title: No. 16 Penn State women's volleyball gets back in win column, defeats Iowa in 4 sets
author: Ashley Felsberg I The Daily Collegian
description:
No. 16 Penn State defeated Iowa 3-1 Saturday night, after losing its No. 1 Nebraska on Thursday.

Alexis Stucky served to start the first set; however, Iowa answered with a cross-court kill from Hannah Whittinstall to take the first point of the match. Kennedy Martin quickly followed up with a kill of her own, foreshadowing the back-and-forth that would persist for set one.

Penn State struggled to get past the front line and keep the ball in bounds with its kills. Two attack errors from Finley Krystkowiak gave the Hawkeyes a two-point advantage. Regardless of the errors, the blue and white were quick to bounce back, gaining momentum from a Whitney Lauenstein cross-court kill from the left side.

A Martin kill and a paired block with Gabrielle Nichols gave Penn State its ninth and 10th points. However, Iowa was quick to follow up with a point after a Lauenstein attack error and a kill from Liv Mogridge.

The two teams traded single points for the next eight scores until the media timeout.

After a Martin attack error, coach Katie Schumacher-Cawley called a timeout, as her team fell down three points.

Whittingstall served for the Hawkeyes coming out of the timeout, while the blue and white couldn’t find a way to defend the kill from Carmel Vares. Lauenstein followed up with a kill of her own.

Iowa widened the point gap with a Mogridge kill and a Jenna Meitzler ace, but Martin added her eighth kill of the set to reverse the offense. This initiated a three-point run for the Nittany Lions, as it was followed by an attack error from Iowa and another Martin kill, putting them within one and forcing the Hawkeyes to call a timeout.

Iowa took the first point after the stoppage, with another Mogridge kill despite a crafty off-the-net save from Stucky that kept the play going. Martin again brought the blue and white within one, but the Hawkeyes answered with a Ksenija Tomic kill, tying it up to match point.

The Hawkeyes took set one after a Krystkowiak attack error following Henlee Moszkowicz’s serve.

A Lauenstein kill toward the back line, combined with three Iowa attack errors, gave the blue and white a 4-0 lead to start set two.

Iowa earned its first point after an attack error on Penn State’s end. However, the Hawkeyes couldn’t go on a run as Nichols answered with a kill.

The two teams traded the next four points until Stucky followed up a Krystkowiak kill with an ace, making Penn State’s lead five.

Iowa went on a two-point run after a combination of attack errors from the Nittany Lions. However, Haley Burgdorf added her first kill of the game, shifting offensive momentum back to the blue and white.

“Knowing I can take any swing, getting a good set from Stucky. And obviously if I don’t have it, I need to control the ball and put it in a spot that's going to make them scramble,” Burgdorf said.

While the Hawkeyes worked to close the point gap, Penn State continued to hold its lead to at least three points.

A Nichols block and kill, separated by a single Iowa point, took the set to the media timeout as Penn State held a five-point lead.

“Even if I’m not getting set, I know I’m still helping my team by holding the block, opening up seams for people like Haley, who had a fantastic night, so just always controlling what I can control,” Nichols said.

Iowa earned the first point after the break, but Kendall Northern quickly answered with a kill. Martin then added on an ace, forcing Iowa to call a timeout. Following the stoppage, the teams, yet again, traded single points until a Lauenstein attack error gave Iowa a two-point run.

“Kendall has done a great job of being herself. Like, she has been gaining so much more confidence in these last two games, and you’ve seen it,” Nichols said.

A Burgdorf kill and an Iowa attack error brought the Nittany Lions within two points of the set win, yet play was extended after a Stucky service error.

Iowa replicated the service error, bringing Penn State to set point. The blue and white officially took the set after a Burgdorf kill, evening the match.

“I think defensively we were much better. We were digging balls, blocking balls, you know, and I think keeping the ball in play a little bit more,” coach Katie Schumacher-Cawley said.

Penn State’s energy continued as Nichols opened up set three with a kill. While Iowa answered with its own kill, Penn State continued to shift momentum in its favor with a Burgdorf kill and a Lexi Gin ace.

Iowa’s three-point run was broken up by a Martin ace, preventing the Hawkeyes from taking their first lead of the set.

Penn State reached its largest point separation, four, taking set three to the media timeout after a Vares attack error.

“I think Ken’s been working on her serve the last two seasons and is really aggressive,” coach Schumacher-Cawley said.

Burgdorf proved to be a consistent point of attack, adding her sixth and seventh kills of the night, separated only by a single Iowa point and Martin’s 16th kill, holding the blue and white’s lead at four.

“I’ve learned that it’s a very hard conference, and you just gotta trust yourself and trust your team,” Burgdorf said on Big Ten Conference play.

Rec Hall stood as another Martin kill brought Penn State to set point. However, Fadulto committed a service error, giving Iowa another chance at completing the comeback.

The Hawkeyes closed the gap to two points, but the Nittany Lions officially took set three after a service error from Jaimie Marquardt.

Penn State entered set four with a vengeance, as Lauenstein earned the first point with a kill. Despite a quick Iowa follow-up, she continued an aggressive front with another kill assisted by Burgdorf.

Penn State built a three-point lead after a Northern kill and two Hawkeye attack errors, forcing Iowa into another timeout.

Iowa then went on a five-point run to tie it at 10-10. After three Penn State errors, Whittingstall earned an ace, and Vares put up a kill, forcing Penn State to call a timeout to regroup.

Following the stoppage, Penn State earned the first two points. Lauenstein and Martin each contributed a kill and began what would be a three-point run for the Nittany Lions.

After a point trade-off for five points, Penn State took a five-point lead on a Martin ace. While it was challenged, the call stood and was followed up by an attack error. Iowa proceeded to call a timeout.

While the Hawkeyes earned the first two points following the timeout, a Burgdorf and Lauenstein kill brought Penn State to 22 points.

Martin’s 24th kill of the night brought Penn State to set point. While Stucky’s service error followed, the Nittany Lions won the match after Lauenstein followed up with a kill.

“It’s nice to win, and I thought we, you know, recovered after the first set and made some great choices, great plays, and though these two played really hard,” coach Schumacher-Cawley said, motioning towards Haley Burgdorf and Gabrielle Nichols.

Up Next

Penn State will play Northwestern in Rec Hall on Friday.

title: No. 4 Penn State women's hockey completes series sweep against Robert Morris
author: Mashiah Mitchell | The Daily Collegian
description:
Following a series loss against No. 2 Ohio State, Penn State looked to get back on track as it started AHA competition.

The early season has already been a testament, even in the last game, when the Nittany Lions had to battle back from a 2-0 deficit. This didn’t deter the blue and white, winning the game 5-3. Coach Jeff Kampersal’s squad returned to the ice on Saturday, looking to complete the series sweep against the Robert Morris Colonials.

Penn State completed the sweep with a 4-1 victory behind a hat trick from freshman forward Sofia Ismael. The blue and white improved to 2-2 on the season, while Robert Morris fell to 1-3.

It was the annual THON game for the Nittany Lions, an ode to the largest student-run philanthropy in the world tailored to raise money for childhood cancer research.

As soon as the puck dropped, the blue and white took control of the match and never looked back. From clean passes to neutralizing Robert Morris’ offensive attack, the first period was a dominant one for the Nittany Lions.

Ismael broke the game open very early on, netting her second goal of the season courtesy of assists from vets Sophie Morrow and Abby Stonehouse.

Ismael was all over the ice the entire, having a hand in all four of Penn State’s points, including two goals in the first period alone.

Freshman forward Kylie Amelkovich also scored her first career NCAA goal after beautiful setups from both Ismael and Stonehouse.

The second period was a bit more pedestrian for the Nittany Lions, but it didn’t come without its surprises and mistakes. For a moment, it looked like a Robert Morris comeback was on the horizon, looking to repay the favor from the previous game.

The Colonials were able to get on the scoreboard following both Grace Tullock and Danica Maynard hitting the penalty box simultaneously, leaving the blue and white in a 5-on-3 power play battle.

The Nittany Lions spent nearly one-third of the second period with someone in the penalty box, a theme that Kampersal’s team is nowhere near accustomed to. While still fairly early into the season, it’s something that should have an eye kept on it, with over 44 total minutes conceded in the penalty box across the first four games.

The Penn State offense got a bit sloppier in this period as well, frequently turning the puck over and missing setup passes. Towards the end of the period, the Nittany Lions played keep-away before star forward Grace Outwater also had a stint in the penalty box.

Penn State’s sophomore goalkeeper Maddy Campbell was on the money in the second period, stonewalling any chances that the Colonials took with the puck, and leaving a lot to be desired for Robert Morris’ power play offensive line.

Ismael completed a hat trick halfway through the third period, sealing the game for the Nittany Lions, which only got more chippy and physical as it continued.

The Nittany Lions posted a shot differential of 52-4, showcasing their dominance on both sides of the puck.

“[Ismael] has either led her entire women’s league in scoring one or two years so we know that she can put the puck in the net,” Kampersal said about Ismael’s performance. “We love that she is stepping up in place of those who have graduated and we hope that she and Kylie [Amelkovich] can continue to contribute.”

Up Next

For the Nittany Lions, they will carry their two-game win streak on the road for another two-game series, this time against the Syracuse Orange in more AHA competition. Syracuse is currently undefeated at 3-0, its best start to a season in over a decade.

title: Penn State's run defense struggles, puts up worst performance since 2022
author: Andrew Mercer | The Daily Collegian
description:
EVANSTON, Ill. — Northwestern totalled 413 rushing yards and four touchdowns en route to a 34-13 victory over Penn State on Friday night in the grand opening of the new Ryan Field.

The figure was the most by any Big Ten team so far this season and the most Penn State has allowed since Michigan racked up 418 yards in 2022.

By comparison, quarterback Aidan Chiles had only 93 passing yards, so it was evident the Wildcats’ offensive coordinator Chip Kelly’s ground game was Penn State’s kryptonite.

“We expected a lot of that, understanding how Chip Kelly runs his typical offense,” defensive tackle Siale Taupaki said. “How they maneuver things. But at the end of the day, it was all technique, details, fundamentals.”

Penn State had a lot of issues across the board on defense, but the team’s biggest problem was tackling. Matt Campbell took notice of that postgame, and he said there were numerous opportunities to shut Northwestern down but the Nittany Lions simply didn’t execute.

“There were a lot of missed tackles tonight, and however that happened and why that happened, we're going to have to evaluate and have a better answer as we come back for next week,” Campbell said. “From my end of it, that part is frustrating because we tackled really well in the first four games of the season. Our ability to get that fixed is first and foremost, then we’ve got to figure out schematically where we’re at.”

Campbell took responsibility for the poor run defense, citing how he failed to get his squad to play the “physical brand of football” required of a winning team. However, the players deferred the responsibility to the entire team, understanding the mistakes made defending the ground game were a key aspect of the loss.

“It starts with us players,” linebacker Tony Rojas said. “We’ve got to be more disciplined, finish tackles, whatever it is. We can't really point fingers. It wasn't you know offense, defense, certain player’s fault. It was all of ours. We got to come out with more intensity in practice.”

The notably weak showing from the defense came as a shock considering how successful D’Anton Lynn’s unit was the week prior against Wisconsin despite a fourth quarter breakdown that spelled defeat.

In that game, the Nittany Lions had pass rush issues, but largely held the Badgers at bay.

Against the Wildcats, Penn State struggled to contain running backs Caleb Komolafe and Joseph Himon II who combined for 35 total carries and each had over 160 rushing yards. Himon found the end zone twice while Komolafe and Chiles each scored once.

Komolafe and Himon dominated with both inside and outside zone rushes while Northwestern’s offensive line established a firm hold on the line of scrimmage. There were gaping holes for the pair and they were slick at shedding contact as well.

Taupaki was asked if he’d ever been bullied in such a manner on the line of scrimmage, but he “wouldn’t call it bullying.”

“It’s really nothing,” Taupaki said. “It's just we need to critique our fundamentals.”

Taupaki said the emphasis now will be on keeping the team together after its first blowout loss, a sentiment echoed by the team following its second-straight loss.

“I still continue to remind them to show up in the good, bad and ugly,” Taupaki said. “Because it's still another day to fight. We all promised each other and this is what we signed up for, but at the end of the day, we still got to show up.”

title: Penn State ‘didn’t practice physical’ for Northwestern, evident in Friday’s defeat
author: Noah Aberegg | The Daily Collegian
description:
EVANSTON, Ill. – Tight end Benjamin Brahmer was very open about Penn State’s struggles throughout the week of practice leading up to the team’s loss to Northwestern.

“We're at a point where we just need to have that physicality in practice,” Brahmer said postgame.

While the coaching staff doesn’t want injuries to pile up outside of game play, the physicality of practice helps prepare for the game. This week, the Nittany Lions’ aggressiveness wasn’t there during the week, according to Brahmer, and that showed Friday.

“It starts with our practice and how physical we want to practice,” Brahmer said. “If we just change that and continue to stay together, that's all we can do right now.”

Penn State struggled against Northwestern in the 34-13 loss, as the offense couldn’t find momentum and the defense gave up 413 rushing yards, leading to its second loss in as many weeks.

Wide receiver Chase Sowell said the Nittany Lions’ week of practice was less physical than a normal week because of “how intense the last game was” and having to turn around and play Friday.

“I feel like (physicality) is a thing that is part of our identity and part of Penn State's identity,” Sowell said. “So I would like to be more physical from everybody, and I think that's just the message of this team was, we got beaten tonight, and that's not the standard of Penn State, and we got to get better for this place.”

Despite the defeat, Brahmer made it a point to not direct blame at any certain players or coaches. He emphasized his trust in Matt Campbell and Taylor Mouser, but he was critical about the team’s lack of physicality throughout the whole game, saying it was a difference-maker against Northwestern.

“I think we’re flying around on the field and we’re hustling as hard as we can,” Brahmer said. “I think just the physicality piece, it’s just got to flip a switch there and just stay together as a whole as an offense.”

The Nittany Lions started the game with a solid defensive drive, holding the Wildcats to a field goal. Once the offense took the field, Rocco Becht connected with wide receiver Chase Sowell for a 26-yard gain, but then gained just five yards over the next three plays and punted the ball away.

The lack of physicality for Penn State’s offense came in the run game. The offensive line didn’t provide many gaps for Carson Hansen or James Peoples, something Cousins knows the team wants to do, but recognizes they’ve yet to achieve.

“I think we need to have conviction,” Cousins said. “I think we need to come off the ball with a nasty intent. I know that's the vision of what we have for ourselves, but we need to start putting that on tape.”

That physicality is something the team works on during practice, but it didn’t seem to be on the level it usually is this week. While Brahmer highlighted that disappointment, Cousins emphasized the need to not focus on those struggles and the importance of pushing past them.

“At this point, you can’t even worry about the practice that we just had,” Cousins said. “You have to worry about the next practice that we have. If you dwell on a week of practice, that's going to keep affecting your process and the team's process.”

With two straight losses, different mindsets have been a topic of discussion among the team, trying to find ways to move past the team’s poor performances against Wisconsin and Northwestern.

The Nittany Lions now move on to their toughest opponent of the season so far, with USC coming to town for the White Out. After seeing what went wrong Friday, Brahmer understands the need to get back to work.

“You just gotta go at it,” Brahmer said. “All I know to do is work, so I’m just gonna come back and work and do my job and practice as physical as I can. I think that’s all we do.”

title: Rocco Becht’s confidence still high amidst poor play in 2-game losing skid
author: Andrew Deal | The Daily Collegian
description:
EVANSTON, Ill. — Rocco Becht had his second consecutive underwhelming performance of the season, both coming against Big Ten opponents.

On Friday, Becht struggled to help Penn State push the ball down the field in its 34-13 loss against Northwestern, showing inconsistencies again with a 63% completion percentage.

“Definitely frustrating. I'm better than that, and I just got to look myself in the mirror and ask myself, why am I doing this? Why am I here?” Becht said postgame.

Becht said he’s “doing it for his family” during his fifth season in college football. His veteran presence is why Matt Campbell still believes in him to be Penn State’s starting quarterback after back-to-back losses.

“I think Rocco's experience, number one,” Campbell said. “I think Rocco's proven that he can work through a football game where it's not perfect, and having the ability to adjust within the football game, and to be honest with you, Rocco's worked through hard before, and he's proven he's got the great ability to do it.”

Becht “worked through a game” that wasn’t perfect Friday. Penn State quickly was trailing 10-0 and didn’t get on the scoreboard until the second quarter, which Northwestern followed up with a three-play drive for a touchdown to make it 17-7.

After the Wildcats’ touchdown drive, they continued to pour it on en route to a blowout victory, which isn’t new to Becht. In 2024, Becht and Iowa State lost in the Big 12 championship to Arizona State, 45-19.

“I've gotten blown out before, just like today against a team like Northwestern, who's good, who's physical on defense, who's sound, and I've won a lot of games,” Becht said.

As one of the leaders, Becht is going to continue to hold himself and the rest of the team accountable to ensure a loss like Friday’s doesn’t happen again. He’s experienced lows of getting blown out in games and not having strong individual games, as well.

His ability to pull himself out of the low parts of games comes from trust while not worrying about anything else. His only concern is from “the people who love you, who trust you, who trust in you, and trust in them back.”

Campbell’s confidence in him to perform at a high level is still there because of his experience, and why his teammates still have all the confidence in him to make the plays. It’s also why, despite his last two games, his confidence is still high in himself.

“It’s high. I know I can play the best football I can right now. I've played in a lot of games,” Becht said. “I know how to win. It's nothing with the confidence level of things. It's maybe a detail here, detail there, accuracy-wise. But again, my confidence is super high, super high in this team, and that's not going to wear.”

The proven ability to win games, albeit not happening yet with Penn State in the Big Ten, is a reason wide receiver Chase Sowell has a lot of trust in him. Sowell noted that “he's been around the Big Ten,” as Becht played Iowa on a yearly basis while at Iowa State.

Becht’s belief in himself and the team to emerge from the losing streak and the inability to put points on the board is there, and the experience he has in college football proves he’s been able to do it in the past.

“I've been down in the dumps like really bad, and I've brought myself back up, and I'm going to continue to do that now,” Becht said. “I'm not going to go and sulk at home and tell myself I'm bad at football. I'm going to continue to do what I do and continue to get better because that's all I know.”

title: 3 takeaways from Penn State's loss to Northwestern
author: Noah Aberegg | The Daily Collegian
description:
EVANSTON, Ill. — Penn State headed to Northwestern following its first loss under Matt Campbell as Big Ten play continued at the newly-opened Ryan Field on Friday night.

The Nittany Lions struggled in all facets of the game as the Wildcats ran away with the game, quite literally, 34-13.

Here’s three takeaways from Penn State’s second straight loss.

Defense can’t contain big run plays

Running back Joseph Himon II had a day against the Nittany Lions, averaging 16.2 yards per carry with two touchdowns.

Going into the game, Penn State knew Northwestern’s offensive coordinator Chip Kelly would run the ball a lot. Despite that preparation, the Nittany Lions still struggled.

“We just didn’t uphold to our standard,” defensive tackle Siale Taupaki said. “Everybody played a role in it, including myself. We could do better on it for sure.”

The biggest hardship regarding Himon was Penn State’s inability to bring him down. He broke multiple tackles, including on what should’ve been a short carry to open a drive. Instead, he tore past linebacker Kooper Ebel on a 36-yard run, followed by a 38-yard touchdown two plays later.

That wasn’t the only time the Wildcats had those looks, however. Later in the matchup, safety Marcus Neal Jr. had to chase down running back Caleb Komolafe on a 24-yard rush, which was again followed by an 11-yard touchdown by Himon.

Himon had three rushes for over 30 yards against Penn State in his 162-yard performance, while Komolafe recorded 188 yards.

Even quarterback Aidan Chiles had his way rushing the ball, converting a third-and-11 with a wide-open rush that could’ve gone for more.

Rocco Becht’s inconsistency is stalling the offense

After throwing his first interception of the season on just 12-for-29 passing against Wisconsin, Rocco Becht said he “expects a different team Friday,” including improvement from himself.

That wasn’t the case against the Wildcats, as Becht was repeatedly off-target. It was also the second straight game where he had multiple passes batted down at the line of scrimmage.

Coming off touchdowns from both teams in the second quarter, Becht was hoping to continue building some offensive momentum. He launched the ball toward tight end Andrew Rappleyea, but overthrew him by so much it appeared to be targeted for wide receiver Chase Sowell.

“That was a bad performance by us,” Becht said. “That's not Penn State football, and we got to be better.”

Midway through the third quarter, Becht had back-to-back attempts that would’ve generated significant yardage in a crucial time for Penn State. Instead, he once again overthrew his receivers, missing Sowell and wide receiver Zay Robinson, who easily could’ve scored a touchdown.

Even when his receivers caught the ball, they were still off target and needed big reaches. Tight end Benjamin Brahmer had to reach across his body to pull in a pass from Becht in the second quarter, while wide receiver Brett Eskildsen had to lean forward and grab the ball before it hit the ground at one point.

Becht’s tipped passes have also become an issue, as his third tipped ball of the day resulted in his second interception of the season. He finished the day with 224 yards, one touchdown and two interceptions.

Penn State’s offensive weapons create options

A week after Sowell was the only receiver with a catch and Penn State’s tight ends were almost nonexistent, Becht found more of his weapons in the passing game.

Sowell was the leading receiver again Friday with five receptions for 68 yards and the sole receiving touchdown. He had several other opportunities — having been targeted 11 times — but Becht was unable to connect with him on each instance.

Sowell was one of six players with multiple catches, nearly doubling the production against Wisconsin.

Eskildsen also had five receptions after Becht underthrew him on numerous targets the week before, tallying 39 yards. Rappleyea had a similar performance with 36 yards on five catches.

Robinson, tight end Benjamin Brahmer, and running backs James Peoples and Carson Hansen were also active on offense, combining for 10 receptions and 94 yards.

“As an offensive as a whole, I think we're playing as hard as we can,” Brahmer said. “There's no one position that's not playing good. It's just we all need to come together.”

Throughout the season, Campbell has discussed the team’s depth on offense and ability for any player to step up and have their moment, which was on display against Northwestern. Despite the success from the weapons, Becht’s inability to find them consistently ultimately resulted in the lackluster performance.

title: Penn State men's soccer falls to Ohio State in the final seconds, remain winless in Big Ten play
author: Ava Aguiar | The Daily Collegian
description:
The Nittany Lions returned to Jeffrey Field to take on Ohio State in their annual White Out match, looking to break their losing streak.

Penn State ended the game in a devastating loss as a goal in the last nine seconds sealed the deal for Ohio State to take the 2-1 win.

First Half

The Buckeyes took possession of the ball in the first minute and a half, with Penn State unable to match the speed of Ohio State. The blue and white redeemed themselves by taking back the ball with the first shot of the game, but Peter Doran just missed the goal off the bottom right of the net.

The blue and white struggled with their aggression, with multiple fouls called in the first six minutes, including a tackle by Doran that narrowly avoided a yellow card.

Etienne Reck made the second shot of the game, but was bounced and caught off the chest of Ohio State’s Patrick McLaughlin.

After a brief moment of fighting in their own box, the Nittany Lions put pressure back on the Buckeyes after a foul on Reck gave him a free kick. Both Reck and Amadou Kone took two shots, both narrowly missing.

Ohio State took back-to-back corners, with Martin Wurschmidt heading an almost guaranteed goal that another Penn State player saved, before missing another attempt at goal.

Nittany Lions’ goalkeeper Daniel Peluffo-Wiese had a third incredible save as he bounced the ball off his head midair, blocking the right side of the net.

More fouls were called as Grant McIntosh picked up his second of the game with a shove on Jack Wayne, before Reck fouled and earned the Buckeyes a free kick.

Off a corner kick, Reck was able to get in perfect position, scoring the first goal of the game in the 33rd minute, to put the Nittany Lions up 1-0.

Second Half

Penn State came into the second half with fire, taking three shot attempts in the first five minutes and dominating possession of the ball.

Ohio State made its way into the blue and white box after multiple fouls were called, giving the Buckeyes three corner kicks, but they weren’t able to convert.

In the 53rd minute Kone saw a chance at a wide open field and sprinted down with the ball to score what looked to be the second of the game, but was barely caught off the hands of McLaughlin.

Penn State started to struggle, as Ohio State began to take control, matching the Nittany Lions with three shots, before a timeout was called to reset.

“It was an injury, I think. We were trying to get the guys together and we just made a mistake. Gave away the ball in our own half," Dow said. "I try to get the guys to come together and to make sure we have the right message, move on it was just one mistake. We managed it well.”

Ohio State kept up their fight, matching every move the Nittany Lions made and beating them to the ball each time. In the 67th minute, Nehan Hassan came in for Doran, marking the first Penn State offensive play in fifteen minutes against the Buckeyes. However, the blue and white quickly lost possession.

A foul on McIntosh let Penn State get back in the Ohio State box, where Vladislav Cherny shot a powerful kick right above the net.

With two minutes to go, Ohio State tied up the game as a corner kick gave Wurschmidt an opening to score on the top left of the goal.

With a game that looked to end in a tie, Wurschmidt once again came in and scored in the last nine seconds to officially end the game 2-1 and give the Buckeyes their first win since Sept. 8.

“I wanted to hear how happy Ohio State was on our field, I wanted them to hear that because we could have been in that position too," Dow said. Throughout the game we got smaller, they got bigger. This one burns.”

Up Next

The Nittany Lions will travel to Ann Arbor to take on Michigan Oct. 9 at 7 p.m.

title: No. 4 Penn State women’s hockey earns first win in high-scoring clash against Robert Morris
author: Gavin Leonard | The Daily Collegian
description:
Following two losses to No. 2 Ohio State, Penn State opened AHA play with an offensive battle against Robert Morris.

The blue and white ultimately earned its first win of the new season with a high-scoring 5-3 result over the Colonials in continuing its homestand in Happy Valley. The result improved coach Jeff Kampersal’s unit to 1-2 on the young season after dropping their opening contests to No. 2 Ohio State.

First Period

After the opening faceoff, both teams began testing the opposing keepers early. Within the first five minutes, the teams had already taken eight combined shots, showing both squads' aggressiveness.

Yet, the Nittany Lions aggressiveness would become uncontrolled, as Lorelai Nelson was sent to the penalty box for tripping. The Colonials capitalized on their first power-play, with Alaina Giampietro scoring the first goal of the game after collecting the puck from a scrum in front of the crease.

Robert Morris continued to hound the Nittany Lions as Rowyn Ringor scored another goal a minute later from the right side, extending their lead to 2-0 with 14 minutes left in the period.

The blue and white earned a power play of its own following a penalty on Shayne Desjardins for holding. The Colonials' penalty kill unit started off strong, stifling Penn State’s initial attack and nearly converting a breakaway of its own.

After the attacking shot went off frame, the Nittany Lions scored a goal of their own, as Kylie Amelkovich raced down the left side and sent in a pass to Nicole Hall for the score. Hall scored her first goal of the season to cut the deficit to 2-1.

“That was huge to give us a little breathing room,” Kampersal said. “There were a lot of effort plays, people diving for pucks, people chipping out, blocking shots, penalty kills.”

The fast-paced, back-and-forth play continued as Abby Stonehouse won the puck in the offensive zone from a stalemate on the left side. Stonehouse laid it off to Sofia Ismael, who finished the play for her first collegiate goal to tie the game as the first period ended.

“On the bench, we just try to hype each other up,” Ismael said when asked what the players tell themselves after being down early. “Cheering on the bench is definitely a big one for us in our culture.”

Second Period

Heading into the period, neither team could sustain possession. Both teams hunted for the puck in the halves, and the attacks were quick to race down the rink in search of goal-scoring opportunities.

The pace of play led to shots filling up the stat sheet, as Penn State held a 15-9 advantage with 15 minutes remaining in the period.

The Nittany Lions decided to go against the grain by creating complete attacks, not just counterattacks. RMU’s Shayne Desjardins was tripped, allowing Kampersal to sub in a sixth skater.

During that stretch, the attack sent five shots at the Colonials’ goaltender Thalia D’Elia, but none got by her. Once the power-play was awarded, the unit could not convert on any of its shot attempts.

The Colonials were unable to score on one of its best possessions, as their attack passed through the opposing defense to earn a one-on-one opportunity with goaltender Morgan Stickney. The freshman made a great save to keep the game tied.

That wouldn't last long, as Penn State’s attack came back down the rink and scored on its own breakaway. Keller sent a pass to Outwater, who wrapped around the net and snuck the puck in to take a 3-2 lead.

Third Period

Possession of the puck returned to even, as the attacks raced down the ice after their defense won it back. The Colonials created multiple chances, but Morgan Stickney stood strong by making key saves.

Ismael was called for cross-checking, leading to an RMU power play that amounted to no attempted shots. Penn State followed with a power play of their own after two Colonials were tagged with penalties.

Nelson soon after added her first collegiate goal to help maintain the blue and white's position in the driver's seat.

During the final nine minutes, the match would be filled with penalty calls for both sides. Penn State were awarded a power play first, which they could not convert on. Kylie Amelcovich would then be called back-to-back for slashing and holding, and Megan Hosman would join her in the penalty box for a Holding call of her own.

Robert Morris could not score on its first power-play opportunity, but made up for the mistake on the second attempt, cutting the deficit to 4-3 with a goal from Alaina Giampietro.

“Yeah, that's on me,” Kampersal said in reference to the various penalty calls. “It gets emotional but… we need more discipline and that comes from me and having a clearer message.”

Stonehouse was then called for Body Checking with about two minutes left, giving the Colonials one last chance to send the match to overtime. Penn State’s penalty kill held strong, and Stonehouse sealed the game with an open-net goal when she returned to the ice.

Up next

The Nittany Lions will complete the series with the Colonials on Saturday at 2 p.m.

title: Penn State field hockey earns clean sheet over Rutgers, Hannah Prince secures first Big Ten win
author: Myles Hannak | The Daily Collegian
description:
Two squads, both tied at .500 each, one chance to shake up the standings.

The blue and white closed out its three-game road trip with a 1-0 win against the Scarlet Knights to improve to 5-4 on the season and leapfrog Rutgers in the Big Ten leaderboards.

Both squads traded possession in the early minutes, as the midfield became the front line. Penn State got an early threat in the circle with a bouncing pass that forced the Rutgers netminder to use her body to play it, but it was a relatively easy stop as the Nittany Lions couldn’t register a shot before the chance was cleared.

As the battle for possession continued, Rutgers was called for physicality, which gave Penn State a corner. Yet when Olivia Marthins fired her pass in, it was fumbled on the edge before being kicked, allowing the Scarlet Knights to push quickly.

That chance didn’t materialize and with five minutes remaining, Penn State got another decent look when Sienna Dunn fired a pass to Katelyn Strawser at the back post, but again the link-up went offline in the blue and white’s attack.

With the physicality continuing, Penn State got another penalty corner chance; this time Cam Standish took the effort, and Strawser fired a shot that was saved on a stacked-pad effort. The rebound started a scrum, and Strawser rushed in, slotting the chance in between the posts for the first score of the game with a little over three minutes to play in the first quarter.

The second quarter opened with stalled play for the first few minutes until Rutgers got its first clear-cut chance, but Penn State goaltender Aby Deverka knocked it away. The half came to a close with a majority of the quarter stuck in back-and-forth play with little action.

However, immediately out of the break, the Scarlet Knights switched it up in quickly raised the tempo, forcing Deverka to make a point-blank save in the half before the second attempt went wide. Not even a full two minutes later, Deverka made her third save within the first five minutes of the resumption out of the break as the scale flipped toward Rutgers.

Penn State got back into the action with an offensive push of its own, but every shot was blocked or went wide, and Rutgers still eventually overtook the Nittany Lions in total shots.

With the third quarter dwindling, Standish fired Penn State’s sixth corner of the game into the circle, but it was shut down as many times before and the early score still stood as the only difference between the two sides.

The last two minutes saw pandemonium ensue. Rutgers fired a shot which almost was the equalizer until Deverka slapped it away and Penn State leading scorer, forward Ella Gaitan, who had a quiet day up to this moment, used her stick to deny the ball from crossing the line.

With the fourth quarter started, the Scarlet Knights began with an urgency toward the blue and white’s net, but early attempts soared off frame. Rutgers got another chance in front of Deverka, but her fifth save with her low pad pushed it away and kept things in Penn State’s favor.

In front of goal, Deverka finished with six total saves in the victory after making another down the wire to keep the shutout intact and to give coach Hannah Prince her first Big Ten win.

Up next

The Nittany Lions return home to Happy Valley with a Sunday clash against No. 19 Lafayette, which is set for 1 p.m.

title: Players to watch | Northwestern QB Aidan Chiles, WR Griffin Wilde pose threats to Penn State
author: Andrew Mercer | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State heads to Evanston, Illinois, to face Northwestern in the first game at the new Ryan Field at 8 p.m. on Friday.

The Wildcats are led by their dual-threat quarterback and their top wide receiver who will see more emphasis should tight end Luke Dehnicke be ruled out.

Here’s who to watch on Northwestern’s side.

Aidan Chiles, quarterback

After two years as Michigan State’s starting quarterback, Aidan Chiles transferred to Northwestern and has been the Wildcats’ offensive engine through three games.

An archetypal dual-threat quarterback, Chiles has 30 carries and four rushing touchdowns, both team highs. Chiles has been an efficient passer too, completing 70.7% of his throws so far this season and accumulating 807 yards.

These scoring numbers are exponentially higher at this point than his final season as a Spartan where he was dealing with an injury and had to miss the final three games, including Michigan State’s matchup against Penn State. Chiles posted 1,392 passing yards for 10 touchdowns and three interceptions while rushing for 227 yards for six touchdowns in 2025.

Chiles put in a worthy performance against Indiana, going 22-29 for 293 yards and two touchdowns. He was sacked four times, but had a gain of 15 on the ground as well, breaking even in rushing yards.

Griffin Wilde, wide receiver

With Dehnicke “doubtful,” Northwestern’s top wide receiver is primed for an even bigger role in the passing game on Friday.

In 2025, Wilde earned All-Big Ten third team honors in his first season as a Wildcat after two years at South Dakota State. He racked up 880 receiving yards and eight touchdowns on 71 catches as a junior.

So far this season, Wilde’s been Chiles’ top target, with 14 catches for 245 yards and two touchdowns, including a 71-yard reception against his old team. Both of his touchdowns came in the loss to the Hoosiers, and he had a season-high six receptions.

Behind Wilde, the next closest wide receiver for the Wildcats has 78 yards on the season, so if they’re going to have a shot at beating Penn State through the air, Wilde will have to be a primary focus.

Joseph Himon II, running back

Although Northwestern more routinely uses running backs Gavin Sawchuk and Caleb Komolafe, Himon has found the most success getting on the scoreboard.

Himon is easily the most versatile running back in the depth chart, balancing his rushing and receiving capabilities to give offensive coordinator Chip Kelly many ways to employ him.

The redshirt senior’s big-play ability makes him a threat from anywhere on the gridiron. On the ground he’s averaging 11.5 yards per carry on 10 attempts, one of which was an 80-yard touchdown against South Dakota State.

But keep an eye on how Northwestern uses him in the passing game in the red zone. Himon balled out in the air against Colorado on Sept. 19, scoring three touchdowns on three catches for 46 yards. He also had a 15-yard catch against the Jackrabbits.

Robert Fitzgerald, safety

Robert Fitzgerald rose the ranks from a depth safety to one of the conference’s best defenders throughout his four seasons at Northwestern. He’s continuing that success early in the 2026 season.

The redshirt senior currently leads the defense again with 38 tackles so far this season, including 15 solo tackles. He also recovered a fumble against Colorado and broke up a pass against the Jackrabbits.

Fitzgerald made a lot of history in 2025, and being named All-Big Ten second team was the least of his accomplishments.

He led the Big Ten with 69 solo tackles, had six tackles for loss, was the first defensive back at Northwestern to make over 100 tackles since 2016 and first defensive back in program history to make more than 110 tackles. Fitzgerald finished with 115 tackles, four pass breakups, a fumble recovery and an interception.

Fitzgerald poses the biggest threat to Penn State’s passing game that struggled against Wisconsin last week.

title: Penn State women’s soccer set to host offensively potent Purdue on Saturday
author: Sara Castrovinci | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State looks to continue its dominance after a defensive-heavy win against USC, where it held the Trojans to zero shots and one corner kick.

The Nittany Lions are hosting this Saturday again, when they will face off with Purdue at 7 p.m.

The last time the two programs met was last Oct. at Folk Field in West Lafayette, Indiana, where the blue and white came out on top 1-0 in its final regular-season road trip.

In the all-time series between Penn State and the Boilermakers, the Nittany Lions have overpowered Purdue by 20-1-3, with a standing of 10-0-1 at Jeffrey Field. With the game being hosted in Happy Valley, the blue and white have the hefty edge against the Boilermakers with its impressive home showcase.

Keys to the game for Purdue

The black and gold are sitting high at 10-1-1 for the season, with an overall win percentage of 0.875 and 0.800 flat in its conference gameplay. Purdue’s success in the regular season so far and current four-game win streak could help give the Boilermakers that edge they need to finally come out on top against Penn State.

Purdue has had a prominent offensive year, eight times as lethal compared to their opponents. Sitting at 45 goals compared to their competitors' five, as well as 291 shots versus 89, the black and gold have put up commanding season statistics both out of and within conference battles.

Personnel breakdowns for junior forward duo Jaiden Anderson and McKenzie Carle are crucial for the Nittany Lions heading into the Saturday game, as they are the top producers for the Boilermakers. Anderson is leading on the stat sheet with 25 points via 10 goals and five assists, while Carle is second on the board with 18 points via eight goals and two assists.

Irene Campo, Rosa Maalouf and Megan Santa Cruz are all tied for third with 14 points. They have all been able to find the back of the net and efficiently connect for goal-scoring opportunities, but Santa Cruz looks to be creating these chances the most with 44 shots on the season, seven behind Anderson.

On the defensive end, Krystina Wolf has found herself in the starting lineup for 11 of the team's 12 matches, logging a save percentage of .882 for the year. With 30 saves and four goals allowed, the sophomore keeper from Wayne, New Jersey, has shown to be a formidable opponent in the net.

What to look for in Penn State

The Nittany Lions are sitting at 5-2-3 on the season and 3-1-1 in conference play. The blue and white have ruled its home pitch this season at 4-0-2 on Jeffrey Field, giving the home-field advantage they might need against Purdue’s offensive firepower ahead of Saturday's matchup.

Aubrey Kulpa has remained an attacking force for Penn State in her three years in University Park and has continued to lead the pack this season. The junior from Cromwell, Connecticut, has tallied 13 points via five goals and three assists, three of the goals coming from her last four matches, showcasing the consistency she has delivered for the Nittany Lions in the final third of play.

With Purdue being offensively heavy with its gameplay, the blue and white back line will look to continue its defensive momentum from its extremely clean sheet against USC.

Defensive backbones Kayleigh Herr, Hannah Jordan and Lily Boyden will be crucial components for a potential Penn State win this Saturday. Redshirt senior defender Herr has seen a team-high 877 minutes of Nittany Lions’ gameplay, 23 minutes shy of reaching the equivalent of their 10 matches.

The blue and white look to continue its defensive drive to keep the Boilermakers away from their final third, with Herr being an indispensable part to success.

title: Lizzy McAlpine keeps it real on new album “Angel”
author: Brennan Kramp I The Daily Collegian
description:
Alt-pop star, Lizzy McAlpine, just dropped her fifth studio album, “Angel,” and is turning heads with a new, honest and gut-wrenching project.

Breaking into the lime-light with her hit song, “ceilings,” which blew up on TikTok back in 2022, McAlpine has been in the game for quite a while now. Starting her musical journey just outside of Philadelphia in Narberth, Pennsylvania, McAlpine has been making music since she was 12 years old.

Her first studio release, “Give Me A Minute,” arrived in 2020, right at the height of the pandemic. Songs like “To the Mountains,” “Nothing / Sad N Stuff” and “How Do I Tell You?” introduce McAlpine's gentle and whimsical voice along with a folksy rhythm to guide her along the track.

She carries this musical consistency throughout her proceeding projects, “...What Are We” from her 2021 album, “When the World Stopped Moving: The Live EP” and “ceilings,” from the famous 2022 album, “five seconds flat.”

In her fourth project, “Older (and Wiser),” McAlpine leans more into the folk and alt-country feel, while still maintaining the album with tracks that highlight more band involvement. The tempos are slow, steady and easy to flow with. The album reflects, musically, what it says: she is older and wiser.

Now, on “Angel,” McAlpine dives headfirst into the tender melodies and soothing voices that gave her her claim to fame.

The album opens up with the delicate “The light in the painting,” where McAlpine confesses to her other half that they’re the brightest spot in her world of colors.

After a warm and loving introduction to the album, McAlpine makes a 180-flip on the proceeding tracks, “Anybody’s fool” and “A car wash and a new pair of pants,” where she takes humble, yet personally unrelenting shots, at past lovers fueled by secondhand fame and abusive hardships.

She continues this theme in tracks like “Ugly things,” where she resents herself for sticking around an emotionally exhausting relationship filled to the brim with constant disappointment.

The album as a whole plays like it was actively being written over years of crashing in and out of bouts of unimaginable love and unrelenting heartbreak. In songs, “I have a friend,” “Our strange ways” and “Angel,” McAlpine swoons you into lullabies of dreamy heart-eyes and cherry-flavored kisses where she, along with the rest of her studio band, explode the production with infatuating gusto.

Then, you’re transported to a darker, emptier time and place, and she reels your heartstrings back with the tracks “Two elevens” and “Mason’s song.” She reflects here on the grim days of betrayal, grief and misery as her acoustic guitar gently keeps her spirits afloat.

Romantic love and memory, however, is not the only source of inspiration for McAlpine on this album. In her tear-shedding “The crowd,” McAlpine rings out an ode to her late father, Mark McAlpine, just as she’s done on every 13th track of her albums.

Her father passed away on March 13, 2020, hence the placement's significance. In “The crowd,” McAlpine said all the things she never got the chance to say, singing “everything I do / I make it big so you can hear the crowd.”

Her efforts and her fame have given her global recognition, chart-topping albums and success that many in the music industry hope they can one day achieve; to her, though, all she does and all that she has done has been to make her father proud.

She even expands her message in the middle of the album with the powerful “Soldier of the road,” featuring Fleet Foxes. On this track, McAlpine turns the mirror onto her global audience and points to the constant, crushing and detrimental impacts that both war and capitalism are starting to have on society.

Through highs and lows, a revolving, almost dizzying door of partners and a constant grappling of success, McAlpine slows her world down and distills it into a charming and reflective project. This album is the culmination of an artist honing in on their strengths while still digging deeper to let out everything that hums around inside the mind of a musician.

A fifth studio album is no small feat, and McAlpine shows here that she still has plenty left in the notebook to keep fans wanting more. More realism, more feelings, more connection.

title: Column | Vegas comes to State College
author: Quentin Jurney | The Daily Collegian
description:
Gambling and sports have slowly merged to form a parasitic relationship that exploits all of the negative aspects of the sports world. Gambling exacerbates massive amounts of fast cash into every facet of professional sports and, more importantly, sports at a collegiate level. Even college athletes are able to place bets on professional sports.

Since May 14, 2018, sports betting has become legalized nationwide. In a 6-3 decision, the Supreme Court struck down House Bill 74, the Professional and Amateur Sports Protection Act (PASPA), which banned all sports gambling in the United States with the exception of Las Vegas.

In Murphy v. National Collegiate Athletic Association, House Bill 74 was overruled, legalizing sports betting and gambling nationwide. A Pandora's Box was opened, and the basis of the professional sports landscape we see today emerged from within it.

39 states and Washington, D.C., have some form of legalized U.S. sports betting, whether online or in person. Sports gambling and online gambling have become bigger than ever, especially with younger generations.

Penn State isn’t immune to gambling’s takeover of sports. As one of the most popular football teams in the U.S., the demographic of people who are actively betting has also expanded. Not just sports betting fanatics but our very own student body as well. With a heavily male-dominated student population, these companies prey on that demographic and cater to their obsession with sports gambling.

Even The Daily Collegian puts out betting odds on Penn State football games, showing how widespread and influential betting is in high-level sports.

Happy Valley Casino, located in State College, had its grand opening in May 2026. There are very few reasons to invest resources into this type of business in State College and the sole reason to do so is to addict the student body. With over 40,000 students at Penn State’s University Park campus, young adults are heavily intertwined in State College’s population, so a casino built here primarily targets students and preys on their vulnerability.

Since sports gambling is such a popular vice among young men, especially at a big sports school like Penn State, it creates a pipeline effect where sports gambling normalizes constant gambling. Now there’s a physical place where students can gamble on a variety of other games of chance. Since they’re already used to betting and gambling, going to a casino often isn’t a big leap from placing bets on their phones.

Now, this doesn't mean you should avoid casinos completely; if you go once or twice for the experience, or if you want to play a poker game at your friend's house every once in a while, that’s a different story.

But casinos have spent millions on research to get people addicted to coming back, and online sports betting has portrayed itself more as skill than gambling.

Gambling has proved to be a very easy way to lose yourself and destroy your life. With the predatory nature of casinos and the susceptibility of college students, it becomes dangerous to have a casino in the State College area. With the pipeline between online sports betting and gambling at a casino being more apparent, leading to addiction, there’s a cause for concern when a casino is built in a college town.

If Penn State cares about the well-being of its students and its public image, as it especially should nowadays, a casino like Happy Valley Casino should be met with heavy scrutiny. As a student debating whether you should go to the casino often or start sports betting online, I would step back and think twice before going into a place that bets on you becoming addicted.

title: Lauenstein and Martin lead charge for No. 16 Penn State women's volleyball in sweep to No. 1 Nebraska
author: Ashley Felsberg I The Daily Collegian
description:
No. 16 Penn State rematched No. 1 Nebraska Thursday night after the Cornhuskers swept them twice in the 2025 season. The Cornhuskers repeated their success, defeating the Nittany Lions 3-0.

Despite the loss, Whitney Lauenstein and Kennedy Martin both put up double-digit kills, totaling 31 as a duo. The pair was persistent in responding to Nebraska with an aggressive counter-attack, keeping the Nittany Lions within reach of a set win all match.

The first set started off a bit shaky for the Nittany Lions, as the Cornhuskers went on an unanswered 3-point run, two of those points coming off Penn State errors. The blue and white couldn’t find a way to receive the serve, and when they attacked, they were met with an aggressive blocking duo in the Cornhuskers’ front line.

“I thought it was a competitive match, and you know, they found a way to finish it at the end,” coach Katie Schumacher-Cawley said.

Though they remained behind for the entirety of set one, they didn’t do so willingly. Along with Alexis Stucky and Kennedy Martin, Whitney Lauenstein came up big in tough moments. The Stucky-Martin duo totaled 12 assists and 11 attacks; however, Lauenstein contributed seven kills of her own throughout the set.

“I thought Stucky did a really good job of being super deceptive and just allowing us to get good looks,” Martin said.

The blue and white struggled all set to go on a multi-point run, with most of their big plays immediately followed by a difficult Cornhusker attack. When the blue and white trailed by only four points, 12-8, Lauenstein put up two consecutive kills to spark the blue and white at near-halfway, despite Nebraska winning the set.

Martin and Lauenstein started off set two leading the blue and white in a 3-point run of their own. This run also gave Penn State its first lead of the match. Martin earned the first point off of a kill, followed by a paired Nichols-Lauenstein block. Lauenstein then added her eighth kill of the night.

While in the first set, the blue and white struggled against powerful kills, small tap-ins helped out the Cornhuskers in the second. Nebraska went on a four-point run, with three of the four points coming from soft kills.

After a Penn State timeout, Kennedy and Lauenstein were the first to a point again. Lauenstein capitalized with a left-side hit, then followed it up with a kill assisted by Danielle Whitemire to bring the Nittany Lions within six.

“Just don’t take any ball for granted. Especially if it’s out-of-system and someone really hustled for that, I’m gonna get as much apparatus as they just did in my swing right there,” Lauenstein said.

Nebraska stayed on top following a communication error from the Nittany Lions to ultimately win the second set.

Despite the difficulty in closing the point gap and the overwhelming red shirts in the crowd, the Nittany Lion student section remained loud and on their feet, energizing the squad as they entered the third set.

“I thought our student section did an awesome job. Just love those guys. They’re awesome, so yeah, really proud to be a Nittany Lion,” Martin said.

For her twelfth kill of the night, Martin reached for a cross-court kill from the left side to put the Nittany Lions within a point of the Cornhuskers. Despite continually creeping back in, Nebraska also kept answering to widen the point gap. Martin persisted and answered with a thirteenth kill.

“I want to put confidence in the people who are setting me, whether that’s Stucky or a non-setter, like, I want this ball. I want it, and I’m going to produce with,” Martin said.

While the rest of the set followed the same one-point upper-hand competition, Lauenstein proved to be relentless.

Martin continued to lead the blue and white bounce-back following their timeout in a one-point lead trade-off style set. Despite the offense's efforts, the Nittany Lions couldn’t find a way to block the Cornhusker front line, especially Harper Murray, who totaled 13 in the match.

The Cornhuskers won in a sweep, finished by a Ryan Hunter kill.

“We can’t dwell on this. We have to learn from this. We have to move forward and we have to prepare to beat Iowa,” Schumacher-Cawley said.

MORE VOLLEYBALL COVERAGE

title: Rec Hall feels the energy in No. 16 Penn State women's volleyball's loss to No. 1 Nebraska
author: Lily Dorf | The Daily Collegian
description:
The No. 16 Penn State Nittany Lions welcomed back the No. 1 Nebraska Cornhuskers at 7 p.m. for the rematch of the season, after Penn State lost 3-0 to Nebraska last season. In last year’s match, the Nittany Lions again suffered the same fate to the Cornhuskers.

Rec Hall was littered with red and white as the crowd revved up for another face-off between the two teams. As the players took the court, the crowd buzzed in anticipation for the first whistle to blow.

With so many fans in the stands, the players had a chance to reflect on the emotions surrounding volleyball and tonight’s match.

“I just think it’s awesome,” Penn State’s Kennedy Martin said. “The growth that our sport has gotten in general. It’s so awesome to see Rec Hall packed out. I am really proud to be a Nittany Lion.”

Martin was not the only teammate who felt this way.

“I think it’s really cool,” Whitney Lauenstein said. “Wherever they traveled from, whoever is in the stands, they all traveled here to watch women’s volleyball and I think that’s like, the coolest thing ever.”

As the first set started, Nebraska claimed two points against the blue and white, with a block and kill by sophomore Virginia Adriano.

While Penn State scored a kill from Lauenstein, the Cornhuskers kept their lead at 6-1.

Afterward, Penn State’s Martin and Emmi Sellman came back with a swing, bringing the score to 9-5 Nebraska.

As the scores continued to creep closer and closer together, Penn State slowly started to shake off the energy from its previous match last year, as the Nebraska faithful continued to drone on.

The blue and white shuffled around the court in unison, almost like a rehearsed routine. Their teamwork, along with Martin and Lauenstein, helped cut the deficit in the first set, building on the crowd energy.

Penn State freshman Kendall Northern entered the game with a bang, helping the team score two points as Rec Hall erupted in cheers.

Although the Nittany Lions fought hard, Nebraska took the first set, 25-20.

However, Penn State returned to the court with new energy, taking the lead 3-1 in the second set.

The blue and white pushed harder and harder, continuing to tie the score and keep from repeating the same outcome as their last match against Nebraska last season.

As both teams entered the third and final set, it looked as though last year’s fate would repeat itself.

While Penn State scored the first point of the set, Nebraska’s Berge Reilly took charge along with teammates Murray, Jackson and sophomore Manaia Ogbechie.

As the Penn State Nittany Lions kept hitting, the Nebraska Cornhuskers kept hitting harder, widening the gap with each shot.

With the score 24-18, Rec Hall stood, Penn State fans waiting in anticipation while Nebraska fans waited for the outcome they hoped for.

That outcome came true when sophomore Ryan Hunter struck the final blow with a kill, ending the third match 25-18, making Nebraska the winning team for the second year in a row.

“I think every team is different,” coach Katie Schumacher-Cawley said. “I thought we competed hard and these guys know what went on last year. It’s a new team, it’s a new season, so we’re moving forward and we might see Nebraska again in the tournament.”

The Penn State Nittany Lions will be back Saturday, Oct. 3, in Rec Hall, for their match against Iowa.

MORE VOLLEYBALL COVERAGE

title: No. 16 Penn State women’s volleyball swept in Rec Hall takeover by No. 1 Nebraska
author: Elliott Inscho | The Daily Collegian
description:
Lincoln, Nebraska, and State College, Pennsylvania, are separated by just over 1,000 miles.

Judging by the quantity of Nebraska supporters in Rec Hall on Thursday, it can't be too challenging a drive.

“I think it's really cool,” Whitney Lauenstein, who played two seasons as a Cornhusker, said of the crowd. “Wherever they traveled from, whoever is in the stands, they all traveled here to watch women's volleyball, and I think that's the coolest thing ever.”

Even with a packed student section and a gaggle of costumed counterparts from the men’s team in attendance, Penn State was swept by the nation's top squad.

The match's heightened stakes showed early. Ava Falduto fired the initial serve into the net, sparking a three-point run by the Cornhuskers to open play.

After Whitney Lauenstein broke the streak with a kill, Nebraska immediately got back on track. A kill by Andi Jackson, a combination block and consecutive attack errors by Kennedy Martin forced Katie Schumacher-Cawley to call for a timeout with the Nittany Lions trailing 7-1.

Penn State won back-to-back points coming out of the break, and another when Bergen Reilly briefly remained down on the court after an attempted dig. Kendall Northern's powerful swing and Alexis Stucky's slick flick drew the blue and white within three points.

Lauenstein jolted the raucous crowd with a trio of kills, but Nebraska held its pace to take a 15-11 lead at the first media timeout. Penn State kept it close in the stretch, but struggled to make the extra push that it needed to take the lead.

A 4-1 swing by the Nittany Lions, capped by kills from Martin and Lauenstein, cut the Cornhusker lead to a single point and forced coach Dani Busboom Kelly to call her first timeout.

Out of the break, Nebraska won six of eight points to fend off the Nittany Lions and take the first set.

The second frame began with another three-point run, but in favor of Penn State. Nebraska won five of six points to erase the deficit and take a 5-4 lead. Neck-and-neck action left the squads even at 9-9 as the set went on.

The Cornhuskers started to pull away, jumping out to a 17-12 edge through a combination of strong kills and mistakes by the blue and white.

Two kills by Teraya Sigler and a Penn State defensive blunder fueled a late four-point run that put Nebraska up 22-14 and drew another timeout from Schumacher-Cawley.

Lauenstein made a pair of kills in the closing stages, but Caroline Jurevicius bounced a spike off a combined block by Harper Murray and Manaia Ogbechie to claim another set.

Nebraska claimed the third set’s first point, but Stucky notched a kill and two aces in a solo three-point run. The Cornhuskers responded with four consecutive points to neutralize the Penn State advantage and take a 5-3 lead.

While the squads stayed close on alternating points, Nebraska pulled ahead to a 10-7 lead on swings from Reilly and Ogbechie.

Martin made back-to-back swings that cut the lead to a single point before a Cornhuskers attack error evened the score at 12-12. A bad set by Martin, an ace by Murray and a block by Jackson gave Nebraska a three-point edge at the third set’s media timeout.

Late in the set, match officials warned the student section after it made comments directed at Murray.

The Cornhuskers won two of three points to follow until Martin made her 17th kill of the match. After a bad set by Jocelyn Nathan, the Nittany Lions seemed to go on a three-point run, but a video review overturned what had previously appeared to be a kill from Lauenstein.

Another review resulted in another overturned call for Nebraska, leading Schumacher-Cawley to use her final timeout of the match.

Martin made a kill before the Cornhuskers went on a five-point run. Lauenstein came through with a kill that delayed the inevitable, but it arrived anyway when Ryan Hunter sealed the sweep.

“There's definitely things that we can be better at in practice, and be more alert and ready to go,” Schumacher-Cawley said. “These guys understand it. We can't dwell on this. We have to learn from this. We have to move forward, and we have to prepare to beat Iowa.”

Injury report

Ryla Jones was injured in the Nittany Lions' loss to Michigan State on Sunday. Schumacher-Cawley said postgame that Jones "will be back before the season is over."

Up next

The blue and white will return to Rec Hall to face Iowa on Saturday. First service is set for 7 p.m. on B1G+.

title: WPSU officially separates from Penn State, joins WHYY
author: Grace Levy | News Editor
description:
WPSU officially joined the Philadelphia-based WHYY station on Thursday, according to an article from WPSU. The move officially separates WPSU from Penn State after a nearly two-year long process.

WPSU serves the greater State College region and was previously managed by Penn State administration. However, in 2025, the university voted to discontinue funding to the station following federal funding cuts.

“For more than 70 years, WPSU has been a trusted resource for the people of central and northern Pennsylvania,” Bill Marrazzo, WHYY president and CEO, said to WPSU. “Our responsibility now is to honor that trust while building an even stronger and more sustainable WPSU for the generations ahead.”

The transfer to WHYY was first proposed in Sept. 2025, but unanimously rejected by the Penn State Board of Trustees (BOT) Finance and Investment Committee. Following support of the station from the local community, a revised plan was accepted by the BOT.

The plan allowed WPSU to transfer its name and assets to WHYY for $1, with the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) approving the sale in Sept. 2026, according to a news release from Penn State.

According to a frequently asked questions page posted by WPSU, the station will keep its call letters, name, PBS and NPR programming and focus on local coverage, with the majority of changes occurring “behind the scenes.”

“This is not about changing what WPSU means to the communities it serves,” Marrazzo said to WPSU. “It is about giving WPSU the foundation to grow, evolve and continue serving this region for decades to come. The call letters remain WPSU. The commitment to this region remains WPSU. And the future we begin building today will be shaped by the people and communities WPSU serves.”

title: Staff predictions | Can Penn State rebound from its first loss with a win at the Ryan Field grand-opening?
author: The Daily Collegian football staff
description:
Penn State has its first true road test of the year this Friday against Northwestern under the lights of the brand-new Ryan Field.

The Wildcats’ fresh stadium cost nearly $900 million with a student section designed similarly to a European soccer arena. No sitting. Banging on the back wall that echoes throughout the air.

It’ll be a tough environment for the Nittany Lions.

Can Penn State brave the noise and bounce back from its first loss of the year?

Andrew Deal: Penn State 24, Northwestern 20

Based on Penn State’s performance against Wisconsin and Northwestern keeping it close against Indiana, I expect this game to remain tight.

The Nittany Lions have been dealing with injuries, but nowhere to the extent of Northwestern. Wide receiver Hayden Eligon II and defensive backs Damon Walters and Braden Turner all were on the Wildcats’ availability report on Tuesday with questionable designations.

While cornerback Daryus Dixson is also questionable for Penn State, he’s the only Nittany Lion impact player who’s availability is up in the air compared to the multiple Northwestern players.

For the Nittany Lions to have success, they’re going to have to establish the run game, especially against a defense that has struggled against the run. If they can somewhat replicate the success they had against Buffalo, maybe not to the extent of 304 rushing yards, they have a good chance to come out on top.

Penn State will have difficulties containing the dual-threat talent of Aidan Chiles, but it’ll stop him enough to hold up and defeat Northwestern in the Wildcats’ first game at their new stadium.

Andrew Mercer: Northwestern 17, Penn State 14

Although Rocco Becht said he expects a “different team” against the Wildcats, it’s extremely difficult to turn an entire offense around in such a short week.

Penn State had both Sunday and Monday off from practice this week, leaving the Nittany Lions three days to execute on the lessons learned on the practice field before its showtime. If the issues presented on Saturday were truly fixable details, it’ll simply come down to showing up when the pressure’s on.

Penn State cracked under the pressure last week.

While D’Anton Lynn’s defense was strong against Wisconsin, the Badgers proved Saturday that a strong defense cannot completely win you a football game. If three interceptions, including a pick six, wasn’t enough to beat Wisconsin, it’s going to take an explosive performance on offense to get over the hump.

It’s that explosivity I believe Penn State lacks at this point. Without Koby Howard, the offense slumped, and if Becht can’t get into rhythm with Brett Eskildsen or Chase Sowell, there’s no reason why this losing streak can’t snowball.

Lexie Linderman: Penn State 21, Northwestern 14

The poor offensive showing against Wisconsin was definitely not ideal for Penn State, and this Friday’s game is going to show exactly what this team and offense is truly made of.

I don’t expect Taylor Mouser’s offense to absolutely dominate now, but he and Becht likely have chips on their shoulders and want to prove they belong in the Big Ten. They’ll do that with a gritty win over the Wildcats.

The Nittany Lions’ run game has a big opportunity to have a statement performance, as Northwestern allowed 272 yards on the ground last week in its close loss to Indiana. Expect James Peoples to show why he should be Penn State’s No. 1 running back.

Even if Dixson doesn’t play, Terry Smith’s position group has loads of depth that can step up in place, such as fellow sophomore Jahmir Joseph. Northwestern’s passing attack also runs purely through two players, giving the Nittany Lions an advantage.

Penn State’s defense will ultimately step up and prevent the Wildcats from winning their debut game at Ryan Field.

Noah Aberegg: Penn State 23, Northwestern 17

Penn State is coming off a rough start to Big Ten play against Wisconsin, as the offense was never able to find momentum and the defense gave up several big plays. While I expect those themes to remain this week, I think the Nittany Lions can do just enough to pull out the win.

One of the biggest struggles for Penn State this year has been the red zone offense, and as long as wide receiver Koby Howard is sidelined and the run game struggles continue, I think those red zone difficulties will continue. That’s where kicker Ryan Barker will come in clutch.

I think Barker will have one of the most productive games of his career, drilling all three field goal attempts. There could be an opportunity for more, but I think Matt Campbell will be a little more aggressive on fourth down after last week.

Defensively, Penn State’s pass rush will once again have a tough time getting to the opposing quarterback. Aidan Chiles was sacked a season-high four times last week, and while I don’t think the Nittany Lions will replicate those numbers, I think they’ll improve from their single sack against the Badgers.

Turnovers, however, will be the major turning point that gives Penn State the wins. A week after intercepting Colton Joseph three times, the Nittany Lions will record at least one turnover that results in a score and eventually the win.
