title: No. 14 Penn State women's volleyball upset by Michigan State in 4 sets
author: Ashley Felsberg I The Daily Collegian
description:
After a 3-1 win against Michigan on Friday, Penn State continued its action Sunday against Michigan State.

The Nittany Lions couldn’t continue their winning ways, falling 3-1.

Kennedy Martin opened up the match with a kill from the right side, giving Penn State the early lead. Michigan State’s Hayley Ogden quickly answered back to even out the playing field. After a quick couple of back-and-forths, the Spartans broke through for a five-point run, taking an 11-6 lead.

The Spartans continued to go on multiple three-point runs to keep the point gap to at least five. When the score reached 19-10, Michigan State had totaled 13 kills and not a single error.

Martin gave the Nittany Lions their 13th point after a central kill. Her momentum continued after another kill. Martin and Ryla Jones combined for a right-side block, bringing the blue and white within five and forcing Michigan State into a timeout.

Following the timeout, the Nittany Lions scored five straight points. A serving error from Ava Falduto returned offensive control to Michigan State; however, Martin quickly reversed it with a solo block.

Back-and-forth play continued until Alanna Bankston earned the Spartans their 23rd point following a powerful kill for her fifth of the set. While it seemed Penn State had a promising comeback, Michigan State continued with back-to-back aces to take set one.

Gabrielle Nichols’ block gave Penn State the first point of set two. Jones contributed three kills of her own, her third giving Penn State its ninth point, while also forcing Michigan State to take its second timeout.

As Michigan State slowly started to creep back in, Penn State was able to extend its lead. Alexis Stucky assisted Martin in a cross-court swing for the blue and white’s 13th point, but a Stucky attack error kept Michigan State within one.

The Spartans took the lead on back-to-back kills from Carmen Waye. After a service error, two attack errors for Penn State and a Michigan State ace, the Spartans extended their lead to four.

After Bankston and Waye contributed a paired block and Malayah Long added an ace of her own, the Spartans lead extended to six points. Waye followed up with a kill, extending the unanswered run to seven.

Whitney Launstein attempted to give Penn State a final push of momentum, contributing two kills to bring the blue and white within five. This aided a spark as a Nichols block, and a Waye attack error added two more points.

Jones committed a service error, putting Michigan State within two of set point. Madi Andrews added a kill for Michigan State, but it was called a lift. Andrews then followed up with another kill, as did Zora Hardison.

The Nittany Lions stayed alive after Launstein answered back with a central kill, however Hardison responded, and Michigan State took set two.

The Spartans opened up set three with a five point run, as Penn State struggled with the serve receive. Coach Katie Schumacher-Cawley called a timeout, yet Michigan State earned the first two points following the stoppage.

Penn State earned its first point after an attack error by Andrews. Martin followed with a kill of her own, yet Ogden responded to halt the momentum. The Spartans lead was halved after a successful Martin attack and an error by Michigan State.

The Nittany Lions closed the gap to three after a block from freshman, Daniella Whitemire. Sellman’s one time swing aided Penn State’s four point run, however a kill by Hardison halted this comeback. Bankston then brought Michigan State to double digits, with a same-side kill.

The Spartans lead was pulled back to three after Martin contributed a kill to the back side of the court. Each time Penn State crawled within the three-point range, the Spartans answered back, this time with an Andrews kill.

When the score reached 14-11, Jones went down, after colliding with teammate Falduto. She headed out for the remainder of the match, and the officials called for a point-redo. Penn State fought for the point, after an attack error from Waye.

Michigan State earned the 15th point through a left-side hit from Andrews, as the game headed into a media timeout.

Penn State evened the score at 16-16 after a Martin kill. The Nittany Lions battled head to head for the next two points, taking the lead on an Andrews attack error.

Penn State briefly kept its lead, as a Martin attack error balanced out the score. The two teams traded one point leads until Penn State earned a two point upper-hand with a Martin kill and Bankston attack error.

The score flipped in favor of the Spartans after they went on a three-point run, forcing Schumacher-Cawley to use another timeout. The Nittany Lions took the lead with attacks from Nichols and Martin.

An attack error from the Spartans brought the blue and white to set point, yet coach Kristen Kelsay burned her last challenge, looking for an illegal attack fault. The challenge was unsuccessful and the call stood, keeping the score at 24-22.

Martin put up her 14th kill of the day to aid the first set win for the blue and white.

The fourth set started differently, as the Spartans didn’t build a big lead early and the teams traded one- and two-point leads.

After the third point for Michigan State, the Spartans continued the lead for the remainder of the set.

Michigan State called a late set timeout after Penn State went on a three-point run, bringing the blue and white within three points of a completed comeback. Following the timeout, Ava Jurevicius contributed an ace.

Back-to-back errors from the Nittany Lions put the Spartans one away from match point. Penn State used a timeout for one last chance of a regrouping to aid an offensive spark.

Ogden extended the set with a kill following the timeout, bringing the blue and white to within six points. Long added another Spartan attack error to close the gap to five; however, Martin's attack error clinched the match for Michigan State.

Injury Report

Jones left the game in set three with a lower-body injury and didn’t return.

Up Next

Penn State returns home on Thursday at 7 p.m. for its match against No. 1 Nebraska.

title: Penn State drops out of AP Top 25
author: Andrew Mercer | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State has been kicked out of the AP Poll after a climatic upset in the Big Ten opener.

The Nittany Lions are now unranked in the wake of their 24-20 loss to Wisconsin on Saturday, the program’s first defeat at the hands of the Badgers since 2011. It was also Wisconsin’s first win at Beaver Stadium since 2003.

Across the Big Ten, Ohio State moved up to No. 5, Iowa rose to No. 14 and Michigan fell out of the top 25 after the Hawkeyes beat the Wolverines 20-19, Oregon advanced to No. 15 and USC dropped to No. 18 after the Ducks won 41-27. Indiana fell to No. 6 after a close win over Northwestern.

title: How improbable was Penn State’s loss to Wisconsin?
author: Andrew Deal | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State held leads of 17-0 and 20-10 during the game and seemingly had the game in control.

Despite that, Wisconsin marched down the field on big-play bursts to mount the comeback and defeat Penn State, against all odds.

How improbable was this loss?

In-game probability

On Wisconsin quarterback Colton Joseph’s third interception, Penn State’s chances to win peaked on ESPN’s win probability metric. The Nittany Lions had a 98.5% win probability with eight minutes left.

After Joseph’s touchdown pass to wide receiver Eugene Hilton Jr., Penn State still had a win probability of 89.1%, as it just needed about two first downs to put the game away.

The Nittany Lions went three-and-out, but the Badgers weren’t doing everything to take the game that Penn State was essentially handing them. A false start on tight end Jacob Harris put the Nittany Lions’ win probability up to 89.4%.

Harris would ultimately catch a pass and go the distance that flipped the probability in Wisconsin’s favor.

Breaking tradition

The loss was even more improbable than just the ESPN metric. Since 2002, Penn State had held a 17-point lead 101 times in Beaver Stadium. In those games, the Nittany Lions were 101-0 until Saturday night.

Even with all of that against it, the Nittany Lions have also had Wisconsin’s number in the last 15 years. Saturday was the first time the Badgers have defeated Penn State since 2011, when a Russell Wilson-led Wisconsin team won against Penn State, 45-7.

Wilson wasn’t the quarterback out on the field on Saturday. Prior to the final two drives, Joseph was a measly 10-of-22 with a 45% completion percentage, and his numbers didn’t even take much of a jump as the Badgers came back to win.

In addition to Joseph’s lackluster numbers, the Badgers were without their leading rusher, Abu Sama III. He went down with an injury in the second quarter, but backup running back Darrion Dupree was key in the comeback.

History for Wisconsin

Joseph and Dupree led Wisconsin to its largest comeback since 2006 and snapped a 64-game winning streak for the Nittany Lions in games it led by 10 or more points entering the fourth quarter. It was also Wisconsin’s first road win since 2024.

The 17-point lead is tied for the largest blown lead Matt Campbell has had during his head coaching career. It’s also the largest blown lead by a Penn State team since 2017, when it led Ohio State 21-3 in the second quarter.

Campbell said Penn State “left it to chance,” and against all odds, chance came out in Wisconsin’s favor.

title: Column | Penn State’s TEs are supposedly the ‘heartbeat’ of the offense. So, where are they?
author: Lexie Linderman | Football Editor
description:
Benjamin Brahmer has said multiple times Taylor Mouser believes the tight end room is the “heartbeat” of Penn State’s offense.

So, where were they Saturday?

Brahmer caught three passes for 33 yards across the Nittany Lions’ first two drives. He moved the chains twice. It looked like in Koby Howard’s absence, Mouser was turning to his 6-foot-7 tight end that was a John Mackey Award finalist last season.

Brahmer didn’t catch another pass until the fourth quarter.

In the time between his third catch and his fourth, Penn State had turned 17-0 and 20-10 leads into a three-point game. It couldn’t get anything going on offense, and wide receiver Chase Sowell was the only other pass-catcher with a reception.

“I think there was just a weird flow to the game, especially in the first half of the football game, where you're in more situational football,” Matt Campbell said postgame. “I think some of it will be really interesting to see what happened in the second half. We're going to have to have more production from the receiving room and from the other players on the opposite side of the ball.”

Mouser has also talked at length about how much he loves Gabe Burkle and was frustrated with him being limited against Temple. Burkle only has one catch this year.

And then there’s Andrew Rappleyea, who had one target against Wisconsin on the second-to-last play of the game. He had a chance to bring it in for the game-winning score, but he jumped slightly too soon and it fell incomplete.

As a whole, the tight end room has 215 yards this season, good for about 54 yards a game. In theory, that’s not bad. But with the talent at Mouser’s disposal there, it’s not where it should be.

It’s understandable for the tight ends to not see as many targets with Howard in the lineup, as he’s far and away the best playmaker Penn State has on offense.

But Howard wasn’t available against Wisconsin, and he seemingly won’t be suiting up for at least the next two games based on the Instagram story he posted earlier in the week. So the Nittany Lions need to get production in the passing game from someone else.

“I'd be a fool to sit up here and say we didn't miss Koby,” Campbell said. “I would also say I have great belief in the rest of our guys, and the rest of our guys had some opportunities, and they got to keep pounding away at it.”

That someone else should be Brahmer. He can tower over opposing defenses and is good at finding space and hauling in contested catches, even if Howard is still better at that specifically.

Brahmer is supposed to be one of the best tight ends in the country this season, and he should be treated by his offensive coordinator as such. Yes, tight ends are important for blocking purposes, even more so when the run game is struggling like it is now, but Brahmer is too good of a pass-catcher to not be utilized.

So moving forward, Mouser has to get the ball to the so-called “heartbeat” of his offense. Especially with Howard out. And especially after Saturday’s offensive performance.

“I think it's on me to spread the ball out,” Rocco Becht said. “We just got to be better on all of our parts. To go out there and make plays when they're there to be made. So again, I put that on me. I got to be able to spread the ball around and be able to make the defense guess.”

title: Penn State’s 4th quarter defensive collapse against Wisconsin was ‘self-inflicted’
author: Andrew Mercer | The Daily Collegian
description:
Down 20-17, Wisconsin quarterback Colton Joseph found Jacob Harris deep up the middle with 1:13 remaining in the game. Harris had only cornerback Audavion Collins to beat and shed the tackle en route to a game-winning 72-yard touchdown.

The Homecoming game crowd at Beaver Stadium on Saturday night was speechless. Not only did Penn State lose its Big Ten opener, but it did so with a shocking defensive collapse in the fourth quarter.

“Defensively, I thought we played a tremendous football game,” Matt Campbell said postgame. “We gave ourselves every opportunity to win, and we didn’t take advantage.”

The Nittany Lions led 17-0 with under two minutes remaining in the first half, and that goose egg on the scoreboard wasn’t without good reason. Cornerbacks Josiah Zayas and Daryus Dixson had back-to-back interceptions in the second quarter, key to the convincing lead.

Zayas first jumped a pass along the flat and ran 51 yards into the end zone for a pick six, the first touchdown of the game before Dixson capitalized on an overthrown pass.

“It's nothing new,” linebacker Kooper Ebel said. “We see that every week, every day at practice. It's a tribute to how they show up and work every day.”

However, momentum flipped when Joseph scored a 7-yard rushing touchdown going into halftime. Penn State wasn’t immortal any longer.

“Obviously we wouldn't have liked to let that up,” linebacker Kooper Ebel said. “We talk about momentum all the time, we talk about winning the middle eight. They did a great job of executing there at the end of the half.”

Cracks had begun to show throughout the second half as Joseph found strings of success but couldn’t finish the job. There were pockets of big gains that proved Wisconsin could take advantage of opportunities, and when Penn State started to make mistakes, the Badgers did just that.

“It was self-inflicted,” safety Jeremiah Cooper said. “We just got to get better at everything we messed up on.”

Ebel echoed that sentiment. He said there were issues with finishing plays because of “pre-snap alignment,” and said the noise volume inside Beaver Stadium was a factor in limiting communication between the defenders.

Wisconsin got the job done late in the fourth quarter after relentlessly pushing forward despite facing immense adversity. Cooper said postgame the main issue was with “fundamental techniques.”

Although Tony Rojas’ fourth-quarter interception made it seem like Penn State had everything under control, D’Anton Lynn’s defense completely unraveled in the Badgers’ final two drives of the game.

It began with an 11-yard touchdown pass to Eugene Hilton Jr., that was by no means an easy grab. Hilton had to toe-tap the side of the end zone and hold on to a ball thrown over his shoulder after blazing by Marcus Neal Jr.

“I know it was on Marcus,” Cooper said. “But I know Marcus is a much better player than that. I know he's gonna fix that, so I have full confidence that he's gonna bounce back from that.”

The next drive was when Harris went the distance to win the game.

Despite the offense’s apparent struggles to capitalize on the chances the defense generated, Cooper made sure to take accountability for the loss, citing that “it’s team football at the end of the day.”

“We still let them score,” Cooper said. “So it's not on them. It's on us.”

title: ‘I’ve got to be better’ | Penn State’s offense struggles amidst season-lows from Rocco Becht, WRs
author: Noah Aberegg | The Daily Collegian
description:
With five seconds left on the clock, Rocco Becht launched the ball to the end zone, needing a touchdown while trailing 24-20.

But similar to his performance through the previous 59 minutes, the deep ball wasn’t there, as it sailed out of the end zone to clinch Penn State’s first loss of the season against Wisconsin.

“I got to be better for this team,” Becht said. “I can’t put us in scenarios where our backs are backed up and we got to have a big play. I didn’t do my part today, so I got to do better.”

It was a season-low performance for the winningest active quarterback in college football. For the first time this season, he didn’t have a passing touchdown and threw his first interception of the year.

“It wasn't a ball that was a bad or poor decision,” Matt Campbell said postgame of Becht’s interception. “It was a tipped pass. I really thought Rocco played well. I thought it was a really good football game for the most part. I'll answer that better after I watch the tape.”

Becht finished just 12-for-29 for 114 yards in Penn State’s 233-yard offensive performance. The Nittany Lions’ offense only found the end zone once, as Becht recorded his first rushing touchdown of the season.

But Penn State’s quarterback was missing his top target, as Koby Howard is currently sidelined for an “extended period of time.” It was clear throughout the game that Becht and the offense missed Howard out there.

“I'd be a fool to sit up here and say, man, we didn't miss Koby,” Matt Campbell said postgame. “Koby's a guy that we all have great faith in.”

Throughout the week, there was a lot of talk of the other wide receivers stepping up. Chase Sowell, Brett Eskildsen and Zay Robinson were all names that were expected to see more targets, while freshman wide receiver Amarion Jackson was also discussed as a potential contributor.

Instead, Sowell was the only wide receiver who recorded a reception against Wisconsin. The former Iowa State receiver had six catches for 70 yards, including a handful of plays in big moments for the Nittany Lions.

“I would say I'm a little bit surprised that that is the statistic in the game,” Campbell said. “We're going to have to have more production from the receiver room, from the other players on the offensive side of the football.”

Eskildsen was back at full strength after being banged up over the past two weeks, but didn’t record a catch. He was almost involved in the passing game many times, as Becht targeted him on several deep balls.

However, Eskildsen wasn’t able to haul any of them in, albeit some were underthrown, including what could’ve been a touchdown late in the game.

“I saw the defense, the corner, kind of stutter his feet, and Brett got behind him. I got to put a better ball out there,” Becht said. “I got to make it easier on these receivers to go out there and make plays.”

While Becht had those struggles in the passing game, Campbell said “some of our issues were probably more so with some protection things.”

Becht faced immense pressure from Wisconsin’s pass rush, which recorded two sacks and two quarterback hits.

At one point, right tackle and captain Anthony Donkoh was subject to a spin move from a Wisconsin defender, who ran unguarded at Becht. There were numerous times he had to scramble out of the pocket and throw the ball away.

“I feel like this game, we have a lot of responsibility,” left guard Trevor Buhr said. “I really just feel like in all those moments and everything, we got to do everything we can to help all those other guys and try to have those guys be able to lean on us. We just gotta get better.”

After scoring just one offensive touchdown and three second-half points against Wisconsin, Campbell stressed the significance of coming back and going head first into next week’s game against Northwestern.

“The reality of it is, these are all correctable things if we’re willing and humble enough to be able to make the corrections,” Campbell said. “It’ll be a great challenge for us. Not going to be easy, but we look forward to the challenge.”

title: Penn State players see growth opportunity following loss to Wisconsin
author: Andrew Deal | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State suffered its first loss of the season, and first under Matt Campbell, in dramatic fashion after giving up two touchdowns in the fourth quarter.

Despite the loss, the team felt it was an opportunity to grow and rally together to push forward, especially given the Nittany Lions have a short week with a road matchup against Northwestern on Friday.

“We just got to learn from this, and we got a great opportunity to bounce back next week with this quick week, and we just got to take everything that we learned from this game,” offensive lineman Trevor Buhr said. “It's pretty good we got some adversity at this point, so just taking everything we can learn from this and then applying it forward.”

The players and coaching staff made sure to keep each other’s heads up following the loss to avoid dwelling on what happened on the field.

Running back James Peoples recognized that “moment to grow” during his conversation with running back coach Savon Huggins postgame as they walked off the field.

That mentality was heard throughout the locker room, as Campbell’s message to the team more so focused on keeping spirits high than the collapse to end the game.

“Win or loss, we're going to come in tomorrow and continue to work, and I think that's just the attitude and the message that he gives us is to continue to just push forward and be ourselves and go out there and compete,” Rocco Becht said.

Buhr noticed the same thing when offensive line coach Ryan Clanton addressed his players after the game. Buhr said Clanton told the offensive line that there’s still “a lot of football left” and to plan to “bounce back tomorrow and just get ready and keep moving forward.”

What stood out the most to the players was Becht’s message to the team in the locker room despite his performance. Becht had an underwhelming day with 129 passing yards and a 41% completion percentage, but he still spoke to the team and kept the spirits high.

“He was very motivated because I think he feels like all the pressure is on him and all the blows on him,” defensive tackle Armstrong Nnodim said. “Just for him to come to the team and just speak highly of everything, it shows his character and through adversity, he can still remain positive.”

Kicker Ryan Barker said the team has already begun focusing on Northwestern and “kind of flushed it, and that's what we have to do when we face adversity.”

The team will still look at the film on Sunday and address what went well and went wrong throughout the game to help it continue forward. Buhr is “really not concerned about (the loss) at all,” knowing there’s still eight games left in the season.

“You gotta keep your head up,” safety Jeremiah Cooper said. “It's literally the first conference game, and we got a whole season to play. So it's keeping our head up.”

title: 3 takeaways from Penn State's shocking loss to Wisconsin
author: Andrew Deal | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State kicked off the first Big Ten slate under Matt Campbell with a home game against Wisconsin in front of a Helmet Stripe crowd.

The Nittany Lions lost their first game of the season to Wisconsin despite three interceptions from the defense throughout the game.

Here’s three takeaways from Penn State’s loss.

Defense collapses late

Penn State’s defense limited Wisconsin to 124 total yards in the first half and forced two turnovers that led to two touchdowns.

In the fourth quarter, the defense collapsed, allowing Wisconsin to make a comeback after being down by 10.

Wisconsin began its first touchdown drive of the quarter with 7:02 left in the game. Running back Darrion Dupree gashed Penn State’s defense, with gains of 17, 13 and 10 yards to get the Badgers into the Nittany Lions’ territory.

After allowing a 13-yard touchdown pass, the defense was tasked with making one final stop with 2:28 left on the clock, and it was gashed once again.

A 72-yard touchdown to tight end Jacob Harris gave Wisconsin the lead with over a minute left. The total collapse of the defense after previously shutting down the Badgers’ offense could’ve come from the lack of time it had off the field.

“I think we had a guy slip on the broken play, and one slip, and that play, that situation, it's kind of like the narrative of the second half, right?” Campbell said. “We left it to chance, and we had so many opportunities to put the game away.”

Penn State’s offense had three straight three-and-outs, giving the defense very little time to rest. The defensive collapse led to Wisconsin’s upset victory over the Nittany Lions in comeback fashion.

Pass rush can’t get success

The pass rush gave Joseph plenty of time to throw the ball. It was a concern entering the game, and it remains a concern after recording just one sack.

Additionally, that sack came from linebacker Tony Rojas, who had to run across the field to get to Joseph.

With that much time in the pocket, Joseph was able to sit and find receivers who got themselves open. When D’Anton Lynn dialed up a blitz, it was able to bring pressure on Joseph and force him to make an errant throw.

Despite the struggles Joseph showed when pressure was in his face, the pass rush didn’t get to him very often. Joseph wasn’t able to beat Penn State through the air much, though, thanks to the secondary shutting down Wisconsin’s receivers.

Penn State’s edge rushers are going to have to find success more often as the season continues, as the level of offenses is only going to get better.

Penn State’s offense struggles without Koby Howard

Penn State seemingly had plenty of weapons to rely on with the absence of Koby Howard.

However, those weapons weren’t showcased in the loss over Wisconsin, as the offense scored just 13 points, with 10 of them from the defense giving it good field position.

“We really struggled to find the rhythm and I think in the first half, we were either backup or on the goal line and we never got into the flow of the game, and I feel like it kind of led into the second half of the football game and kind of being in the same spot because we struggled,” Campbell said.

Tight end Benjamin Brahmer was utilized early, catching three passes when the offense was moving the ball in the first quarter, but he wasn’t targeted after that despite being Rocco Becht’s largest target.

After 304 rushing yards in Week 3 against Buffalo, the run game didn’t show much, running for an average of 3.4 yards per carry. James Peoples led the way with 67 yards on the ground.

In the air, Becht connected with just three receivers, with the missing big-play ability from Howard giving the rest of the weapons less favorable opportunities in the pass game.

The offense was stagnant throughout the game and kept Wisconsin in the game, allowing it to mount the comeback and defeat the Nittany Lions.

title: Maddy Campbell stars as Penn State women's hockey goaltending impresses in losses to Ohio State
author: Rafael Rivera | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State might have a decision to make in between the pipes.

The night after Morgan Stickney had a stellar collegiate debut, saving 42 shots against Ohio State in a 2-1 overtime loss, sophomore Maddy Campbell had a great performance of her own, saving 31 shots against the Buckeyes.

After yesterday, it looked like Stickney put herself firmly in the driver's seat to be Penn State's starting goaltender, but Campbell put up just as impressive a night against the scarlet and grey.

“It’s actually a good problem to have,” coach Jeff Kampersal said. “Maddy played really well. I gotta talk to coach Moe (Bradley), but we will probably rotate in the beginning to kinda see who emerges. Both goaltenders gave us a chance to win; Maddy did great so I’m happy for her.”

Entering the year, Kampersal echoed that sentiment in preseason media, where he first confirmed that both will split the starting role to open against Ohio State. It was a real switch on the ice in the wake of program icon Katie DeSa departing in between the pipes, who held down the crease in a majority of games. Although it’s early, the competition may have sparked something special in Happy Valley.

“Both of us have been pushing each other so hard we both want to play, and I think that’s really helped us both just be on our A game,” Campbell said. “In practice, if she doesn't let a goal in, I don't want to let a goal in and vice versa. I think us together makes such a great pair.”

Despite a winless opening series to the season, the situation in net appears to be a catalyst for widespread improvement not just on the ice as it did tonight, as it’s already occurred within the position group.

“I think as we saw this weekend, we both played really, really well, and (Stickney) has been great,” Campbell said. “It's a super positive environment for both of us, and then me personally, just coming back as a sophomore, I just really want to take everything that I go last year and improve and just keep getting better and better.”

The novice netminders' performances are nothing to scoff at against an Ohio State team that will most likely compete for the National Championship. Next week against RMU, the coaching staff will get another opportunity to see who’s best suited for the job, as it’s likely to be another series where fans see shared brilliance.

title: Penn State men’s basketball notebook | Mike Rhoades holds open practice, discusses outlook
author: Myles Hannak | The Daily Collegian
description:
For the first time since late July, Mike Rhoades spoke to the media.

After over two hours of a sweat-filled practice that involved drills and live game action directed by an animated Rhoades, the boss spoke on player personnel, expectations and style of play ahead of the Nittany Lions’ season.

Here’s a recap of what the blue and white coach had to say.

Practice performance

As the Nittany Lions enter next season with an entirely refurbished and more experienced roster, Rhoades pumped up the gas in a practice that included fastbreak drills, designed loose ball chases and cardio work built in.

Rhoades already discussed earlier this summer his team’s off-the-court bonding efforts and his need for a different on-the-floor identity.

“This group so far, all summer, all fall, they've been a blast to be around and a blast to coach. We have a little bit of everything,” Rhoades said. “We got some young guys, we got some older guys, got some skilled guys, we got some big athletic guys and we have good character, good bones right now — but it's early, and there's not much adversity.”

The coach stayed vocal throughout practice, wanting players not to go down and, if they do, to bounce right back up. It wasn’t just that; his pauses in practice to give advice or the drills, designed with sprints or tire work for the losers or if a mistake was made – there was a clear uptick in intensity

“Last year we were being so young and weak, I thought in my 30 years it was the weakest, softest team I’ve coached,” Rhoades said. “That ain’t happening anymore, so it's all about physicality, playing through physicality, being good, strong and tough.”

Identity of play

While Rhoades wasn’t ready to name his starters yet when prompted, he remained giddy for the tools at his disposal and gave a majority of his roster props by name. The coach already said this summer he desires his team to play differently, and after first seeing his squad, Rhoades expanded on what he meant.

“Best shooting team I've had since I've been here. It's probably one of the best shooting teams I've had since I was at Rice,” Rhoades said. “If you have guys that can really shoot it like Brant (Byers) and Roberts (Blums) and Thomas (Allard) and Josh (Reed), then you can't really help off those guys.”

Penn State finished last season in the bottom of the Big Ten in both percentages scoring and defending the shot from beyond the arc.

As for both 7-footers, Buffalo transfer Tim Oboh spent time in practice directly against returning Ivan Jurić, who Rhoades confirmed gained six to seven pounds going into his sophomore year, with an emphasis on improving his verticality and using that experience to his benefit.

Guard Andy Gemao got reps on both of them via defensive switches, as he enters next season as someone Rhoades said postgame has a real chance to earn minutes early in the season. Joining the backcourt with the true freshman is Dasonte Bowen, who’d also earned praise from his coach to the media. Neither of the pair, however, got quite the same praise as Davidson transfer Roberts Blums, who Rhoades compared to a “daredevil”

“He's just not afraid. He's tough, plays super hard, his energy is contagious, and then he can make plays and make shots — The dude wants to win in everything we do,” Rhoades said. “Sometimes I got to pull him back, but you'd rather pull the dog back than try to get him on.”

Also practicing with the squad is fifth-year Josh Reed, whose status remains gray in the midst of his legal battle for eligibility. While Rhoades admitted the confusion in the situation gets to him at times, remarking that “the timeline is never on our time,” he reaffirmed the solid communication among all parties.

Rhoades was also asked about international additions François Wibaut and Roko Prkačin, praising both for their veteran presence and coachability.

Noticeably on the sideline was freshman forward Aleksandar Zečević, who didn’t participate in any drills with contact due to what Rhoades confirmed was an ankle sprain, which shouldn’t limit him come the start of the season.

The noise

As he enters his fourth year, the urgency for Rhoades to improve Penn State’s standing on the hardwood becomes even more dire. With what looks like a season to make or break the process at work in Happy Valley, as it already looks stacked against the Nittany Lions, those questions are only months away from rearing their heads at all avenues.

“You can only be controlling what you can control, and if you're worried about outside these doors, what people say and opinions, you are already beat,” Rhoades said. “Nobody else matters, but inside this gym, it's always going to be like that. That's just how it goes, and all that other stuff to me is smoke.”

The open practice served as a public display of Rhoades focus to the task at hand through his intensity, vocal care for the program during practice or even his pause to accuse media members of recording practice.

“This is the best part of my job, being in the gym and having fun. I'm always like this. It's been cool with these guys because there's a lot of teaching because we got all these new guys, but that's why you get into it.”

title: No. 14 Penn State women's volleyball defeats Michigan behind dominant 3rd and 4th sets.
author: Gianna Dowling | Sports Editor
description:
After ending its nonconference slate with a loss to then-No.16 Tennessee, No. 14 Penn State returned to action on Friday night. The Nittany Lions opened Big Ten play at the Crisler Center in Ann Arbor, taking on Michigan.

The blue and white opened conference play with a bang, defeating Michigan 3-1.

The Big Ten foes traded points to start the set, but Penn State broke through for a 5-2 lead behind three kills from Gabrielle Nichols.

The Wolverines didn’t let up, though, taking four of the next six points, three of which came on Nittany Lion errors.

The back-and-forth continued until both teams were deadlocked in a 9-9 tie. Michigan took its turn to go on a run, scoring three straight points behind kills from Cymarah Gordon and Ella Demetrician.

Three points was the longest run either team would go on in the early portions of the match, as the Wolverines held a close 15-13 lead heading into the first media timeout.

Michigan extended its lead right after the break with Jenna Hanes’ first kill of the night. The point couldn’t help the Wolverines gain momentum, though, but did quite the opposite.

Penn State responded with a four-point run, thanks to three Michigan errors and an ace from Lexi Gin. The Wolverine miscues called for coach Erin Virtue to take her first timeout.

Coming out of the timeout, the maize and blue found its footing, taking five of the next seven points, which forced Nittany Lions’ coach Katie Schumacher-Cawley to talk things over with her squad, trailing 21-19.

The blue and white got a couple of points back on Alexis Ewing’s third kill of the night, along with an attacking error from Demetrician.

However, Michigan continued to answer the call, breaking out to a 24-22 lead, and with set point looming, Schumacher-Cawley burned another timeout.

Back into play, the Wolverines served for set point, but Kennedy Martin recorded her fourth kill, extending the opening set action. However, Michigan wasn’t denied for long as Demetrician’s set-high sixth kill clinched the first set.

It was a sloppy set on both sides, with a combined 13 attacking errors.

The second set didn’t tell much of a different story as Penn State opened with back-to-back attacking errors from Nichols and Whitney Lauenstein.

After falling behind 4-2, the Nittany Lions broke through for five straight points behind a balanced effort from all their attackers.

The Wolverines took the next two points, but it wasn’t enough to slow the blue and white down. Penn State went on another scoring run, this time for three points off another kill from Lauenstein and both a kill and service ace from Emmi Sellman.

The effort guided the Nittany Lions to a 15-10 advantage heading into the media timeout.

After the opponents traded points coming out of the break, Penn State once again stretched a three-point run from Nichols’ sixth kill of the match and Martin’s eighth, as well as another attacking error from Demetrician.

Back-to-back attacking errors from Sellman and Alexis Stucky helped Michigan cut its deficit down to 21-15.

However, the Wolverines couldn’t claw their way back, as a powerful performance gave Penn State the 25-17 set two win.

The Nittany Lions started the third set with Lexi Gin’s second service ace of night. From here on out, things looked much like they did in the first set, with both teams trading points.

This was until, the blue and white scored four straight points on two Martin kills, guiding Penn State to 6-2 lead.

The Nittany Lions maintained an advantage throughout the next stretch of points, turning a 9-4 lead into a 14-10 lead. The blue and white got kills from Ryla Jones, Lauenstein and Martin, with Michigan answering with kills from Eco Senyapici and Demetrician.

Schumacher-Cawley’s squad proved that there was still much more left in the tank, and Penn State pushed for a six point stretch, taking a 10-point lead. The stretch was fueled by four Wolverine attacking errors, along with a fourth kill for Jones and a game-high 14th from Martin.

The Nittany Lions continued to overwhelm Michigan, taking four of the next six points, finding themselves at set point with a 24-12 advantage.

Sydney Schnichels kept the maize and blue alive briefly, but Martin put the cherry on top of a dominant third set.

Penn State opened the fourth set scoring on an error from Schnichels and a Stucky service ace. Michigan answered with back to back kills from Gordon.

The Nittany Lions built a 12-7 lead after briefly trailing 4-3. Martin opened the stretch with a kill, while Jones, Sellman and Lauenstein all contributed. Michigan closed the gap with kills from Gordon, Demetrician and Schnichels, but Penn State still stood firm.

After the fourth set media timeout, Penn State’s 16-8 lead quickly became a 20-12 advantage as Martin continued her powerful night with the help of her setter Stucky, who finished the night with 40 assists.

Three straight points put the Nittany Lions one step closer to taking the match, but the run was halted by a kill from Lydia Johnson.

The Michigan threat was brief as a Stucky kill and attacking error from Gordon sealed the deal for the blue and white.

Up Next

The Nittany Lions remain in the Mitten State for their next conference matchup, taking on Michigan State at 2 p.m. Sunday.

title: Penn State women's hockey's offensive struggles prove detrimental in second loss to Ohio State
author: Gavin Leonard | The Daily Collegian
description:
Correction: After the game, officials changed the stats to credit Penn State's assists on its goal to Grace Tullock and Megan Hosman; the original version of this story attributed it to Kylie Amelkovich. The Daily Collegian apologizes for this error.

After a heartbreaking overtime loss in the first game of the series, the Nittany Lions failed to bounce back with a 2-1 loss to No. 2 Ohio State at the Pegula Ice Arena on Friday afternoon.

With the Buckeyes having the 33-to-11 shot count advantage, it was clear throughout the game that Penn State’s offense struggled to consistently break through the opposing defense.

In the opening minutes of the match, Grace Outwater gave the offense an ounce of life, scoring the first goal of the game. Outwater made a run down the middle on a breakaway and delivered the pass through the air.

“Shooters shoot, and she shot,” coach Jeff Kampersal said. “We expect Grace to hopefully average a goal a game or more; that’s her role to get us offense.”

Outwater’s goal was a sign of what was to come, as the majority of Penn State's opportunities came from counterattacks where defense turned into offense.

After Ohio State tied the game on a power-play goal, the blue and white endured a shot-attempt drought, including a failure to convert on a power-play of their own in the final minutes of the first period.

Heading into the second period, the Penn State defense showed up in its own right with plenty of blocked shots and saves. Yet, the Nittany Lions were unsuccessful in playing complementary hockey.

On Penn State’s second power-play of the game, the offense couldn’t get the puck out of their D-Zone, leading to multiple two-on-one opportunities that weren’t converted by the Buckeyes.

“It’s frustrating; it’s not for lack of trying but the breakouts were just meh,” Kampersal said. “In these big games we have to have a threatening power-play. It’s just a mindset of being really hungry when they have those opportunities.”

Ohio State completely controlled the game’s momentum, and the same defensive-zone struggles resurfaced as Penn State lost the puck in its end of the rink, leading to a Buckeyes goal. Ohio State increased its lead in the shot count tally, holding a 19-to-5 advantage.

In the final period, Penn State’s offense finally began to find its footing, setting up an attack in the offensive zone that led to a shot that went wide of the net. As time progressed, so did the offense, with more opportunities coming from counterattacks.

Those opportunities didn’t lead to shot attempts, however, as the blue and white offense couldn’t thread the final pass through nor retain the puck when pushing down the rink for attacks.

The last-second offensive push was too little too late, and the Nittany Lions now begin the season with back-to-back losses.

Ohio State dominated the shot count, notching 33 shot attempts in comparison to Penn State’s 11.

“We want to be a little bit more selfish shooting the puck and taking our own shots,” Kampersal said. “We need more urgency, especially on the puck.”

While Ohio State’s physicality and ability to disrupt passing lanes proved to give the Nittany Lions serious trouble, the team understood the challenge ahead and can use the loss as a way to improve.

“I think our team knew that we could be in this game with them, and I think we proved that,” sophomore goaltender Maddy Campbell said. "A lot of people didn’t think that we really could have as close games with them.”

title: No. 4 Penn State women's hockey drops second-straight game to No. 2 Ohio State
author: Mashiah Mitchell | The Daily Collegian
description:
Correction: After the game, officials changed the stats to credit Penn State's assists on its goal to Grace Tullock and Megan Hosman; the original version of this story attributed it to Kylie Amelkovich. The Daily Collegian apologizes for this error and any confusion.

After an overtime thriller on Banner Night that didn’t fall in Penn State’s favor, losing 2-1, the Nittany Lions looked to prevent falling to 0-2 early in the season at all costs, primed for the second leg of their series against the Ohio State Buckeyes.

In another close contest, Penn State came up short, once again falling 2-1.

This entire series was an early testament to the grit and resilience of this Nittany Lions team, and it was the theme of both these games from start to finish.

The Nittany Lions’ 2026 PWHL draftees Tessa Janecke, Leah Stecker, Maddy Christian, Katie DeSa, Katelyn Roberts, Kendall Butze and Mya Vaslet all returned to Happy Valley for the ceremonial puck drop. The alumni received a standing ovation not only for what they provided for the program, but also for what they will provide at the next level as well.

From the moment the players hit the ice in Pegula Ice Arena, the physicality was evident from both teams, with hits coming at what felt like immediately into the action.

Star forward Grace Outwater showed her prowess early and never looked back, getting the blue and white in the scoring column less than five minutes into the first period off of a picture-perfect breakout pass. Credited with setting up the goal were Grace Tullock and Megan Hosman.

This small lead would only last so long, with Ohio State’s sophomore forward Hilda Svensson scoring swiftly on a power play. This power play came after Sofia Ismael and Mira Jungåker got into a small shoving match, which resulted in Ismael hitting the penalty box, something that would become a common theme for this match for both teams.

There were over 14 combined minutes spent in the penalty box by both teams, with 12 of the 14 minutes coming across the first two periods alone. To say these two teams wanted to thoroughly prove that they were better than the other is an understatement.

Though the Buckeyes were able to net two goals in each of the first two periods, goaltender Maddy Campbell was the savior of the back line today, with 24 saves before the third period got underway.

It felt almost inevitable that the Buckeyes would score in the second period with how they controlled the puck for what felt like the period’s entirety. With 15 shots in the 20-minute frame, it was only a matter of time before the defense caved.

Furthermore, the shot differential was a big tell for the flow of the game up to this point. The Buckeyes outshot the blue and white by nearly three times their total, 26-9.

There was a lot of noticeable frustration from the Nittany Lions, more specifically from Outwater, who had multiple verbal exchanges with her opponents. Even at the end of the period, Outwater and sophomore forward Kassidy Carmichael had to be separated as they were jawing at one another.

The third period offered up many opportunities for the Nittany Lions; unfortunately, they were opportunities that the blue and white were unable to capitalize on, falling short to the Buckeyes once again.

The attack from the blue and white was an interesting tale for the day, with it looking like two different teams at certain line changes and substitutions. With it still being early into the season and coach Jeff Kampersall still integrating all the new talent, this is more than expected.

Up Next

Following this series, Penn State will get a week off before returning to Pegula to welcome the Robert Morris Colonials to Hockey Valley for their first AHA conference series. This comes after the Colonials’ series against Post University.

On the opposite end, this will mark the third game of the Nittany Lions’ four-game homestand before hitting the road.

title: Penn State men’s soccer remains winless in conference play after falling to No. 2 Indiana
author: Zach Schroder | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State traveled to Bloomington to face off against No.2 Indiana early Friday afternoon. The Hoosiers came in leading in points and without a conference loss, while the Nittany Lions looked to secure their first Big Ten win of the season.

The blue and white faced off against a Goliath, with Indiana ranked second in the country and undefeated on the year.

Ultimately, Penn State lost 2-1 to the No. 2 Hoosiers. Remaining winless in conference play.

1st Half

The Nittany Lions earned the first free kick of the match after a foul from junior defender Nick McHenry. The free kick flew into the box, but junior keeper Michal Mroz ran out to catch it.

Indiana had the first shot of the game; redshirt senior midfielder Alex Matthews' kick was saved by freshman goalkeeper Daniel Peluffo-Wiese. The Hoosiers heated up after a passive first ten minutes of action with two additional shots in the 12th minute. One was blocked while the other was saved by Peluffo-Wiese.

The blue and white took their first true shot when junior forward Etienne Reck put one right on Mroz’s chest. The Nittany Lions followed up with a couple of corner kicks, with the second high-flying out of bounds.

Penn State’s offense added some pressure of their own; they kept the ball on Indiana’s half for an extended period of time. The Hoosiers had a fast possession with another great save from Peluffo-Wiese. The Nittany Lion defense was aided by a couple of over-the-crossbar shots from Indiana.

McHenry earned the first yellow card of the game for unsporting behavior in the 24th minute of action. Senior forward Oliver Moller-Jensen broke free and put a shot in the bottom right corner after a nice run for the first score of the game. Penn State fell behind 1-0 in the 28th minute. The blue and white earned two yellows quickly after they conceded, one coming from an assistant coach for dissent and another for unsporting.

Both squads traded offensive possession deep in each other's territories to end the half, trading many fouls as well. The Hoosiers applied heavy pressure in the final five minutes. The first half was very chippy; Penn State had nine fouls while Indiana, which leads the conference in fouls, had seven.

2nd Half

The chippiness continued into the second half with three fouls in the first three minutes of play. After a quiet first 7 minutes of play, Penn State tied the game. Senior defender Morgan Marshall curved a beautiful shot into the top left corner of the net; he was assisted by senior forward Amadou Kone. The match was tied 1-1 in the 53rd minute of play.

Marshall applied more pressure with a shot through a defender's legs; Mroz made the save. On the other side of the pitch, the other goal-scorer in the game, Moller-Jensen, created his own pressure with a shot off target. After the equalizing goal, the Hoosiers upped their energy back to what it was before they scored their goal. Four throw-ins and a corner later, Moller-Jensen takes another shot that is blocked by the Nittany Lions.

The two squads traded more shots: junior defender Noah Forster for the Nittany Lions and Wes Carnevale for the Hoosiers; Mroz saved his while Penn State blocked theirs. Indiana earned a free kick in a great scoring opportunity for them, but junior forward Stephane Njike skyed it over the crossbar.

The blue and white quickly made it to the other box, and Reck shot top left, but Mroz saved it; a second opportunity went over the net. The back-and-forth continued when Mollar-Jensen placed a kick in top center between the posts for his second goal of the match, assisted by Njike. The Hoosiers now led 2-1 in the 76th minute.

After Indiana’s go-ahead score, the Nittany Lions struggled to get any offensive rhythm against the Hoosiers defensive lines. Senior midfielder Noah Andreas drew a foul that resulted in a penalty; he also went down with a leg injury on the play; Njike’s kick was blocked by Peluffo-Wiese; he had a second opportunity, but it soared over the goal.

The physicality and chippiness continued until the end of the game with three more fouls between the 85th and 86th minute. A VAR review was conducted for a handball, but Penn State did not receive a penalty kick. The match would end with a near-miss shot from Carnevale taking too much time off the clock for the blue and white.

Penn State returns home to Happy Valley to face off against UCLA at 7 p.m. Monday at Jeffrey Field.

title: Supreme Court clears way for Trump administration to deploy ‘expansive’ voter database ahead of midterms
author: Jonathon Chiu | The Daily Collegian
description:
The Supreme Court ruled on Friday to approve the deployment of an “expansive” voter screening system by the Trump administration ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections, according to reporting from the New York Times and National Public Radio.

The ruling, which is not attributed to any individual Supreme Court justice, reverses a June 22 federal court ruling that prevented the use of the Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements (SAVE) data system to collect the citizenship information of Americans for the purposes of searching for noncitizen voters.

Justices Ketanji Brown Jackson Sonia Sotomayor and Elena Kagan dissented Friday’s ruling.

It is unclear how the use of SAVE’s data will impact who can vote in the upcoming midterms, as federal law bars the removal of people from voting roles within 90 days of a federal election.

In a dissent authored by Jackson, she warned that Friday’s Supreme Court ruling ignores the potential harms of allowing states to use SAVE’s data to “cancel the voter registrations of at least some recently naturalized citizens or force such persons to provide proof of citizenship before voting."

SAVE, was originally created in 1986 to allow “federal, state and local government agencies to verify the citizenship and immigration status of noncitizens applying for public benefits,” according to Friday’s ruling.

President Donald Trump signed an executive order on March 31, 2025 to allow for the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to expand SAVE with new systems to allow state and local authorities to verify the citizenship status of both registered voters and those in the process of registering to vote.

On April 22, 2025, DHS, in conjunction with the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) and U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS), announced plans for "comprehensive optimization” of SAVE, which Friday’s Supreme Court ruling said were completed and released the following month.

According to the ruling, the “modified” SAVE program now allows state and local authorities to input someone’s first and last name, date of birth and full or partial social security number into the database’s portal. This information would then be checked with the Social Security Administration’s (SSA) records to verify that the searched individual has U.S. citizenship.

Failure to obtain this status requires authorities to contact the person being searched to confirm their citizenship in order to remain eligible to either remain registered or be able to register to vote, according to the ruling.

Several legal challenges were filed following the release of the updated SAVE database and its use for searching the citizenship status of voters, including a lawsuit from the Electronic Privacy Information Center and affiliates of the League of Women Voters which alleges the Trump administration had unlawfully compiled sensitive information into SAVE and set up the data system as a potential tool for voter suppression.

title: New Bellisario Dean Emily Metzgar’s first goal is to ‘listen and learn’
author: Neel Ved | The Daily Collegian
description:
On July 1, Emily Metzgar started her role as the dean of the Donald P. Bellisario School of Communications. Metzgar succeeded Interim Dean Denise Bortree after the departure of former Dean Marie Hardin.

Prior to joining Penn State, Metzgar was the director at the School of Media and Journalism at Kent State in the College of Communications and Information. There, she led the media school through rapidly changing journalism and higher education landscapes.

When Metzgar learned that Bellisario was looking for a new dean, she said she applied for the position without any hesitation given that the college has a great reputation.

“There are fantastic students here, and wonderful faculty who really care about the students,” Metzgar said. “On our website it says ‘Big School Resources, Small School Feel,’ I know that this is actually true. Our staff colleagues are just as committed as the faculty to helping students succeed.”

Metzgar described that her job is not a “clean up job,” as Bellisario is in a fantastic position.

Prior to working in higher education Metzgar served as a Foreign Service Officer for the U.S. Department of State in Beijing and worked in policy analysis. She said working in public diplomacy helped influence how she views media education in today's society.

“The experience that I have had has shown me how important communication is,” Metzgar said. “One of the most important things I learned with some of the policy and political writing that I had done in the past was that it is really important to choose words carefully.”

As this is Metzgar’s first year, she said one of her main goals is to listen, learn and ask questions. She said she wants to get a sense of what’s working well and what can be improved, as well as developing pre-existing relationships.

Since joining Penn State, one of Metzgar’s favorite discoveries of the Penn State community is how kind and supportive everyone is.

“When my appointment was announced, I had nothing but supportive and kind outreach from people via email, social media and interacting with people,” Metzgar said. “Penn State is a large institution but there is really an environment that feels supportive in ways that can be really hard to foster. It is remarkable.”

During her time working across different colleges at Kent State, there was an interest in developing a course that had to do with artificial intelligence, ethics and privacy.

“She understood the importance of exposing our students to this,” Amy Reynolds, dean of the College of Communications and Information at Kent State, said. “She also worked with faculty who were interested in supporting professional development.”

Reynolds added that there were lots of workshops and initiatives across the country for AI, and Metzgar made it a priority to support that work. One thing that stood out about Metzgar’s leadership, Reynolds said, was that she was ready to lead from day one.

“My first goal is to listen and learn. I think that's the number one rule for someone stepping into a new role like this. Just listen and learn, ask lots and lots of questions, and get a sense of what's working, what's working really well, what might be able to work a little bit better,” Metzgar said.

In fall 2019, the College of Communications and Information at Kent State conducted a national search for a director of the School of Media and Journalism. In the spring of 2020, Metzgar accepted the position.

“We had faculty searches going on across the college as well as university leadership positions across Kent State,” Reynolds said. “At the start of the pandemic a lot of people were nervous about changing jobs, which were beyond the normal ways one might transition to a new position. Emily was not phased by that.”

Gary Abdullah, the assistant dean for diversity and inclusion at Donald P. Bellisario School of Communications, said when some leaders come into a new role, they immediately make changes and put their stamps on everything.

One of the shared goals between Metzgar's office and Abdullah’s office is that they want to make sure that the community and culture of the Bellisario college stays on point. Metzgar has encouraged Abdullah to continue the work they do across the college with the faculty, staff and students to make sure that Bellisario is a welcoming place for everyone.

“She has wholeheartedly believed in the Belisario college family mantra. We're gonna keep pushing that. I believe she's going to help us continue that,” Abdullah said.

Abdullah said Metzgar’s level of observance will be beneficial to the college. He also said one of the areas she’ll have the biggest impact on is the college's long-term planning.

Abdullah added that they want to make sure they maintain the small-school feel by getting to know each other.

“I truly do believe that she has the vision and the leadership necessary to help us continue to be good at what we do, but to get even stronger in other things,” Abdullah said.

title: Penn State vs. Wisconsin preview | How to watch, betting odds and more
author: Noah Aberegg | The Daily Collegian
description:
It’s homecoming week at Penn State, with the Nittany Lions welcoming Wisconsin to Beaver Stadium to open Big Ten play with the Helmet Stripe game.

Things will kick off in Beaver Stadium at 5 p.m. Saturday. Penn State has a slim, 12-9 lead in the all-time series and looks to improve that in Matt Campbell’s first-ever game against the Badgers.

Here’s more information on the weather, betting odds and a look at both teams ahead of Week 4.

Forecast

With the late afternoon kickoff, the game will start with the sun shining and end under the lights.

The temperature will be a high of 69 degrees during the day. In the evening, it will drop to a high of 47 degrees.

There’s a 24% chance of precipitation during the contest.

Betting, how to watch

The sportsbooks currently predict the closest margin of the season for Penn State, with the Nittany Lions entering as a 9.5 point favorite over the Badgers, according to FanDuel.

The over-under is set at 44.5 points.

The game will air on Peacock, with tickets available for the game as low as $40.95 on Ticketmaster.

About Wisconsin

While Penn State faced a trio of easy teams to start the season, the Badgers opened their nonconference slate hosting then-No. 4 Notre Dame, resulting in a 41-13 blowout.

Wisconsin enters this weekend with a 2-1 record, but has the experience playing against a top-five team, something the Nittany Lions don’t have.

The Badgers are led by quarterback Colton Joseph, who has proven to be a dual-threat option. He’s passed for 752 yards and five touchdowns while also rushing for 82 yards and another score. However, he’s thrown two interceptions so far, something Penn State’s lockdown secondary may look to bite on.

On the ground, former Iowa State running back Abu Sama III is coming off of an injury that forced him to miss last week's matchup against Eastern Michigan. He still leads the team with 156 rushing yards and may be the most established running back the Nittany Lions have faced so far.

A week after Penn State locked down wide receiver Chance Morrow against Buffalo, it’ll have another wide receiver threat in Tyrell Henry, who recorded 14 receptions in Week 3.

The Badgers defense has allowed an average of 20 points per game, with a majority coming in Notre Dame’s 41-point outing in the season-opener. However, they’ve forced three turnovers — including a pair of interceptions — and could be looking to hand Rocco Becht his first turnover of the year.

About Penn State

The Nittany Lions have shown through three weeks that they’re a team capable of putting a lot of points on the board and locking down opposing offenses.

Becht has developed strong connections with many of his weapons. With Howard out for Saturday, Becht will likely look for Chase Sowell and Brett Eskildsen, as well as the three tight ends who started against Buffalo — barring Andrew Rappleyea is healthy enough to play.

Wide receiver Zay Robinson has also been a threat in the passing game, tallying five receptions for 80 yards and a touchdown this season. He’s also shined while returning punts and is waiting for his moment to return one to the end zone.

Defensively, Penn State’s pass rush took a big step forward against Buffalo and has paired with the linebackers and secondary to allow an average of 7.3 points per game.

Injury updates

The injury to Howard dealt a major blow to Penn State earlier in the week, as Campbell said he’d be out an “extended period of time.”

Outside of the star wide receiver, center Brock Riker, tight end Andrew Rappleyea and linebacker Cam Smith were all listed as questionable on Thursday’s availability report.

The team had several other players listed as out and questionable, including safety Omarion Davis as probable. However, they are mainly depth pieces who likely wouldn’t play on Saturday.

title: Players to watch | QB Colton Joseph, LB Cooper Catalano headline Wisconsin’s notables
author: Andrew Deal | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State’s first Big Ten game will begin with a home matchup against Wisconsin at 5 p.m. Saturday, with the Badgers coming into the matchup on a two-game winning streak.

Wisconsin’s lead running back Abu Sama III — a former rusher under Matt Campbell at Iowa State — is currently questionable but is expected to play, which could leave the pass game as more of a focal point considering Sama might not be 100%.

Here’s some players to watch on Wisconsin’s side of the field ahead of Saturday evening’s Big Ten battle.

Colton Joseph, quarterback

The first name to watch is Colton Joseph, who transferred to Wisconsin from Old Dominion after two seasons with the Monarchs.

Joseph’s dual threat ability has continued with the Badgers after rushing for just over 1,000 yards last year at Old Dominion. Currently, Joseph has the most rushes of any Wisconsin player, running 25 times for 82 yards and a touchdown. While it does count towards his mark, Joseph has been sacked for just 12 yards, not playing too much of a factor in his total.

On the passing side, Joseph has a 63.5% completion percentage and is best when he’s rolling out of the pocket. His 752 yards are good for eighth in the Big Ten, just ahead of Penn State’s Rocco Becht.

Joseph’s mix of running and passing could cause issues to a Penn State team who hasn’t quite dealt with a quarterback as dynamic as Joseph this season.

Tyrell Henry, wide receiver

The Nittany Lions’ defense will once again have to face a receiver who’s far and away the quarterback’s top target. Tyrell Henry has caught 22 passes for 293 yards through three games, which is significantly more than the next closest wideout. Chris Brooks Jr. is second on the team with eight catches for 168 yards.

However, Henry’s numbers are inflated due to Wisconsin’s blowout win against Eastern Michigan, where the senior caught 14 passes for 160 yards. This also could mean he comes in with a lot of momentum albeit against a team from the MAC.

In Wisconsin’s first game of the year, and facing a secondary that lines up with the talent that Penn State has, Henry caught four passes for 42 yards in the Badgers’ 41-13 loss to Notre Dame.

If that stays constant against statistically one of the top secondaries in the country, it could be a lot of Joseph and the run game against the Nittany Lions. Cornerbacks Daryus Dixson and Audavion Collins will likely be tasked with slowing down Wisconsin’s top receiving threat.

Cooper Catalano, linebacker

On the defensive side of the ball, Cooper Catalano has proven to be the team’s leading linebacker early in the season.

Catalano was one of the standouts on defense in Wisconsin's opener against Notre Dame, where he totaled nine tackles. The sophomore emerged as a viable linebacker last year as a true freshman in some of Wisconsin’s toughest games. In the Badgers’ upset win over then-No. 23 Washington, Catalano recorded 19 tackles.

This year he’s been given the keys to the defense as the MIKE linebacker, meaning he’s responsible for relaying play calls with the green dot. Catalano leads the team with 26 tackles through three games.

Matthew Jung, safety

In the back end of Wisconsin’s defense, Matthew Jung has been a turnover producer through the Badgers’ nonconference slate. While recording 20 tackles, he also forced a fumble and an interception.

Statistically, Jung had his best game in the season-opener, where he notched nine tackles. The senior can add extra size in the run game with his linebacker-like build, standing at 6-foot-3, 213 pounds.

Jung’s experience in his final year could play a major factor in the defense’s production against Penn State’s offense. While the Nittany Lions don’t have Koby Howard, Jung and the defense still have to focus on other threats in the pass game.

The safety will likely have to play as he did against Notre Dame for Wisconsin’s defense to shut down Penn State’s offense.

title: Penn State women’s soccer loses control in second half, ties Iowa in a back-and-forth match
author: Ava Aguiar | The Daily Collegian
description:
After a weekend win at Maryland, Penn State women’s soccer returned to Jeffrey Field on Thursday night, taking on the Iowa Hawkeyes during this season’s White Out match.

Coming off back-to-back wins against Minnesota and the Terrapins, the Nittany Lions looked to go 3-1 in conference play and continue their offensive dominance from key players Aubrey Kulpa, Paige Kalal and Anna Babcock.

However, what was sure to be another strong offensive showing quickly turned for the worse in the second half.

Within minutes of the first half, the blue and white put the pressure on the Hawkeyes, taking immediate possession of the ball and control of the game. One minute into play, Kalal took a shot that just missed off the net, before Kulpa was able to score her fourth goal of the season just three minutes later.

The two have been a force to reckon with all season, being tied for 12th in points in the Big Ten, and consistently building plays together. Kulpa attributes their partnership to their friendship outside of the sport.

“I think it’s building an authentic relationship outside of the soccer field. I remember she came in last spring and I had dinner with her, and we just enjoyed each other’s presence,” Kulpa said. “I got to know her, and I think a lot of our play on this field and in games starts on the training field.”

The Hawkeyes continued to struggle through the first half on defense, as Penn State continued to take up space in their box. Iowa didn’t see its first chance to score until ten minutes into the game.

The gold and black failed to make the play, taking another shot in the 32nd minute that was caught by keeper Mackenzie Gress.

Trying to get the momentum back, Iowa saw five substitutions, as Kalal, Kulpa and Babcock came off the field. Iowa’s Liana Tarasco took another shot towards the goal, but it was blocked again by Gress.

The Hawkeyes made their move in the second half, taking control of the game with the blue and white working over time to keep them off the board. After 70 minutes of trailing, Iowa’s Sara Batchadji scored to tie up the game at 1-1, and left the Nittany Lions fighting to defend their goal.

“I think obviously in the first half, we had plenty of opportunities to put this game away. I thought we came out of the second half like it was just going to come,” coach Erica Dambach said. “I think we played the first half on our terms and the second half on their terms.”

The second half was full of whistles, competition and aggression, as multiple yellow calls were made against Iowa for unsporting, and a missed call on a shove by an Iowa player saw everyone up in arms.

“I think the biggest thing is feeling prepared when those moments happen, so they know what they’re going to say in the circle. They know what they’re going to say when they come over to the sideline; they know when there’s going to be tactical changes,” Dambach said. “We’re really just trying to take the element of surprise or shutting off, making sure you’re keeping it in.”

A near goal by Hawkeye Lucia Englund in the 81st minute almost put the game away to leave Iowa going home with their first conference win of the season and Penn State their second Big Ten loss.

Going into their game against USC on Sunday, Dambach emphasized the importance of focusing on six 15-minute segments and playing hard for the full 90.

“The strength of this team is in our depth. We’ve got players that can come in and change the game, and we want to make sure that not only when we make subs do we maintain,” Dambach said. “But we get stronger, and that happened in the first half. In the second half I thought the starters didn’t do the job; it’s whoever is on the field and needs to make sure that they dominate.”

title: “Nothing to lose out there” | Stickney stands out for No. 4 Penn State in collegiate debut
author: Elliott Inscho | The Daily Collegian
description:
Even before Morgan Stickney skated between the pipes at Pegula Ice Arena for the first time, Jeff Kampersal knew that he’d found a competitor in the 5-foot-8 goaltender.

However, the tenth-year coach certainly didn’t expect his first-year netminder to make 42 saves in her collegiate debut on Thursday.

“We knew she would compete her butt off, but maybe not to the extent she did [tonight],” Kampersal said.

A St. Charles, Missouri, native, Stickney has played in big games before. She represented Team USA at the U18 Women’s World Championship in 2025 and 2026, claiming silver and gold medals, respectively, in the two tournaments.

That experience was part of the reason Kampersal threw her into the fire to open both Penn State’s season and Stickney’s tenure as a Nittany Lion. Stickney said that despite the stakes, she approached the matchup the same way she would any other.

“There were some nerves,” Stickney said. “But I think if you play nervous, you’re only going to regret it. I just went into it and embraced it. Nothing to lose out there.”

Stickney’s stops were good for a 0.957 save percentage against the No. 2-ranked Buckeyes as part of a solid all-around defensive performance. Skaters in front of her blocked 26 shots, led by Ashley Kokavec, who blocked four.

“We talked a lot about blocking shots coming into this weekend, and every time they block a shot, I'm just very grateful,” Stickney said. “I was like, 'Hey guys, keep up the good work.’”

15 of Stickney’s saves came in the first period, and she made five more in the second before Kaia Malachino pounced on a rebound and flicked the puck into the net.

Grace Outwater scored Penn State’s lone goal off the third period’s opening faceoff. The junior forward scored 24 goals last season en route to totaling 40 points.

“She's our go-to player at this point,” Kampersal said. “She's come back and been able to play long minutes and be as good in the third period as she was in the first, so that was huge.”

After allowing the first goal, Stickney denied every Ohio State shot for the rest of regulation. She surrendered the game-winner on the first shot of overtime when Joy Dunne skated in front of the net, worked past a pick by Hilda Svensson and fired a wrister past her blocker and into the nylon.

Dunne’s winner came on the Buckeyes’ 46th shot of the game, more than double Penn State’s total of 21.

“We're generally in the other position where we're out shooting people,” Kampersal said. “It's just a matter of being urgent, but being patient. Because they play so aggressively, they will give up odd rushes, and we need to finish those.”

After the game, Kampersal was hesitant to commit to Stickney as his season-long starter.

Maddy Campbell, a sophomore who saw action in 11 games last season, is also in the mix to battle for the starting role. She logged a .935 save percentage, 1.44 goals-against average and four shutouts as a freshman behind Katie DeSa.

“Campbell is really legit as well, so it's coming down to week-by-week competition,” Kampersal said. “A big game like today for Morgan obviously helps her cause, but they both will compete against each other and try to raise each other's effort.”

Kampersal said that he and goaltender coach Moe Bradley will decide on Friday’s starter after watching Thursday’s tape. Still, he was impressed by Stickney’s poise in her debut, especially given the raucous student section that set the tone in Pegula.

“Even though the Roar Zone is for you and they're behind you, that can be intimidating,” Kampersal said. “She stepped up and played great.”

For Stickney, it was a game long in the making, and a moment that she made the most of.

“It was awesome,” Stickney said of her debut. “I was really looking forward to this day, and it didn’t let [me] down.”
