title: Penn State women's soccer draws Iowa in high intensity match
author: Sara Castrovinci | The Daily Collegian
description:
Battling under the lights at Jeffrey Field for Penn State’s annual White Out match, the Nittany Lions took on Iowa for their fourth conference game of the season.

The Hawkeyes forced Penn State to a 1-1 draw, ending its streak of consecutive wins.

The blue and white kicked off offensive action in the second minute of gameplay with a shot placed just right of the net by senior forward Paige Kalal. Penn State dominated the pitch through the first ten minutes, confining play to the Hawkeyes’ final third.

Building off of their attacking momentum, Brooklyn Antonucci found Aubrey Kulpa in Iowa’s box, where the junior forward was able to find contact with the ball on her right foot and netted an early goal for Penn State in the fourth minute of play.

The Hawkeyes took back some of the momentum after Kulpa’s goal, with some offensive pressure and breakaway moments.

Iowa's pressure stints slowly faded as the Nittany Lions regained most of possession. The Hawkeyes’ back line thwarted the attacking pressure from the blue and white and landed the ball in Hannah Jordan’s feet. The sophomore defender lacked pressure from Iowa and struck a hard-hit ball just over the crossbar.

Iowa began capitalizing on Penn State’s missteps, sending consistent through balls to Lucia Englund on the right wing and pressuring defender Lily Boyden.

Kulpa almost had goal No. 2 in the 26th minute of the match after striking a powerful ball to the top center of the net, saved by Galt. The Cromwell, Connecticut, native has proven to be a major offensive threat for the blue and white, leading with nine points on the season via three goals and three assists.

“We just wanted to come out strong, focus on us, dominate what we need to dominate and you guys definitely can see that in the first half,” said Kulpa.

Not much offensive opportunity came for either program until the 34th minute of the match when Kaelyn Wolfe rocketed a shot just off target, her first attacking appearance for the night.

The level of physicality between the two teams continued to rise throughout the match, leading to Hawkeyes’ Abby Skiff earning a yellow card just outside the top of their 18-yard box, the first time any player had been booked all match.

Penn State couldn’t capitalize on the free-kick awarded to them. The final six minutes of play were back and forth between the programs, leading to no goal-scoring opportunities.

At the end of the half, The Nittany Lions tallied four corners and nine shots on goal, proving their offensive domination and winning the first half of play 1-0 over Iowa.

The blue and white opened up second-half play with a set piece in the 47th minute that was easily countered by the Hawkeyes’ back line led by Sara Batchadji and Millie Greer.

Iowa showcased more composure in its formation throughout the half, slowing down Penn State’s offensive efforts.

Coming into this matchup, Iowa allowed only one goal against its defense in its three Big Ten games, showcasing defensive strength and a formidable challenge for Penn State's attack.

In the 57th minute, the Nittany Lions were shown a yellow card for dissent that was quickly followed by a yellow card in the 58th minute on Molly Martin for unsportsmanlike conduct.

Unlike in the first half of play, the blue and white were unable to capitalize on its counterattack efforts. The Hawkeyes’ offense found themselves sitting more comfortably in the blue and white final third.

“They made some tactical adjustments. I thought we played the first half on our terms and the second half on their terms, said coach Dambach.

Despite Iowa turning the tide offensively, the Hawkeyes still sat at five shots to Penn State’s 15 on the match at the 68th-minute mark.

In the 70th minute of the high-intensity match, Batchadji appeared to attempt to place the ball into the box, looking for a white shirt to run onto it. The ball took an awkward bounce and ended up over Mackenzie Gress’s head and into the back of the net, tying the match at 1-1.

“I think she thought there was going to be a header from a defender and kind of misread it a little bit, and you know that stuff happens,” said Dambach. “She's been incredible for us all season long, and I thought that for 89 minutes she continued to be incredible today.”

With the Nittany Lions unable to create any major goal-scoring opportunities in the final few minutes of play and Iowa’s switch in offensive pressure and late equalizer, the blue and white ended the match at 1-1, leaving them at 4-2-3 for the season.

Up next

The Nittany Lions are back at Jeffrey Field, set to host USC at 1 p.m. for their Military Appreciation game.

title: Penn State women's hockey suffers 2-1 defeat to Ohio State in OT to open season
author: Rafael Rivera | The Daily Collegian
description:
It was a special one in Pegula Ice Arena on Thursday night as Penn State suited up for its first game of the season against No. 2 Ohio State. The team honored the 2025 squad by unveiling the Frozen Four and AHA Championship banners from the rafters before the game.

Ultimately, the ceremonies and home advantage couldn't benefit the blue and white en route to a narrow 2-1 overtime defeat to the Buckeyes.

First period

The game started off physical as the Buckeyes and Nittany Lions traded big hits. Ohio State possessed most of the puck, with the blue and white getting the occasional counterattack.

12:48 into the first half, Ohio State received a power play after freshman Lorelai Nelson was sent to the box for a tripping penalty.

The penalty kill ended up holding it down with freshman netminder Morgan Stickney denying every shot that came her way. After more Ohio State possession of the puck, Penn State got a power play for interference on the scarlet and gray's Jenna Raunio, yet nothing formulated.

The period ended with Ohio State leading 15-0 on shots.

Second period

The Second period started off more of the same until Grace Outwater got a breakaway one-on-one with the goaltender. She got the shot on target, but Ohio State's Genny Klein saved it, but it was the first on-goal for the blue and white all game.

With 14:07 left in the second period, the Nittany Lions got another power play after Maxine Cimironi was called for slashing, but nothing flourished, as only one shot was put on goal. Soon after, with 10:44 left, Ohio State found the net after a shot by Kaia Malachino that slid past Stickney.

It was only a matter of time before the Buckeyes scored, as prior to the goal, Ohio State put up 20 shots on Stickney before the goal, compared to Penn State's three on Klein.

The Nittany Lions then got into penalty trouble midway through the period, with Nelson and Abby Stonehouse each getting penalized. The blue and white’s penalty kill ended up thwarting Ohio State's power-play unit. Penn State's attack seemed to still have trouble possessing the puck, with the Buckeyes hounding for every loose chance.

Stickney continued to impress, flashing the leather and saving some dangerous shots on goal. The Nittany Lions attack looked better to finish the second period, getting some shots on goal to test Klein. The frame concluded with Ohio State leading shots 26-9, again dominating offensively for another stretch.

Third period

Penn State started the period off with a bang 11 seconds in as Nittany Lions captain Outwater sifted through the Buckeyes' blueline to tie the game 1-1. The blue and white seemed to play with a newfound intensity after the equalizer, looking more confident and physical overall. After a stretch of end-to-end hockey, the Nittany Lions got into penalty trouble as Nelson got her third penalty of the game with 14:31 left on the clock. It didn't matter; true freshman Stickney continued her stellar first game as Penn State's netminder, fending off Ohio State's power play effortlessly.

Things got chippy with 9:18 to go as Ohio State's Joy Dunne and Penn State’s Danica Manyard each got two minutes in the box for roughing. After returning to full strength, the Nittany Lions got a power play after the scarlet and grey got a penalty for too many men on the ice. Penn State's power play looked the best it had been all day, having many good looks, but Klein ended up stopping every shot that came her way.

The momentum seemed to shift the Nittany Lions way on a dime with the squad getting another power play after a roughing penalty on Kate Viel. The blue and white’s power play looked electric, creating many opportunities to score, but yet again Klein stifled the attack. The teams then battled it out for the next six minutes, sending the game to overtime.

Overtime

Unfortunately for the Nittany Lions, overtime didn’t last long, as Dunne scored the game-winning goal on a slap shot.

Penn State suffered a stinger, having a top team in the nation on the ropes, although it still signals a contest with optimistic takeaways. After a slow start, the Nittany Lions rebounded with an energetic third period, as they showed flashes of what they could be. Leading the performance for the blue and white was Stickney, who had a stellar true freshman debut for the blue and white, saving 42 shots against the No.2 team in the nation.

Up Next

The Nittany Lions will finish the series with the Buckeyes on Friday in a White Out game at 4 pm.

title: Penn State men’s lacrosse defender Owen Tasse selected No. 11 overall in 2026 NLL Draft
author: Elliott Inscho | The Daily Collegian
description:
Jeff Tambroni will have an NLL Draft pick to work with in 2026.

The Las Vegas Desert Dogs selected defenseman Owen Tasse with the No. 11 overall pick in the 2026 NLL Draft on Sunday. Tasse, a graduate student who transferred from St. Bonaventure over the summer, has yet to sport the blue and white.

The 6-foot-4 long pole recorded 30 caused turnovers and scooped 59 ground balls in his final season with the Bonnies, totaling 54 and 97 respectively in his four years with the team.

NLL connections run deep in the Ottawa, Ontario, native’s family.

Tasse’s father, Jason, played professionally for the NLL’s Ottawa Rebel, posting four goals and three assists in 16 games played. His brother, Payton, was drafted by the Halifax Thunderbirds with the No. 73 overall pick in 2025.

While he’ll play field lacrosse this spring at Penn State, Tasse has vast box experience that will translate to the NLL. With his brother, he won the Founders Cup, Canada’s Junior B box lacrosse championship, in 2022 as part of the Nepean Knights.

Tasse also claimed the Minto Cup, the Junior A championship, the next year with the Burlington Blaze.

Penn State’s last NLL Draft picks came in 2023, when Jack Posey and Chris Jordan were both selected by the Calgary Roughnecks. The Nittany Lions’ last first-rounder was Mac O’Keefe, who went No. 15 overall in 2020.

According to NLL rules, teams can draft any player who has completed four years of college lacrosse, even if they plan to return for a fifth season like Tasse. The Desert Dogs will retain his exclusive rights until he wraps up his collegiate career in Happy Valley.

title: Federal military offices rescind order pausing sponsored Penn State projects
author: Jonathon Chiu | The Daily Collegian
description:
The Office of Naval Research and Army Research Office contacted several members of the Penn State research community on Friday ordering the pause of several research projects, according to an email sent to faculty members obtained by The Daily Collegian.

On Monday, the directive ordering the pause was rescinded, Penn State’s Senior Vice President for Research Andrew Read wrote in the email.

The directive was issued on Friday to the university’s Office of Sponsored Programs as well as several members of Penn State’s research community.

Read said in the email that there has been “minimal disruption to research activities” as a result of the directive, but admitted that its issuing had caused “a weekend of serious concern” among Penn State researchers. He stressed for any researcher who had received word of the order to contact the university’s Office of Sponsored Programs for assistance.

The directive came after the U.S. Department of Defense (DoD) ordered Penn State and 29 other academic institutions to review their ties and collaborations with “foreign entities of concern” in late August.

Read said Friday’s directive “appears to be related” to the DoD’s order, and that several other universities also saw the now-rescinded order to pause sponsored research projects.

He said his office, in conjunction with Penn State President Neeli Bendapudi, the university’s Office of Government and Community Relations and Office of General Counsel, will continue to engage “constructively” with the federal government to learn more about the nature of the DoD’s initial request.

He added that Penn State is working with the Association of American Universities and Association of Public and Land-Grant Universities to understand the nature of the Aug. 21 request, and to remain in contact with the 29 other universities impacted by the order.

“We recognize that the grant suspension messages were unsettling for those affected, given the potential impact that disruptions to sponsored research can have on research programs and individuals’ livelihoods,” Read wrote in the email. “Although the suspensions have been lifted, we understand that questions and concerns remain, and we are committed to supporting you and keeping you informed as we continue to monitor developments and engage with the Department of Defense/War.”

The Collegian has reached out to the university for comment. Officials confirmed it received the requests but have not sent a response in time for publication.

In July, Penn State and the U.S. Army signed a 10-year partnership agreement in which the university will provide environmental, architectural and engineering support services to the Army.

title: Penn State DT Armstrong Nnodim ‘felt great’ in return from injury, looks ahead to Wisconsin
author: Andrew Mercer | The Daily Collegian
description:
Armstrong Nnodim was set to be one of Penn State’s top defensive tackles to start the season, as the transfer from Oklahoma State improved exponentially in 2025, starting in four games and playing in 12.

However, the beginning of his first season as a Nittany Lion didn’t start as many expected. Nnodim suffered an injury in camp and missed the first two weeks of action.

But Nnodim returned to the gridiron against Buffalo on Saturday, and he voiced his relief to have made it back on the field.

“It felt great being out there with my guys,” Nnodim said Wednesday. “It felt great being able to be cultural. A lot of respect for Buffalo, but it was just a great feeling to get back out there.”

He said it was difficult being sidelined because of his love for football and his desire to help the team in any way he can. However, Nnodim had a conversation with Matt Campbell, who said he needed Nnodim to be fully healthy to play to avoid additional risk of injury in the nonconference schedule.

Nnodim called his first game in Beaver Stadium “electrifying.” He had two tackles in the 55-13 victory over the Bulls, and when he felt some rust, he could count on his teammates to lift his spirits.

“Every time I had my head down, it was only somebody in my corner to pick me up,” Nnodim said. “Remember that we have a bigger goal.”

Not only did Nnodim have the support of his teammates, coaches and fans, but also his family. His father was in attendance, and Nnodim said he is expecting to see more of his family in the crowd as the season goes on.

“It meant a lot because my pops sacrificed a lot for me,” Nnodim said. “Him, my mom and all my siblings. He’s one of the milestones that got me to this place.”

Going into Week 4 against Wisconsin, having Nnodim and fellow defensive tackle Alijah Carnell — who was also injured — back is really important. D’Anton Lynn said having injured players meant others were on the field too long and got fatigued.

Lynn said he wants to have four to five defensive tackles in the rotation, and Nnodim said having the depth back is important for keeping “fresh legs” on the field. He also said it’s a motivating factor, as everyone’s looking to fight for the right to play, one of Campbell’s philosophies.

“Every player is going to go 100% for the amount of plays we're in,” Nnodim said. “When you have that depth, it's like you can count on everybody and know that everybody's going to do their job.”

Although he’s only played one game under Lynn’s defensive scheme, he feels confident in his and his teammates abilities to get the job done and start the conference slate in the win column.

“Ever since I came here, I've been trusting what all the defensive coaches have been putting out there,” Nnodim said. “I've been trusting the process, and from that it's just been helping me expand my game.”

title: Penn State men’s soccer notebook | Coach Rob Dow talks matchup against No. 2 Indiana
author: Ava Aguiar | The Daily Collegian
description:
After a hard-fought match that ended with a loss in the last five minutes, with a goal from Michigan State, the Nittany Lions are gearing up for another tough game against No.2 Indiana.

Before heading to Bloomington to face off against the Hoosiers on Friday, coach Rob Dow met with the media to discuss the upcoming match.

Here is what was discussed.

The competition and mental preparation

The matchup with the Hoosiers marks the third Big Ten game in the blue and white’s schedule, and might just be their most competitive yet. Indiana’s record currently sits at 7-0-2, after tying against Wisconsin and Louisville. The Hoosiers are ranked second nationally and first in the Big Ten.

“Wisconsin played Indiana really well last night; they’re tough, they’re resilient, hardworking, they showed value points in which we want to show on Friday,” Dow said.

Penn State has faced the typical trial and error of working together as a new team and will look to take what they’ve learned from their previous Big Ten competitions to continue improving.

“The biggest thing I think we’re going to take from Michigan State, losing the game in the last five, six minutes of the match on a restart which is uncharacteristic for us is that we can’t just play 60 minutes, or 80 minutes or 89 minutes we have to be prepared to play 95,” Dow said.

The pressure is on as the Nittany Lions have a chance to put their potential on display, something that can take a toll on an athlete, but it’s early in the season and anybody’s game.

“The elephant in the room is every player chooses to come to Penn State and play in the Big Ten. There is no easy game. Indiana may be ranked in the teens a few weeks ago and now they’re number two,” Dow said. “When we get into the Big Ten and start playing each other we keep boosting each other’s rankings, and that’s what we wanted, it's about the small margins.”

Key players

Penn State forward Etienne Reck was back on the field after a hamstring injury saw him on the injury list since the team’s second match against Missouri State. Reck had an incredible last game bouncing back with multiple shot attempts and will look to continue playing while trying to stay healthy.

“He had a good week of training. We had some good continuity out of him, but he’s very important for us. Especially how we progress a ball out of our own half, he can hold the ball up,” Dow said. “I think he had a chance early in the match against Michigan State. If you caught him a week later, I think it’s just sharpness, his finite execution, his technique, and his head; he would have scored that.”

Referred to as an old-school nine, Dow will look for Reck to make some forward plays and to hopefully put some points on the board.

“It’s hard to find nines anymore. He’s a goal scorer; he’s in the box. Talking about defending out half, he can anticipate a clearance and hold and allow numbers to get up on the field,” Dow said. “He’s creative about when he has to lay it off and spin and also find gaps between the backline, especially over his right shoulder onto his left foot.”

However, he can’t do it alone, and players like Toby Grant and Beckham Brown will look to assist.

“But we need service until we get the ball into the box and whether that’s our inverted winger’s cutting in and finding him or my backs getting forward or wing backs getting forward, Brown, Grant to get service into his head is critical,” the Penn State skipper said.

Beside Reck, the team has a solid fullback squad, including Arian Recinos, who made his collegiate debut last week.

“Arian (Recinos) has some abilities to play in the center mid, so he’s somewhere in the depth chart too, but you have to have depth,” Dow said. “You can’t expect Arian in his second game to go 90, so Beckham’s going to have an important role to play.”

title: No. 14 Penn State women’s volleyball set for Mitten State matchups with Michigan, Michigan State
author: Elliott Inscho | The Daily Collegian
description:
Autumn has arrived, and so has Penn State’s conference slate. After compiling an 8-2 record to begin the campaign, the Nittany Lions will take a trip to the Mitten State for their first pair of Big Ten matchups against Michigan on Friday and Michigan State on Sunday.

Penn State’s schedule so far this season has only consisted of one true road game, against DePaul in Chicago, which ended in a sweep. Besides that, Penn State faced Kentucky at Wrigley Field for its only other match away from Happy Valley for the Nittany Lions, which ended in a blue and white defeat over four sets.

As expected, Kennedy Martin led the blue and white with 4.47 in points per set in the nonconference schedule as he entered the year. A vast majority came from former Florida teammate Alexis Stucky, who posted 9.78 assists per set in the ten matches.

Penn State sank to No. 14 in the latest AVCA poll after being upset by No. 16 Tennessee on Sunday, and challenges will start to get even stiffer on Friday. Conference play will see the Nittany Lions take on six top-25 opponents, though neither of this weekend’s foes were ranked.

“I’ve never played in the Big Ten before, but I've played a bunch of Big Ten teams,” Stucky said after the loss to Tennessee. “This conference is a gauntlet. It's good to be challenged because I know our conference schedule is going to challenge us.”

Michigan went 9-2 in the nonconference, falling to South Carolina and TCU. The Horned Frogs were the only ranked opponent that the Wolverines faced through their first 11 games.

There haven’t been many tests for Michigan so far, as it’s swept in six of its wins and never dropped more than a single set in any victory. The maize and blue are riding a high streak of form, with four consecutive losses in a stretch where only one set was lost.

The main offensive threat for Michigan is Ella Demetrician who leads the Wolverines with 4.23 kills per set, a mark that ranks No. 24 nationally. Earlier this season, she posted a career-high 23 kills in Michigan’s win over Eastern Michigan on Sept. 17.

The Wolverines sport a high-level attack that ranks No. 7 nationally with 14.51 kills per set and No. 13 nationally with a hitting percentage. There’s less to write home about defensively, as Michigan’s 2.26 blocks per set ranks No. 100.

Historically, the Nittany Lions have been flat-out dominant against Michigan, holding a 57-7 all-time record over the Wolverines. In coach Katie Schumacher Cawley’s tenure as coach, the blue and white lead 3-1 in a split stretch between Happy Valley and Ann Arbor.

After the trip to Ann Arbor, the blue and white continue with another tall task, despite the Spartans currently sitting as an unranked opponent.

Michigan State received votes in the latest AVCA poll, but not enough to break into the rankings.

The Spartans were unblemished through their nonconference slate, being one of three Big Ten teams to hold an undefeated record, sitting at 10-0. While they haven’t played a single ranked squad all season, they’ve dropped just three sets in the campaign’s first ten matches.

Those lost frames came in a 3-2 win over Miami in the season opener and a 3-1 win over Oakland on Sept. 15. Michigan State will face off with Washington, another team that’s receiving votes, on Friday before hosting Penn State on Sunday.

Offensively, the Spartans are led by Alanna Bankston with 3.81 kills per set. Middle blocker Carmen Waye has also been a weapon for the squad, ranking No. 1 in the country with a .542 hitting percentage on 118 swings.

Defensively, Michigan State also stands firm, with Carmen Waye and Zora Hardison leading the charge. Both Spartans currently rank in the top-20 in blocks per set in the Big Ten.

Michigan State is a better defensive team than Michigan, ranking No. 3 nationally with a .118 opponent hitting percentage and No. 18 with 2.79 blocks per set. The offense isn’t as hot as Michigan's, but it’s posted a solid 13.67 kills per set. The real stardom for the Spartans comes at the backline where they post a conference high of 2.36 aces per set.

Malayah Long sits as the leader in most statistical categories, but her numbers pace amongst the middle tier of the Big Ten.

Penn State boasts almost the exact same historic record against the Spartans at 57-8 all-time. The Nittany Lions have won the last four meetings, and 20 of the last 21 dating back to 2013. Schumacher-Cawley only lost once in her six games against the Spartans, which happened during a five-set thriller in 2023.

First serve against Michigan is set for 7 p.m. Friday in Ann Arbor, and the blue and white will face Michigan State at 2 p.m. Sunday in East Lansing. The matchups will be televised on B1G+ and Big Ten Network, respectively.

After this road trip, the blue and white return home for a four-game homestand, including the Dig Pink Match, before taking a West Coast series.

title: ‘He brought the team back to life’ | Terry Smith's values shape him through long Penn State career
author: Noah Aberegg | The Daily Collegian
description:
For nearly 50 years, Terry Smith has built his life around football.

From playing on Firethorn Drive in Monroeville, Pennsylvania, with childhood friends to playing wide receiver at Penn State, coaching at both the high school and college before eventually taking over as the Nittany Lions’ interim head coach, football has remained the constant in his life.

But even after stepping into the most prominent role of his career as the Nittany Lions’ interim head coach, Smith said he’s more comfortable being behind the scenes coaching his players.

“This is what I’ve done for my entire life, I’ve been coaching,” Smith said on Aug. 7. “There’s no better feeling than to be on the grass. To be on the grass, getting after your guys, coaching them up, and then unleashing them on game day. That’s where I’m most comfortable. I'd rather coach and kind of be hidden.”

That comfort was built long before Smith returned to Penn State as a coach. It started as a kid, where Smith spent his childhood playing football and other sports with a group of friends who would eventually go on to play Division I football.

At Gateway High School, Smith quarterbacked his team to back-to-back WPIAL titles in 1985 and 1986. He was the star in his second championship, scoring the only touchdown in the 7-6 victory.

“Terry’s just a competitive athlete from the very beginning,” Verne Howard, one of Smith’s childhood friends and high school teammates, told The Daily Collegian. “Coming from Aliquippa, PA, that was his roots where he came from and brought that with him to Gateway. That’s where you get that initial toughness from.”

His success at Gateway eventually led him to Penn State, where he established himself as one of the top receivers. As a three-year starter, he finished his career with 1,825 receiving yards.

But his playing career didn’t end in Happy Valley. Smith went on to play in the NFL, Canadian Football League and Arena League before transitioning to coaching, with his first role coming at Hempfield High School.

He then spent four years at Duquesne before returning to Gateway in 2001 as the offensive coordinator.

Over the next 12 years, Smith took on the roles of head coach and athletic director at his high school, making an impact both on the field and in the community.

Howard said Smith was a hard coach who consistently produced high-level athletes, but enjoyed forming relationships with his students.

In addition to the numerous All-Americans athletes and those who played in the Big 33, an all-star game featuring Pennsylvania’s top high school players, Smith was also known for giving opportunities to athletes who weren’t necessarily at the same level as their peers.

Smith would help athletes learn how to study film and aided them in the recruiting process.

“That was stuff he wasn’t getting paid for, he just did on his own,” Howard said.

Smith’s impact extended beyond the football field. He would often give lunch money to students who were struggling financially, and “would never tell a kid no,” according to Howard.

In 2013, Smith returned to the collegiate ranks as Temple’s wide receivers coach. A year later, he returned to his alma mater, this time coaching the cornerbacks and serving as the defensive recruiting coordinator.

Smith quickly became one of the most trusted members of James Franklin’s staff. He was named assistant head coach in 2016 and associate head coach in 2021.

“He exemplifies what Penn State is,” D’Anton Lynn said on Aug. 25. “He’s a great leader, not just for the players, but for the staff. He puts his ego aside and he cares about Penn State football more than anything else.”

Over his 13 seasons at Penn State, Smith has helped develop a dozen players who went onto play in the NFL, but those accolades were never the point. His focus remained on the daily work of coaching and building relationships with his players.

Entering the 2025 season, Smith had spent his career helping develop Penn State’s cornerbacks. But after Franklin was fired following three consecutive losses, Smith was promoted from associate head coach to interim head coach.

For a coach who had spent much of his career working behind the scenes, the opportunity put Smith in the center of Penn State football. His approach, however, remained the same.

“I just want to be a really, really good coach,” Smith said. “I want to be a really good role model to these guys and lead by example, and hopefully they can learn some lessons to navigate their waters as they become adults and grow men in their own life. Just live right and do right by people, and then the good Lord takes care of everything else.”

Smith hadn’t been a head coach since his time at Gateway, but helped guide Penn State through a difficult stretch. The Nittany Lions nearly defeated Iowa before losing by three points to eventual national champion Indiana.

“We were just so happy that he got the opportunity to do what he did at the time,” Howard said. “Terry was deserving, and he had earned that.”

The Nittany Lions won their final three games of the regular season to become bowl eligible, going onto defeat Clemson in the Pinstripe Bowl. The results mattered, but so did the way Smith brought the team together.

“The way he led us off the field and on the field, everyone has a connection with him, and just the way he leads, I feel like he’s a great leader,” Tony Rojas said Aug. 7. “The way he brought the team back to life when he was named that coach was crazy to see, and it just showed how much everyone loved Terry.”

Smith said the culture when he was interim reminded him of his own playing days at Penn State, calling it “a little bit of a throwback” to the way things were when he played.

“We’re building a great culture. We’re building a team. We’re building togetherness,” Smith said on Aug. 7. “We’re building guys that really care about each other and want to play for each other.”

After Penn State hired Matt Campbell on Dec. 5 to be the next head coach despite some players and many fans alike advocating for Smith to get the full-time job, Smith was faced with a decision: Should he stay or should he go?

“It was a dire situation of whether I’m going to stay, I’m going to leave, I’m going to take other opportunities,” Smith said. “Who’s going to be the next head coach here? Do I fit his style? Do I fit his culture?”

But after speaking with Campbell, Smith knew there was a fit alongside him. He had known Campbell for over a decade, with Campbell even recruiting players from Gateway when Smith was the head coach. Smith knew “he was my kind of guy that I can get behind.”

And Campbell felt the same way, as it was reported just hours after he was hired that Penn State’s new head coach would be staying on staff.

“My gratitude and honor to be able to work forward with Terry and lead forward with Terry means a great deal to myself and it certainly means a great deal to our young men in our football program,” Campbell said.

Since the beginning of the Campbell era, Smith’s influence has continued to shape the program. Nearly half of Penn State’s roster entered the transfer portal after Franklin’s firing, but the cornerback room had the highest retention rate.

According to cornerback Zion Tracy, Smith was a key reason he stayed in Happy Valley, saying, “Terry’s somebody I really trust, so I was so glad he stayed.”

Smith’s impact has also extended beyond football, as he was named an honorary grand marshal for the 2026 Homecoming Parade, signifying his impact on the State College community and what he truly means to Penn State.

“The greatest thing Terry brings is he’s such a wealth of living knowledge of what it means to be a Penn Stater,” Campbell said Tuesday. “I think how Terry has lived and how he’s led as a player and a coach here in this community, it continues to be the essence of what it means to be a great Penn Stater.”

title: Staff predictions | Will Penn State open Big Ten play with a win over Wisconsin?
author: The Daily Collegian Football Staff
description:
Big Ten play has arrived.

Penn State is set to play its first conference game of the season this Saturday against Wisconsin in what’s doubling as Homecoming and the Helmet Stripe game. It’ll also be the first chance for Matt Campbell to earn a Big Ten win.

Here’s how we think the Nittany Lions will perform in their first real test of 2026.

Andrew Deal: Penn State 24, Wisconsin 13

There weren’t many questions answered for Penn State during the nonconference slate given the competition. While Wisconsin is likely one of the weaker conference teams on the schedule, it’s still a Big Ten opponent.

The Nittany Lions will have to begin the Big Ten schedule without wide receiver Koby Howard, who currently leads the team in receiving yards and yards per reception. While that production can certainly be filled in by Chase Sowell and Brett Eskildsen, they’ll still be without their top receiver.

I expect the tight ends to get more looks throughout the game, especially given the skillset of its top three, barring Andrew Rappleyea plays after being given a “questionable” designation from Matt Campbell on Tuesday.

The Penn State defense will have its biggest task of the year — containing the dual-threat capabilities of Wisconsin quarterback Colton Joseph. The Badgers’ quarterback ran for over 1,000 yards last year, so if the Nittany Lions want to limit the scoring, it’ll need to be hyperfixated on Joseph’s legs.

The athleticism of linebackers Tony Rojas and Kooper Ebel will be a main factor in containing the rushing ability of Joseph, and while Abu Sama III, a former running back under Campbell, will be the lead back, but given the strength in rush defense for Penn State, I expect him to have a slower game.

Penn State will stay in control of the game, but it’ll remain close throughout. The Nittany Lions will answer their first “test” in the Big Ten with a convincing win over Wisconsin.

Andrew Mercer: Penn State 21, Wisconsin 14

Penn State’s nonconference opponents were just the warm up, and now that the Nittany Lions are in the Big Ten stretch, things are getting real. Campbell’s first conference outing will be far closer than many expect even though the Nittany Lions have an easier schedule.

I have this game being a touchdown-or-bust situation, with two of Penn State’s scores coming at the hands of tight end Benjamin Brahmer and the other from running back James Peoples.

The running back room found a lot of success against Buffalo, but that was a MAC team, and the Big Ten is a different beast. Therefore, I’d expect punter Nathan Tiyce to appear more than usual, at least in the first half while the Nittany Lions figure out the run-pass balance with Howard out.

Temple’s Jaxon Smolik ran all over the Nittany Lions in Week 2, and Joseph is similarly efficient calling his own number when the pocket breaks down. When the pass is open, Joseph’s accurate deep ball will keep Penn State on its toes.

I’d expect at least one of the Badgers’ touchdowns to be through the air and the other coming from Sama, someone who the Nittany Lions praised all week leading up to the game.

It’ll be tight, and Penn State’s defense may experience a culture shock upon playing a Big Ten offense. But I believe the Nittany Lions will successfully adjust and hold the Badgers to only two touchdowns.

Lexie Linderman: Penn State 28, Wisconsin 17

The real question moving forward after three nonconference blowouts is whether Penn State is a competitive Big Ten team. It gets to start with a relatively easier test, but still one that could pose problems.

Joseph is one reason why the Badgers could keep things close. His ability to run is something Penn State is going to have to respect, and it wouldn’t be surprising if the defense struggles with that slightly at first.

As for the offense, missing its biggest weapon is going to sting. However, there are plenty of other players who can step up for the Nittany Lions, most notably the tight ends. They haven’t been involved in the passing game a ton up to this point, but without Howard, that will surely change.

How the run game looks this week will be interesting after great performances from all four running backs against Buffalo. Carson Hansen will likely be the announced starter, but it wouldn’t be surprising to see the staff run whoever the hot hand is at the time.

The offense might start a bit slow against a Big Ten defense, but the Nittany Lions will eventually pull away in front of an electric home crowd Saturday evening.

Noah Aberegg: Penn State 30, Wisconsin 13

Penn State’s offense shined in the nonconference opener and closer. While it won’t reach the 55 points scored against Buffalo, the team will still find the end zone multiple times and add nine more points from field goals.

The absence of Howard will be a major loss in the offense, but the team has several additional weapons that can help fill the void. I’d expect Sowell and Eskildsen to score, while Brahmer will contribute significantly in the passing game.

On the other hand, I don’t think the run game will have the same impact it did against Buffalo. The top three backs will all likely see the field, but a majority of the yardage will once again come through the air.

The pass rush was a major topic of conversation this week, and the team will face another mobile quarterback in Joseph this week. Similar to performances against Carlos Del Rio-Wilson and Smolik, the Nittany Lions will have a hard time bringing down Joseph in the backfield.

Wisconsin’s offense will go the distance for just one touchdown, but will make several big plays resulting in a pair of field goals Saturday, giving Penn State a comfortable victory to open Big Ten play.

title: Caramel Afternoon brings pastries, coffee to Penn State students
author: Talia Rittenhouse | The Daily Collegian
description:
It's finally fall, and what pairs better with fall than lattes and pastries?

Located at 214 E. Calder Way, Caramel Afternoon is the place to get delicious drinks and pastries, bringing as many options as your heart desires.

Not only that, but you can also get breakfast or lunch here, such as their granola bowl, avocado toast, pesto mozzarella panini or the turkey-cheese panini.

As I came to the store on a chilly, rainy day, I was searching for some feel-good lattes and desserts and got just that.

Fruit Tart

With strawberries, blueberries, raspberries and blackberries on top, this dessert not only looks delicious but also tastes fresh and truly homemade.

The tart has a buttery, sweet, flaky crust, holding together the shape of the dish, bringing structure to the tart without breaking into any pieces. Inside is a thick layer of creamy, vanilla pastry cream — I could eat it with a spoon because it was so delicious.

Altogether, this dessert is perfect if you want something sweet, but not too sweet, because of the fruit and light cream in the middle.

This fruit tart is perfect for one person, not only because of its single-serve size but also because you won’t want to share.

White Chocolate Mocha Latte

On the menu, there are many different flavored lattes, iced coffees or matchas to try.

One of which was the white chocolate mocha latte. I personally got it with oat milk, but there are many other options.

This latte isn’t overpowered by the milk, so you can really taste the espresso, which itself has a great taste.

At times, there was an aftertaste that I can't fully identify — it might have been from the flavoring — but it was more bitter than I would like in my coffee. However, I'm sure it wouldn't affect others who want to try this.

So, if you like the flavor of coffee and aren't into the sugary drinks at other coffee shops, this latte allows you to have the espresso taste and a little flavoring to make your drink even more special.

Apple Crumble

Caramel Afternoon’s apple crumble tastes just like apple pie at Thanksgiving dinner, bringing back fun family memories in just one bite.

The apple crumble is perfect as we approach fall weather, and I think it would pair well with a hot latte on a rainy day, perfectly setting the autumn mood.

In this dessert, you get a square of the apple crumble with sweet sugary crumbles on top, pastry dough on the bottom and baked apples in between.

This dessert is perfect for someone with a sweet tooth, as it’s very sweet from the sugar in the apple mixture and the crumbles.

With the sugar and juices from the apples, the apple crumble has even created its own sweet caramel-like sauce that spreads all throughout the treat.

Caramel Macchiato

After seeing the extensive drink menu, I knew I had to try a classic caramel macchiato — one of my all-time favorites.

Again, like the white chocolate mocha, this latte has a great ratio of milk to espresso, allowing you to still get that coffee taste in the drink. The taste of the caramel is subtle, though I wish there were more in it, or even a caramel drizzle.

You can get this latte either hot or iced. I think after trying it iced, I might prefer it hot, as I tend to enjoy a warm macchiato, especially on a fall day.

I'm not sure that this caramel macchiato is my favorite that I've had, since it was on the more bitter rather than sweet side, but I still enjoyed it and would have it again.

title: Penn State field hockey suffers 2 consecutive losses, raising stakes against Bucknell
author: Annie Alberts | The Daily Collegian
description:
The Nittany Lions began play in the Big Ten with their first road contest of the season, but the stretch left the blue and white staggered as it continued away from Happy Valley.

Penn State took two losses this week as it faced now No. 2 Maryland in the conference opener and current No. 19 Monmouth on the road.

The Nittany Lions ended their previous week with a loss to then-No. 4 Princeton as the blue and white struggled through a tough part of its schedule. Despite the fractured result in action, here are the major takeaways from the clashes with high-profile opponents.

Nonstop action

In both of this week’s matchups, whenever a goal was scored, there was action that followed. In the Nittany Lions’ meeting with the Terrapins, the first goal was scored early by Maryland’s Brinkley Eyre. Moments later, it was followed by a corner shot. The same thing happened two quarters later, with the Terrapins scoring back-to-back goals, almost instantly.

However, there was action even before the goals as well. Penn State’s first contribution to the scoreboard was made shortly after Olivia Marthins made a corner shot. The blue and white quickly rebounded and turned it into a goal. Whether for or against the Nittany Lions, pace stood out as a real staple of the play on the pitch in recent performances.

Rapid saves

Throughout this action before and after goals, the opposing team wasn’t always successful. Penn State junior goalkeeper Aby Deverka made back-to-back saves whenever Maryland and Monmouth brought the heat. In the second quarter of the Maryland matchup, Deverka made three saves in a row, one of them being from a penalty shot attempt.

In the third quarter of the Monmouth game, Deverka stuck to her run of form that she’s had all year and continued to carry into last week. The Hawks fired four shots in 45 seconds, two of them being penalty corner shots. Deverka saved all four, which were the Houston native’s only saves of the game.

Throughout the week, Deverka totaled 11 saves, stacking performances for a nationally prominent year in net. However, in the Maryland game, the netminder saved seven shots, but let in three.

Fouls galore

If there was anything Penn State got from its game against Monmouth, it was fouls. The Nittany Lions totaled 44, which is the most they have committed all season. In fact, the blue and white hadn’t committed any fouls until its meeting with the Hawks.

The match was constantly interrupted by penalty corner shots and various cards. As a result, Penn State took only 10 shots and scored one goal, as breaks limited a consistent speed of play.

Monmouth received 47 fouls and a yellow card during the final minutes of the game.

However, the Hawks had two more shots on goal than the Nittany Lions did. In the end, Monmouth defeated the blue and white 2-1. Overall, the game was very hostile and unlike Penn State’s usual style of play that had been established early in the Hannah Prince tenure.

After a weekend getaway to Monmouth University, Penn State couldn’t seize a win. After suffering losses in two games in a row, the blue and white stayed off the ranked polls. Penn State has hit a bump in the road in Prince’s first season, currently riding a three-game losing streak.

Penn State continues its road trip with a match against Bucknell on Sept. 28. The Nittany Lions hold a 47-2-2 record all-time against the Bison, winning all the matchups this millennium; it’ll be a familiar matchup in both programs’ history.

title: Column | ‘Lord of the Rings’ shows how ‘We Are’ is a Fellowship
author: Kippi Hall | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State has had a dark 15 years, enough to stop a “We Are” chant dead in its tracks.

Now is no exception. Amid a burgeoning investigation of an alleged cocaine-trafficking ring run by Penn State fraternities, sex offender and former Penn State defensive coordinator Jerry Sandusky seeking a federal appeal and the sale of two out of seven branch campuses scheduled to close coming underway, Penn State is struggling for a PR and morale win.

Finding community while we’re surrounded by scandal, tragedy and darkness is a tall order at times. For the Fellowship of the Ring in J. R. R. Tolkien’s series, “The Lord of the Rings,” corruption and despair cloud their pursuit of goodness, too.

The series, published from 1954 to 1955, with the movie series being released from 2001 to 2003, has easily held its ground as the best foundational fantasy series of all time.

The Fellowship consists of four hobbits (short, hedonistic people), an elf, a dwarf, a wizard and two men. They’re tasked with destroying the One Ring, a cursed artifact with the immense power to corrupt its wearer and onlookers, before its evil creator, Lord Sauron, finds it. The volunteer carrying the ring to its demise? An unassuming hobbit named Frodo Baggins.

Frodo and the rest of the hobbits are from the Shire, an evergreen land where trouble never seems to fall and the people remain satisfied, complacent and averse to discomfort of any kind. This peacetime lasts until Sauron’s followers come to get the Ring from Frodo, spreading darkness and death across Middle Earth. Thus, Frodo is forced to begin his journey to destroy the Ring — but not without his friends Sam, Merry and Pippin, who refuse to let him make the treacherous journey alone.

Penn State and State College act as a kind of Shire for students and alumni alike on the surface. Traditions of eating grilled stickies, taking pictures at the Nittany Lion shrine, even signing each other’s T-shirts during bar crawls are all welcoming symbols of the mountain ridge that cradles our university. Like a blissful hobbit, joy seems to be the defining characteristic of Happy Valley.

Penn State, at the height of this joy, has been repeatedly thrown into chaos with its community left in the lurch on how to react. In the summer, as everyone was winding down from the school year or starting up their internships, Penn State student Billy Schmidt was shot dead in Philadelphia. All the while, resurfacing wounds from 2011 and 2023 appear at the Bellefonte courthouse.

It feels like the eye of Sauron is on us, too, without giving us a chance to feel like a community. Frodo, on his trek to Mount Doom while feeling the burden of the Ring on his mind, says to Sam: “I don’t like anything here at all. Step or stone, breath or bone. Earth, air and water all seem accursed. But so our path is laid.”

Like Frodo and the dangers that surround him, the corruption and tragedy that plagues Penn State is a part of our path. But Penn State has the remarkable ability to remain together anyway.

Part of what makes both the Fellowship and Penn State such strongly bonded communities is, ironically, their respective weaknesses.

Everyone in the Fellowship is susceptible to the corruption of the Ring and the power it holds, including Frodo, and reacts to it in different ways. The wizard, Gandalf, refuses to touch the Ring because he knows his power along with the Ring’s would be disastrous. One of the men, Aragorn, tries to protect Frodo from harm to right the wrongs of his ancestors that caused the Ring to still exist. The dwarf, Gimli, attempts to smash the One Ring with his hammer upon seeing it (to no avail, of course).

At Penn State, the attachment to tradition and the rosy-colored perfection of it can cloud judgment. At times, commentary on current and past scandals feel like attacks on everything this institution does rather than just the harm it has the ability to wield.

But, like in “Lord of the Rings,” even the purest person in the room fails to rise above darkness without the support of the community around them to help move forward.

Frodo doesn’t succeed in destroying the One Ring on his own and only ends the tyranny of Sauron when the Fellowship, however strong or small the member, fights to keep the darkness at bay. In doing so, they keep each other accountable and protected from the Ring’s corruption.

Along with Frodo, we Penn Staters often fail to check ourselves. The spirit of “We Are” can almost feel like armor against the onslaught of bad publicity, like a club (or cult) no one else can get into. But that’s exactly the opposite of what “We Are” should mean.

In the second installment of the movie series, Frodo asks Sam what they’re holding on to in the face of immense suffering and the threat of death and evil at every turn.

Sam tearfully tells Frodo: “That there’s some good in this world, Mr. Frodo. And it’s worth fighting for.”

A friend told me they didn’t think I was the “school spirit” type for this column, but that’s not true. I love being a Penn Stater, and I think, like Sam Gamgee, it’s a community worth fighting for and improving, even when it feels like all I can offer is heavy-handed criticism.

“We Are” isn’t armor, or a Ring, to abuse when bad things happen, but rather a promise to support and hold our community accountable, which we all have the burden to keep when crisis strikes.

title: First Friday brings community to State College
author: Lily Dorf | The Daily Collegian
description:
State College is one of many towns to participate in First Friday, a monthly event held on — as you may have guessed — the first Friday of the month. Some may see it as a way to go out with friends and take on the town, while others see it as a way to connect with the community in many different ways.

The vendors of State College's First Friday celebration range from food to toys to art demonstrations. While they get to know the community better after every event, these Fridays are also an opportunity for Penn Staters to get up close and personal with the vendors as well.

Drip Studio is a piercing and tattoo shop located at 248 E. Calder Way. The studio was opened in 2022 by Jenny Eisenhower and her husband.

“I've been here in State College for 17 years, and I've always been a part of the community,” Eisenhower said. “Even before I opened my business, I ran community events and donated to charities within the area, so the community is extremely important to me.”

When she was approached to be a part of State College’s First Friday, her yes was a no brainer.

During First Friday, Drip Studio offers 20% off piercings and 10% off jewelry purchases for all attendees. This idea sparked from the studio having limited existing sales and wanting to provide an out-of-the-box experience for all.

When it comes to First Friday, it's clear Eisenhower and her shop love the community, and they love her right back.

If you're in the market for a trinket or sweet treat, It Is What It Is has everything to satisfy that want. Originating in Lock Haven, Pennsylvania in 2018, It Is What It Is serves as a gift shop, selling everything from candles to Snoop Dogg crochet kits. Owner Fabrae Sanders, along with her husband Larry Miller and father Art Sanders wanted to bring the magic of the store to State College. However, the idea for It Is What It Is started long before its opening day.

“The business was actually the brainchild of my mom and dad,” Sanders said. “They had always wanted to do a retirement gift shop business.”

While her parents were still putting together the pieces to make their dream a reality, Sanders’ mother passed away.

“It was nine years ago now, and after that, I thought, ‘Okay, well he's not going to do anything,’ but he called me six months after she passed and said, ‘I'm ready to open the gift shop.’”

So, they started planning and opened up not only the gift shop, but also a candy store next door, which made its way to State College as a pop-up.

Once Sanders got settled with the pop-up shop on 236 E. Calder Way, she was approached to join First Friday.

“I thought it would be the perfect opportunity to have our grand opening at the same time,” Sanders said. "We have a similar program in Lock Haven called final Friday, which is the last Friday of the month. We're pretty used to doing these events in Lock Haven, and I think it's going to be the perfect day for us to open.”

It Is What It Is took on their first First Friday on Sept. 4, offering sweets and joy to the State College community.

Another recent addition to downtown State College is Happy Valley Polish Water Ice, which opened its doors in April 2026. Owner Miklos Vajda wanted to bring the familiar taste of the boardwalk to State College.

“It's been a Jersey Shore tradition,” Vajda said. “They have their place in Maryland, Wildwood, Ocean City, Seattle and Jersey Shore.”

As a Penn State alum himself, Vajda wanted to include the energy of Penn State into his store, like with a recycling bin from Beaver Stadium as a way to strengthen the immersion even more.

When Vajda opened his doors, he knew he wanted to get involved with First Friday, so his inaugural First Friday was the following month. He gave out samples of Hershey’s ice cream to locals, which worked in more ways than one.

“It kind of brings people in because I'm at the front,” Vajda said. “Then some people will be like, ‘Oh, there's a band on stage here,’ and then they'll go past me and sit and watch the band. So, it's kind of a collaboration.”

For Happy Valley Polish Water Ice, First Friday is a way to connect with the diverse community of Penn State.

“One takeaway from First Friday, there's so much to do,” Vajda said. “It's free, it's regular and it's not just for one set of people either. In the summertime, most of the students are back at home and the locals come out. They bring their kids to hang out, listen to the band and get free ice cream.”

title: Penn State reveals initial availability report for matchup with Wisconsin
author: Andrew Deal | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State revealed its first availability report Wednesday night ahead of its matchup against Wisconsin at 5 p.m. in Beaver Stadium.

Wide receiver Koby Howard is listed out, which isn't a shock, as Matt Campbell said he'd be out for an extended period of time. Offensive lineman Will Tompkins is also out after Campbell announced he'd miss the rest of the season on Wednesday.

Defensive ends Lavar Arrington II, Max Granville, Mason Robinson and Dayshaun Burnett are all listed as out ahead of Saturday's matchup. Cornerbacks Joshua Johnson and Tyler Armstead alongside tight end Cooper Alexander, were also listed as out.

Armstead was banged up against Buffalo, Campbell said Tuesday.

Offensive lineman Brock Riker and tight end Andrew Rappleyea are both listed as questionable. Both players were dinged up following Penn State's victory over Buffalo.

Linebacker Cam Smith, cornerback Christian Askew, offensive lineman Dominic Rulli and wide receiver Ethan Black are also listed as questionable.

title: SPA announces lecture by influencer Trisha Paytas
author: Colleen Cratty | The Daily Collegian
description:
The Student Programming Association (SPA) announced a free lecture by influencer Trisha Paytas, taking place in the HUB-Robeson Center on Tuesday, Sept. 29.

Paytas also hosts a podcast called “Just Trish,” in which she discusses entertainment news and all things pop culture.

title: Penn State gears up for Big Ten opener against Wisconsin, meeting former Iowa State teammates
author: Andrew Mercer | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State’s victories in the nonconference slate were only the prelude to a Big Ten schedule that will determine the program’s success in the first season under Matt Campbell.

It all begins with Wisconsin, which will be many Nittany Lions’ first taste of Big Ten action. Linebacker Kooper Ebel said the Big Ten is “closer to NFL style of play,” and the increased physicality of the conference presents a unique challenge.

Despite that, Penn State feels ready for the moment. While Rocco Becht said he’s not preparing any differently than he would for any other game, the defense has yet to dig into its bag of tricks.

“We have a ton of confidence going to Big Ten play,” Ebel said Tuesday. “I think we're just scratching the surface of our defensive schemes. I'm super excited to just attack it with the team.”

Adding to the many layers of the upcoming contest, the transfers from Iowa State are set to face their former teammates and coach who are all now in key roles in their first season as Badgers. Running back Abu Sama III, safety Carson Van Dinter and cornerbacks coach Robert Steeples will be on the opposite sideline of Matt Campbell after time with the Cyclones.

Although he was listed as healthy in Week 2, the Badgers didn’t play Sama against Eastern Michigan to avoid aggravating a shoulder injury. However, he’ll be back in action against the Nittany Lions and will offer Penn State’s run defense a significant challenge.

Safety Jeremiah Cooper battled with Sama at practice throughout their three years together as Cyclones, so he knows a lot about his style and can use those experiences to his advantage.

“Just knowing him, knowing his tendencies, we all know that there's so many coaches here that coached him,” Cooper said Wednesday. “So, I'm picking on him. He's a great player, though, very athletic, very strong, fast. I can't wait to play him because I kind of know what he's gonna do.”

Becht also had high praise for Sama, saying he’s “one of the best athletes I’ve ever seen.” He added the Iowa State transfers on defense have been relaying what they know about Sama to the defensive staff.

Van Dinter was one of wide receiver Brett Eskildsen’s roommates at Iowa State. In Ames, Van Dinter was a role player who played 180 snaps, with 88 of them coming in his final two games of the 2025 season. He redshirted in 2024 after appearing in two games.

Eskildsen voiced his excitement to see his former roommate play in an expanded role.

“He’s a great kid and a great football player,” Eskildsen said. “So it'll be cool to see him out there. We've gone against him like when we were at Iowa State, but it'll be cool to see who he is now and how he's developed as a football player.”

Wisconsin had a tough matchup against No. 3 Notre Dame in Week 1, falling 41-13. That game gave the Badgers experience against a highly-ranked opponent, something that Penn State lacks at this point.

Regardless of Week 1’s results, Big Ten action causes teams to play with heightened intensity. Penn State’s defense knows this all too well and are preparing for a ferocious start to the conference stretch.

“They're going to try to punch us in the mouth,” defensive coordinator D’Anton Lynn said. “They're a physical team, they run the ball downhill, they do a good job of creating explosive plays in the passing game. They're going to take shots and test us downfield.”

title: ‘Next man up mentality’ | Penn State WRs confident in unit after Koby Howard injury
author: Andrew Deal | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State’s wide receiver room took a hit when Matt Campbell announced Wednesday that Koby Howard will be out for an “extended period of time.”

The confidence in the unit hasn’t wavered despite the loss of Howard, especially with the return of Brett Eskildsen, who’s now at 100% after being dinged up the last two weeks, according to Campbell.

“I think again, that rest of that room has got to continue to step up and make plays,” Campbell said. “I think when they've had the opportunity, they've shown to make plays too. So we'll just continue to navigate that. The next man up will be ready to roll.”

Howard’s loss, no matter the confidence in the room, is detrimental to the offensive production. Through three games, Howard leads the team in receiving yards with 344 and yards per reception with 28.7, both of which rank top 10 nationally.

“He's handling it well,” Eskildsen said. “I mean, injuries suck. Being out, like getting off to the start he has, contributing to the team and being the player that he is, it sucks. But he's a hard worker, so he's just getting in the lab in the training room, and we know he'll be back as soon as he can be.”

With the recency of the injury for Howard, the receiver room has helped him keep his spirits up. The closeness of the team and receiver room, which was developed in the offseason, will once again be put to work to help Howard recover.

“Just picking him up, telling him we got him, and he knows that,” Eskildsen said. “Just helping him out in any way we can to get him back as fast as possible.”

Eskildsen and the former Iowa State players have experience with preparing for games without players due to injury. That teaching and preparation has transitioned to Penn State to help with a team that’s already dealt with a few injuries early in the year.

“I think something that is always preached to us is prepare like you're the starter because you never know,” Eskildsen said. “Like everybody's one play away from being the starter if you're a backup, and I think that's something that we learned and have brought over here, and everybody's kind of adapted to is like, injuries are going to happen. That's part of the sport of football.

While Howard is out for an extended period of time, with the wide receiver implying on his Instagram story he’s targeting a return for Oct. 17 against Michigan, Eskildsen and the rest of the receivers have taken the “next man up mentality.”

In that role could be Zay Robinson, who’s been the fourth receiver on the depth chart. He’s made the most of his limited time and could be a player who produces even more given bigger opportunities.

“He's come a long way, but obviously, Zay's always been a great playmaker, and so I think that's Zay's best ability,” Eskildsen said. “He's just a playmaker. He's able to make something out of nothing, so it's been really cool to see him develop on his route running.”

Additionally, freshman wide receiver Amarion Jackson is a player Campbell could see playing more given the circumstances. Jackson hasn’t seen offensive snaps with the top unit yet, but without Howard, he could be in line to see the field this weekend.

“Just his preparation, how he goes about that, knowing what he's doing, and just how he's always come to work every single day since the day he's got here, gives me confidence and everybody on the team confidence that he's ready to go,” Eskildsen said.

Howard’s out for the foreseeable future, so multiple players are likely to see added time compared to what they have in the past three weeks. The confidence in those players to take that step is there.

“Being able to bounce back, be ready for your moment is something that a lot of guys in here are ready for, and so it gives us confidence even when something unfortunate happens and you have a guy down,” Eskildsen said.

title: Penn State women's hockey notebook | Jeff Kampersal speaks on challenges, opening series
author: Mashiah Mitchell | The Daily Collegian
description:
It’s just over 24 hours away from puck drop in Hockey Valley, where the Nittany Lions will welcome a renewed matchup in the Ohio State Buckeyes, raising the banner in front of a team that is widely regarded as one of the best in the country.

Before that, though, coach Jeff Kampersal took time to speak to the media ahead of his 10th season as the leader of the Nittany Lions, answering some questions and leaving others to be determined as the season grows larger.

Kampersal offered insight into his plans as starting goaltender, lessons learned from the prior year that he’s carrying into this season and what opening the season with such a physically demanding series means for the team.

Here’s a recap of the media availability.

Lessons learned

Penn State is following up on their best season in program history, a tough precedent set by a group of senior leaders that have transitioned to the PWHL. Having to live up to this can put an extensive amount of pressure on not only returners, but those fresh into the program as well.

Kampersal has used his veteran talents to assist him and his staff in getting the freshmen and transfers better integrated into their lines.

It has been well documented that he does not want to put too much pressure on the newcomers, having a knack for allowing them to develop through the error-making process, which Kampersal admits is going to be an early topic.

“I think the chemistry is coming along. I think the biggest thing is the physicality for the new players,” Kampersall said. “When we played Ohio State last year, it was a full-on physical body-checking, little-penalty series, so defensive habits and physicality are what we’re really gonna have to get the first years used to. Once they get that under their belt, they are on their way.”

Experience vs. new blood

At AHA media day, Kampersall lightly touched on internal plans for who will start at goalkeeper against the Buckeyes, eyeing a position battle between Maddy Campbell and freshman Morgan Stickney.

Kampersall went further into depth on his intention to keep it split between the two to start the season and let early play decide who gets the long-term starting nod. As for now, Kampersall, it seems to be a tough choice between the two talents.

“Maddy played 5 periods against Ohio State and Mercyhurst, so she has the experience within the program and Morgan struggled a little against RIT,” Kampersall said. “But we look at the entire body of work throughout the fall to see who goes. Me and Moe (Bradley) will sit down in a few hours and decide who gets the go for Ohio State.”

Ohio State

The aforementioned Buckeyes have been a big topic of discussion for Kampersall and his staff. They fully understand how important a series like this is in terms of competing not only to return to the NCAA tournament in March, but to win a national championship this time around.

A series like this, as early in the season as possible, means plugging in more and more contingencies and the physicality of the game.

“We do a lot of small battles, 1-on-1, 2-on-2; you know, we try to teach them shutting the door, checking, trying to separate the puck from the player rather than chucking the player through the boards,” Kampersall said.

Kampersall also shouted out RIT for its physical style, which he attributes to help tune up for the start of the season.

title: Weekly Recap | Penn State’s women’s volleyball picks up pair of wins and loss
author: Ashley Felsberg I The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State is now 8-2 overall after last week's trio of matches in Happy Valley. The blue and white hosted Villanova, USF and Tennessee. Villanova’s matchup took place Tuesday, while USF and Tennessee were part of the Penn State Classic taking place over the weekend.

The Nittany Lions began their week of play against Villanova, winning 3-1. The team then had a two-day break before taking on USF on Friday night, winning in a sweep. To close out non-conference play and the Penn State Classic, the blue and white battled with the Volunteers, falling 3-1 in an upset loss.

Here’s what stood out in the three matches, despite ending nonconference play on a loss.

All Hail Haley Burgdorf (Villanova)

Penn State won the first set by nearly double the points with a score of 25-14. Haley Burgdorf led the Nittany Lions’ defense, playing a large part in keeping the Wildcats under 20 points.

Burgdorf was named Freshman of the Week by the Big Ten ahead of the Villanova matchup. The 6-foot outside hitter lived up to the title, totaling 13 digs in the match. Along with her defensive presence, Burgdorf also contributed seven kills, an assist and an ace.

The Nittany Lions fell in the second set but claimed the first two.

The third set saw alternating three- and four-point runs on both sides. Stucky, Nichols and Jones worked to put up late-set kills to give the blue and white a burst of energy when the score tied up at 22-22.

After a set-point extension gave the Wildcats one last breath, Haley Burgdorf claimed the set for Penn State off a kill.

The fourth set saw wider point differentials, as Penn State led early on with a score of 15-6 at the media timeout. Burgdorf paired with Caroline Jurevicius to put the blue and white in reach of set point. The match ended after Nichols’ 13th kill – team-high of the night.

Strong Nichols Attack (USF)

Garbielle Nichols paired well with multiple players on Penn State to construct an effective attack in the match against USF.

Nichols and Kennedy Martin worked together on the right side, putting up several blocks and forcing USF to focus its offensive attention centrally. The Nittany Lions escaped with a 25-18 first-set win.

Throughout the second set, Nichols and Launstein worked to put up kills, combating the Bulls’ aggressive front line. The duo each totaled seven kills at the conclusion of the match.

Nichols proved to be a hard obstacle for the USF front line in the second set. The first three Nittany Lion points came from the sophomore middle blocker, off of two kills and a solo block.

The Nittany Lions claimed the second set at 25-23, after a USF reception error from Emelyn Stettin.

The final set of the match was no different than the first two, seeing a competitive back-and-forth each time for the one-point upper hand. While Penn State stayed ahead until the 16th point, the Bulls put up a tireless fight.

Penn State was forced to call a timeout late in the set, after a Burgdorf service error. Following the timeout, Launstein put up her seventh kill of the match for match point. The point was challenged but stood, and the Nittany Lions won the match in minimum sets.

Stucky-Kennedy Duo

Penn State ended its weekend on a lower note, as it picked up its first loss since Sept. 6, when it lost to No. 3 Kentucky at Wrigley Field. The loss was an upset, as Penn State was ranked No. 9 and Tennessee No. 16.

While both the Blue and white and the Lady Volunteers began the match in a sloppy fashion, Alexis and Stucky proved to be a powerful duo yet again. Together, they put up 58 offensive contributions: Martin with 20 kills and Stucky with a stunning 38 assists.

Martin struggled with her serving, picking up four total service errors. She battled head-to-head with Tennessee’s Kennedi Rogers, as there was only a one-point difference in kills for the two powerhouses.

Tennessee saw a resurgence following a four-point run, claiming the third set.

The blue and white claimed the third set. Penn State led 10-5 halfway through the set after going on a six-point run. The lead nearly slipped away after Martin picked up a fourth service error; however, Burgdorf's kill allowed the Nittany Lions to officially pick up their first set win.

Along with Stucky’s 38 assists, she also contributed 12 digs, making this her third double-double of the season so far.

While this third set spark seemed promising, especially with an early fourth-set lead for Penn State, attack and service errors halted any true progress, and the Lady Volunteers ultimately captured the set and match after a seven-point run. The

This loss concluded Penn State’s nonconference span of matches. The Nittany Lions will open conference play up against Michigan on Friday. Penn State will enter this match ranked No. 14, dropping from its previous No. 9 rank.

title: Penn State notebook | Matt Campbell discusses next-man-up mentality after confirming WR Koby Howard's injury
author: Noah Aberegg | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State’s Big Ten slate is here.

Matt Campbell took the podium in the Lasch Building ahead of the team’s conference-opener against Wisconsin to discuss the team’s depth following Koby Howard’s injury, Rocco Becht’s importance to the team and more.

Here’s a look at what Campbell had to say.

Stepping up

Campbell provided a handful of injury updates in the beginning of his presser, most notably that Howard will be out for an extended period of time.

Despite the absence of the team’s top receiver from the first three weeks, Campbell wasn’t shy to praise the depth outside of Howard.

“We’ve had this mentality from the get-go, this kind of next man up mentality,” Campbell said. “The rest of that room has got to continue to step up and make plays. I think when they’ve had the opportunity, they've shown and made plays too.”

Following Howard, Chase Sowell, Brett Eskildsen and Zay Robinson have been the three wide receivers to make the most impact so far this season and will likely be the three starters moving forward, with Robinson replacing Howard.

While he’s second on the team with nine receptions, Eskildsen has been dinged up recently and hasn’t seen the field in the same capacity he did in Week 1, when he recorded five receptions and a touchdown against Marshall.

“He’s finally back to full strength, which is great to see,” Campbell said. “I think again, one guy goes down and one guy comes up.”

Outside of the wide receiver room, Campbell also noted offensive lineman Will Tompkins is out for the season and Dom Rulli “worked himself through some tough situations” and has had “a couple setbacks along the way physically.” Thompkins was a depth piece in the team’s first game, while Rulli has yet to see the field under Campbell.

Rocco Becht’s importance

As the gunslinger, Becht is the focal point of the offense. Campbell echoed that, saying “we've tailor made this offense for the last four years around him.”

Through three games, that focus on Becht has been successful, as he sits third in the conference with nine passing touchdowns and has the second-best passer rating at 215.3.

“One of his greatest strengths is his ability when the defense presents whatever, his ability to get the ball to the right space at the right time,” Campbell said. “Whether that’s a run pass option with the play call, I think Rocco has this elite ability to put the offense in the best position now.”

Developing entire roster

Amidst the injuries impacting the Nittany Lions, Campbell discussed the importance of developing each man on the roster, regardless of where they sit on the depth chart.

“The reality of it is that’s why you got 105 guys on the roster,” Campbell said. “The growth has to happen for everybody. We have to develop the whole roster, not just the guys at the top of the roster. Some guys will get some opportunities if we keep moving ourselves forward for sure.”

The nonconference schedule proved to be an important building block in growing those younger players. Against Buffalo, quarterback Jack Lambert saw his first collegiate playing time, while running back Amar’e Glover recorded a pair of rushes.

Penn State’s starters have established themselves as legitimate threats offensively and defensively, but it’s what the rest of the team can do when they can’t play that’s equally important.

“It’s the teams that have the depth and the ability to develop the next man up,” Campbell said. “That’s the kind of teams that I think have the ability to persevere through the season and the ability to be their best on those 12 guaranteed Saturdays.”
