title: Penn State keeps it groovy at FTG Dance Competition
author: Brennan Kramp I The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State students and alumni gathered into the rows of Schwab Auditorium on Tuesday with intense anticipation as they waited for the start of the annual Homecoming "For The Glory" (FTG) Dance Competition, hosted by Penn State’s Homecoming committee.

The competition is designed to showcase the talents of Penn State’s many dance troupes and genres with a grand prize of a stage performance at THON weekend. As the doors opened, several parents and friends of dancers made their way to the front rows of the auditorium to vie for their best spot at capturing their beloved stars performing eccentric and powerful dance numbers.

Terrell Hoffman, a student engagement specialist and advisor for the Homecoming committee, praised just how special this competition is to the campus community.

“It’s usually one of our bigger, well-attended events,” Hoffman, 39, from Albany, Georgia said. “The performances are always really good.”

In the upper level of the auditorium, dance troupes hung over the rails, waving and smiling ear to ear as they greeted their families. Some of the dancers passed the time by making TikToks, while others munched on last-minute bags of peanuts and finished brushing their hair.

Below, masses of friend groups lined through the rows, saving seats with backpacks, coats and sweaters, occasionally looking up to take photos of their dancers. Some supportive boyfriends sat alone, quietly, waiting to see the products of their partners’ hard work. Still, they smiled and waved to everyone else just the same.

As part of Penn State’s Homecoming festivities, the FTG Dance Competition is a stapled tradition and has been running for over a decade. While the Homecoming committee is a fully student-run organization, they still get help from the university.

Even fellow dancers, who weren’t competing, came out to show their support.

Jamil Dawahra, 20, from San Juan, Puerto Rico, came to show some love to his dance group and enjoy the numbers of others as well.

“I’m a big dance fan in general," Dawahra, a second-year studying health policy and administration, said. "I dance, and I’m in the same company as my friend who’s performing for Vole.”

When the lights faded, so did every word of the audience as they waited for the emcees to introduce the first act.

Vole Dance Company kicked off the night with a rousing performance, followed Whiplash Dance Team, Urban Dance Troupe, Penn State Dance Alliance, Orchesis Dance Company, Nittany Dance Project, Penn State Line Dance, Reve Dance Company, Rince na Leon (Penn State’s Irish dance company) and Tapestry Dance Company.

Each performance was unique. From the beat-heavy hip-hop selections from Urban Dance Troupe to the boot-kickin' step tunes of Penn State Line Dance, all held a crafted groove, putting on various displays of dance.

During the break between each performance, there was little silence. Following the conclusion of one act, booming uproars of cheerful fans would echo in the auditorium hall, and the proceeding introduction of the next act created the same effect.

After Tapestry Dance Company closed out the show, it was time to reveal the winners of the FTG Dance Competition. One member from each group went down to center stage in a tight line (dancer’s instinct, presumably) as the main lights focused in.

Patience started to fade and tension grew as the emcees revealed the second and third place winners, Rince na Leon and Orchesis, before revealing which troupe ended up on top.

“Drum roll please…Urban Dance Troupe,” said the emcees.

The entire auditorium lit up like fireworks as they chanted “UDT” towards the stage. During the competition, UDT got a handful of impressed gasps throughout each portion of their performance, yet were still screaming with glee from the upper deck of the auditorium when their name was announced.

After the competition ended, seas of kids, parents, grandparents and students headed for the doors. There was an upbeat feeling in the air, no doubt a byproduct of the performances and music just shown on display. One attendee, John Held, 19, from State College, Pennsylvania, commended all of the dancers.

“They got a lot of energy…there’s some groups that come here and they’re just really electric,” Held, a second-year studying earth sciences, said.

title: ‘I want my sack’ | Penn State pass rush looks to carry momentum into Big Ten play
author: Noah Aberegg | The Daily Collegian
description:
Through the first two games of the season, there were legitimate questions about the effectiveness of Penn State’s pass rush.

The Nittany Lions recorded just three sacks total against Marshall and Temple, leaving the defense searching for ways to consistently disrupt opposing quarterbacks. That changed against Buffalo.

Penn State’s pressure affected Bulls quarterback Jason Wright throughout the team’s 55-13 victory, providing a glimpse of what the pass rush could become as the Nittany Lions enter Big Ten play.

“I still think that group has grown,” Matt Campbell said on Tuesday. “I feel like what area has made the best growth in three weeks, it’s probably been the ability to watch that group grow forward.”

While the entire edge rush unit has improved, it also faced a major setback after Campbell announced after Penn State’s win over Temple that Max Granville would miss the remainder of the season due to injury. He also said on Sept. 8 that LaVar Arrington II would miss 4-6 weeks.

Despite the injuries, the group has succeeded in part because of its versatility. In August, Caleb Bacon made the move from linebacker to defensive end, adding to the depth of the group.

With that flexibility, D’Anton Lynn has put four edge rushers on the field on obvious passing downs, including Bacon, Yvan Kemajou, Alexander McPherson and Ike Ezeogu.

“The more guys that you can put in different positions to win the one-on-one pass rush, whether it’s against the back or whether it’s against different protections or different players on the offensive line, I think those things are really important,” Campbell said. “But I do think it’s grown immensely over the first three weeks.”

Kemajou said the opportunity to rush alongside the other edge players creates a chance to use their strengths together.

“It’s good having all of us out there ready to just rush and get after the quarterback,” Kemajou said. “Being able to be with guys where you can play off each other, rush off each other, is really good.”

Despite the pass rush’s improvement, Penn State hasn’t consistently translated its pressure into sacks. Lynn said Tuesday that opposing quarterbacks have been getting the ball out quickly, limiting the defense’s opportunities to finish plays.

“I want to get there, I want my sack,” Kemajou said. “I think affecting the quarterback is definitely important, but I want to be able to finish the job.”

Kemajou has been the only edge rusher to record a sack through the first three games. The sophomore has also made an impact against the run, with Lynn calling him “one of our best guys inside.”

With Granville and Arrington sidelined, Jackson Ford has an opportunity to earn playing time. He’s appeared in all three games, and Lynn said his continued development could lead to more snaps for the freshman.

“Jackson Ford, he’s been improving each week,” Lynn said. “He’s in the rotation, he just needs to keep on showing it in practice on a daily basis so that we can keep on entrusting to give him those reps on Saturday.”

As Penn State prepares for its Big Ten opener against Wisconsin, the Nittany Lions will face a quarterback capable of creating plays with his legs in Colton Joseph.

Campbell emphasized the importance of continuing to develop the pass rush as the season progresses, particularly against dynamic quarterbacks. But for Kemajou, the approach remains straightforward.

“Rushing together, making sure we’re closing the pocket down,” Kemajou said. “Make sure QB doesn’t have any place to go outside of just being sacked.”

title: No. 4 Penn State women’s hockey welcomes No. 2 Ohio State for season opener
author: Rafael Rivera | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State starts its season this Thursday in a marquee series against the No. 2 team in the nation, the Ohio State Buckeyes.

It’ll be a special series in Pegula Ice Arena, as the team will raise a banner on Thursday to honor the program's monumental first Frozen Four appearance from last season. To add to the festivities, the second game of the series on Friday will be a White Out.

Even with many new faces on the roster, the Nittany Lions still have the same goal: to build on their success from last season and win a National Championship.

Here's a look at how the blue and white fare against the Buckeyes.

Matchup history

In last season's series against Ohio State, the Nittany Lions lost both games in Columbus by a solid margin: 5-1 in the first and 4-1 in the second. The Buckeyes outshot Penn State 85 to 45 in the two games, seeming to dominate possession of the puck. Six of the seven players who scored against the Nittany Lions last season are returners.

Penn State will try to flip the script from a year ago and hold back the explosive Ohio State attack, which has plenty of returning experience. Penn State was missing a major key player in the matchup last year, though, as the team's top scoring threat Grace Outwater was out due to injury. The forward will get a chance at the scarlet and gray this season, however, as Outwater entered the AHA Preseason Player of the Year ahead of the season.

It’ll be a real test for this Penn State team to go up against a Buckeyes attack that has gotten more mature and is also playing with a chip on their shoulder after losing in the National Championship last year to Wisconsin 3-2.

2026 Buckeyes

Ohio State is led by senior forward Joy Dunne, who’s been a goal-scoring machine since entering college. Dunne has 80 career goals and leads all active NCAA players.

The O'Fallon, Missouri, native was nominated to the All-WCHA preseason team and is considered to be one of the top picks in the upcoming PWHL draft. The Buckeyes have two other All-WCHA preseason players in Jocelyn Amos and Mira Jungåker.

Amos, who was recently named co-captain, had a stellar season last year, finishing third on the team with 48 points and second with 22 goals. She was also the main anchor in Ohio State's faceoff group that won 539 faceoffs last year, the second most in the nation.

Penn State's backline will have to be cautious of the playmaking and scoring ability of Dunne and Amos if it hopes to walk out of the series with a tally in the win column.

Jungåker, the junior defenseman, is the new leader of the defensive unit after Ohio State lost several graduated stars. Last season, she tallied six goals and 19 assists, scoring 25 points in 29 games.

Penn State brings in lots of new faces after seven players were selected to the PWHL, losing Tessa Janeke and Maddy Christian, leaving lots of scoring production to be picked up.

Freshmen Lorelai Nelson, Sydney McIntosh, and Kylie Amelkovich are some names that may be important to the team's success this season.

Outwater returns as the team's top scoring threat after a season where she was crowned AHA scoring champion, scoring 31 points in league play and finishing the season with 40 total points.

Penn State returns more quality at forward with Abby Stonehouse, who scored 14 goals while adding 10 assists for 24 points last season. The junior forward has improved her numbers every and is someone who can make the jump to elite.

One thing that Penn State can take advantage of in this series is the youthfulness of Ohio State's blueline.

Emma Peschel and Sara Swiderski were both selected in the first round of the PWHL draft, leaving the unit without its top defensive pairing from last season.

Ohio State still has Jungåker and Jenna Raunio, a sophomore with Olympic and big game experience. However, behind their top skaters, the Buckeyes are relying on underclassmen like Leah Wicks and true freshmen to fill out their depth. Penn State can potentially look to score on the Buckeyes' blue line while their experience is still low.

Overall, this matchup has all the makings of a fun series in Happy Valley this week, as both teams have serious championship aspirations.

title: Penn State Homecoming through Collegian’s Archives
author: Teresa Phelan | Opinions Editor
description:
Penn State’s Homecoming remains one of the university's most valued traditions. From football to floats, students, alumni and community members come together to celebrate the beginning of the semester and what’s to come.

Follow alongside the Collegian’s archives as we outline over 100 years of homecoming.

1920

Penn State’s first “Alumni Home-coming” took over a year to plan and welcomed back alumni for fraternity meet-and-greets and a performance by the New York Symphony.

Students and alumni paraded through the streets to the stadium on Oct. 9, which kickstarted the traditions of floats and a featured football game.

1938

The Penn State Collegian reported that the Nittany Lions would face the Bucknell Bison in their 29th meeting of the universities. John Patrick, who had scored the deciding touchdowns in previous games against Bucknell, would miss the game with an injury sustained in a scrimmage. The game at New Beaver Field started at 2:30 pm, and the Bison would go on to win 14-0.

There were 1,500 alumni registered for the weekend, with a tour of the new Atherton Hall and Mary Beaver White Recreation Building at the forefront of the celebrations. Fraternity and business dinners took place in the Old Main Sandwich Shop during the day, with a nighttime Cider party concluding the weekend.

1948

To boost alumni attendance, a “Homecoming Special Train” traveled throughout Pennsylvania and the surrounding areas, picking up people and bringing them back to State College. Alumni living in New York, Philadelphia, Pittsburgh, Greensburg, Baltimore, Washington, Lancaster and York were able to buy a ticket that would take them from their home to Bellefonte.

The tickets included meals on board, Pullman reservations, use of a club car en route and on campus and tickets to the football game against Michigan State.

1972

For the first time in a decade, the homecoming committee didn’t elect a homecoming queen; instead, five “outstanding women” were honored. The Undergraduate Student Government Executive Council, Association of Women Students and the Interfraternity Council’s president representative heavily protested the elimination of the contest altogether.

Despite progress towards eliminating the contest, the University’s Union Board said that “general appearance” and “poise” were the main qualifications for an outstanding woman.

1983

In a jam-packed week, there were concerns about the goalposts at Beaver Stadium being taken down, regardless of whether or not the team beat West Virginia. Two weeks prior, the goalposts were carried away by students after a victory against Alabama, which cost the university over $4,000 to replace.

“WVU hasn’t beaten Penn State in 28 years. I don’t know if their fans would carry the post to Morgantown, but (tearing down of the goalposts) is definitely a possibility no matter who wins,” Dave Baker, sports information director, said. “West Virginia is a highly-ranked team, and there’s going to be a lot of excitement.”

Damage to the campus wasn’t only predicated on the football field; there were concerns about the Lion Shrine being defaced, which required immense cleaning and sandblasting. This process began to soften the corners of the sculpture and resulted in a wax substance being used to prevent paint from seeping into the cracks.

1996

Much to the confusion of students and alumni, homecoming took place two weeks earlier than it had occurred in the past. Homecoming took place on Oct. 12 against the Purdue Boilermakers.

Despite the changes, Greek life and the homecoming committee reported no immediate issues and everything went off without a hitch. Although homecoming dates are set years in advance, the home football schedule, ticket allotment, and television schedule are all factors considered, and athletics works with the Alumni Association to find a suitable date.

2006

Registration for homecoming was moved to a digital format due to potential confusion between the committee and independent organizations. Online registration allowed more accessibility for people than signing in and out of the “other paper book.” This was a year of change, as there were only two categories of registration: overall competitors and event competitors, eliminating the noncompeting organization category.

Homecoming also partnered with Centre Volunteers in Medicine, who covered cover charges for Homecoming Night Out and day of service events. The philanthropic partnership intended to get more community involvement, while maintaining organization.

2010

Heidi Kloster and Elias Warren became Penn State Homecoming’s first-ever emcees after videos of their auditions were shared with the student body and were voted the favorites. They hosted the pep rally and parade and served as the face of the week.

Warren, a University Park Undergraduate Association representative, and Kloster, a PSN co-host, used their theatre experience to elevate the week with their humor and performance qualities, giving students a “show.”

“I’m looking forward to the pep rally the most because it’s when the alumni come back, the band plays and the lion is there,” Kloster told the Collegian.

2020

Due to the COVID-19 pandemic, homecoming was moved to a virtual format. A pre-recorded special was broadcasted and uploaded to their social media platforms. Organizations’ pre-filmed videos were compiled and paired with videos from alumni and community members who weren’t able to be on campus.

Homecoming 2021 was a hybrid of in-person and online events, and strictly followed CDC, university and state guidelines regarding the virus.

title: 3 things I think, 3 things I know after Penn State’s nonconference slate
author: Lexie Linderman | Football Editor
description:
Penn State has officially concluded its nonconference slate, throughout which it showcased what kind of team it could be in the first year under Matt Campbell.

Across these last three weeks, the Nittany Lions have risen four spots in the AP Poll, faced some needed adversity and revealed what kind of playmakers it has.

But the nonconference matchups can only show so much about a team, and Big Ten play is going to be way different for this squad.

So here’s three things I think and three things I know after Penn State’s first three games of 2026.

I think the run game is going to be just fine

Taylor Mouser said it best after Week 2: “To say that I wasn’t thrilled with where the run game’s at would be an understatement.”

At that time, Penn State was averaging 3.9 yards per carry as a team. So it came out against Buffalo with a clear conviction to get the run game going, and that included spreading the ball around more to different running backs.

The result? 304 rushing yards and five rushing touchdowns.

As long as Mouser continues giving all four running backs meaningful carries throughout each game, the ground game is going to be just fine.

I know Rocco Becht can carry Penn State to wins

Rocco Becht has had the best start of his collegiate career with Penn State this season. He has 751 yards, nine touchdowns, zero interceptions and a 70.3% completion percentage, even with backup Alex Manske taking over in the third quarter of two games.

Becht’s 215 passer rating ranks fourth nationally, trailing only Georgia’ Gunner Stockton, Indiana’s Josh Hoover and Miami’s Darian Mensah, and his numbers through three games are just slightly better than they were in 2024 — his best season at Iowa State.

While Becht has had some blunders, such as running out of bounds behind the line of scrimmage multiple times rather than throwing the ball away or missing a few wide-open guys in the end zone, he’s otherwise been consistent through the air and has taken great care of the ball.

But arguably most importantly, Becht’s leadership capabilities are why he can put Penn State on his back when times get tough and carry them to a victory. He did just that when the Nittany Lions were struggling against Temple.

“The thing that I really appreciate it's like who responded,” Campbell said after defeating Temple. “It's the guys you expect, right? Rocco steps up, he makes big plays in big moments to kind of get you back into the football game.”

I think the edge rushers need to get more pressure

Penn State’s defensive end room was a bit of a question mark this offseason, and almost still is in a sense now that Max Granville is out for the year.

The Nittany Lions have just five sacks this season, three of which have come from the linebackers. Their edge rushers need to step up as Penn State begins conference play, especially with multiple dual-threat quarterbacks on the upcoming schedule.

Sophomore Yvan Kemajou has been the most consistent defensive end this season and had a big game against Buffalo with two tackles for loss and two quarterback hurries. The Nittany Lions need him to keep that up moving forward.

“I think at first it was kind of spotty,” D’Anton Lynn said Tuesday. “He'd make flash plays, and then you wouldn't feel him for a little bit. Then he'd make a play, and I think the more he's been in this system, the more consistent he's been.”

I know Benjamin Brahmer needs to be involved more

Benjamin Brahmer was Penn State’s leading receiver against Temple, putting the offense on his back when it needed him most with a 23-yard touchdown right before the half and another score later in the game.

But besides his five-catch, 79-yard performance in Philadelphia, Brahmer has been quiet in the passing game, with just one reception in each of the Nittany Lions’ other two games for 18 yards combined.

Brahmer is one of the best tight ends in the country and was a semifinalist for the John Mackey Award — given annually to the top tight end nationally — last year. He needs to be involved in the passing game more, especially if leading wide receiver Koby Howard is out multiple weeks.

“He's a very fluid athlete,” fellow tight end Andrew Rappleyea said last Wednesday. “He's a good playmaker, and I love being able to share the field with him.”

I think a healthy Brett Eskildsen will be a game-changer

Matt Campbell said Tuesday that wide receiver Brett Eskildsen has been “dinged up” the last two weeks, which is likely a reason why his production has dipped since having 48 yards and a touchdown against Marshall.

Whenever Eskildsen is back to full health, whether that’s this week or the next, he immediately becomes a dangerous threat to opposing defenses because of his speed. The Iowa State transfer is easily the fastest wide receiver Penn State has, and that helps open up the passing game even more.

“Every opportunity he's got, he's made some dynamic things happen,” Campbell said Tuesday.

I know the secondary is one of the best in the Big Ten

Through three games, Penn State’s secondary has allowed 270 passing yards, good for an average of just 90 per game. It only allowed 60 passing yards to Buffalo, albeit a quarterback starting his first-ever college game, but locked down wide receiver Chance Morrow, who had been incredibly productive in the Bulls’ first two matchups.

The Nittany Lions having an elite secondary is not necessarily unexpected, as the cornerback and safety rooms feature some of the most veteran talent on the entire roster with Jeremiah Cooper, Audavion Collins, Marcus Neal Jr. and Zion Tracy all having plenty of game experience under their belts.

But even the younger players in the secondary, most notably sophomore Daryus Dixson, have shined, and the unit was the highest-graded in the country by Pro Football Focus in Week 1 against Marshall.

Penn State currently ranks second in both total passing yards allowed and passing yards allowed per game, trailing only Kansas State in both categories.

title: Column | Women in sports still face significant hurdles. The AI video of Holly Rowe shows that.
author: Lexie Linderman | Football Editor
description:
It’s been one week since Arch Manning was asked whether he’d seen any viral edits or videos after Texas’ incredible comeback win over Ohio State. His response spurred some of the most discourse I’ve seen in recent months over women in sports media.

“I saw the AI edit of (Steve Sarkisian) slapping Holly Rowe … That’s a good one,” Manning said.

Manning and the room of journalists broke out in laughter.

Women have spent decades working to earn the respect of men in the sports industry, and this disrespect of Rowe, who was the subject of the Texas’ head coach slap in the AI video, only proves there are still ways to go.

Rowe is one of the most respected female sideline reporters out there. She’s been with ESPN since 1998 and has never stopped working, literally. She didn’t take time off when she was battling metastatic melanoma.

But even she is still subject to intense scrutiny. People online make jokes about her weight. And now a group of men were laughing about a video that wasn’t really even circulating until Manning brought it up.

The video came about after Sarkisian didn’t let Rowe ask any questions postgame and instead yelled “Texas Fight, Hookem” into the microphone and walked away.

Rowe walked off visibly frustrated. Texas officials told The Athletic there were technical issues on ESPN’s side, so Sarkisian was waiting for about a minute. Fellow ESPN sideline reporter Laura Rutledge had said previously that Sarkisian declined the halftime interview due to technical difficulties.

Manning and the journalists in the room received loads of criticism online for making light of the AI-generated video that was clearly disrespectful to Rowe. He wrote an apology on his Instagram story on Wednesday, saying “I know my words and actions were hurtful to a lot of people.”

Rowe reposted his apology, thanking Manning and disclosing the two had a conversation that will “remain private.”

But this is only one of many recent instances of disrespect toward women in sports, joining Sydney Sweeney’s ad for sports prediction market Novig in which she was fully naked, and Callaway’s ad where a woman is pushed to the ground after reaching to touch a man’s driver.

Both sparked intense controversy, but Sweeney’s ad was more indicative of how sports media and advertisements are painting women recently. For example, the NFL used influencers Alix and Ashtin Earle to advertise its game in Australia at the beginning of the season, where they posed as clueless football players who only care about their appearances.

Painting women this way in sports advertisements has been a recent phenomenon. The girl knows nothing about sports, so the guy helps them out. It’s almost like leagues and companies have taken steps backward, not forward, when it comes to integrating women into their marketing campaigns in a way that isn’t rooted in misogyny.

As for the Callaway advertisement, that showed clear disrespect to women both in golf and just in general. The ad has since been taken down, but the fact it was ever approved in the first place is shocking.

But the most shocking part of all of this disrespect toward women in sports is simply that it’s still happening.

At least Manning apologized, and Callaway took the video down. Sweeney doubled down, though, which is concerning considering she is somewhat of a role model to a number of young adults.

Just because there were apologies doesn’t erase the damage that was done. It doesn’t erase the discourse online. And it certainly doesn’t erase how women feel about these things.

As a woman working in sports, all of this upsets me. I hope it upsets you, too.

title: Penn State women’s soccer hosts Iowa during midweek, welcomes USC for weekend
author: Zach Schroder | The Daily Collegian
description:
Penn State returns home from College Park after a dominant offensive victory over the Maryland Terrapins. It will try to extend its win streak with a three-game homestand at Jeffery Field.

The Nittany Lions will first play the Iowa Hawkeyes in the White Out at 7 p.m. on Thursday. Then on Sunday, the USC Trojans travel to Happy Valley for the Military Appreciation and THON game at 1 p.m.

The blue and white are now in the thick of conference play, tied for second in points with six other teams. Here’s what to expect for Thursday and Sunday.

Iowa

The last time these two teams met was in September 2024, when Penn State lost 2-1, and the blue and white’s last win against the Hawkeyes came in March 2021.

Iowa clocks in at No. 43 in the NCAA RPI rankings and is still looking for its first conference win of the season.

Third-year forward Berit Parten is the team's points leader with four goals and five assists. The St. Paul, Minnesota, native also leads her team in minutes, shots and shots on goal. Parten is also tied for third in points in the conference with 13.

Another Hawkeye to look out for is fourth-year forward Reilly Heman, who leads the team in goals with five. The Springfield, Missouri, native is the second point leader and also tied for second in shots on goal.

On the other side of the pitch, the Nittany Lions will see Channahon, Illinois, native and first-year goalkeeper Braelynn Galt guarding the goalposts. Galt has 23 saves on the year and has only conceded five goals, which ranks in the lower end of Big Ten starters.

Before conference play, Iowa overpowered teams with a 23-5 point differential. The Hawkeyes are coming off two scoreless draws against Nebraska and Illinois at home, respectively. They were outshot by Nebraska but shot more than Illinois and held a slight edge in possession. Facing Penn State Iowa will look to earn a first conference victory of the year and get back on track from the start of the season.

USC

The second-to-last time the Nittany Lions faced the Trojans was when they traveled to sunny Los Angeles for the second round of the 2021 NCAA tournament. Regulation ended with the two squads tied 2-2, but the blue and white won the penalty shootout 5-3 to advance to the next round.

In 2024, the two had their first matchup as Big Ten opponents on the Golden Coast, as the Trojans defended home turf with a 2-1 win.

USC is another Big Ten team that has yet to get its first conference win. The Trojans have had a tough year, with three draws and only scoring nine total goals. Since entering conference play, they have been outscored 8-1.

Leading the charge for the Trojans is junior forward and defender Lily Biddulph. The Irvine, California, native leads the team with three goals. Sophomore midfielder Jaiden Rodriguez leads her team in shots with 20, with 10 on goal, but only one has found the back of the net.

Defending the net for USC is freshman keeper Josie Biehl, who is tied for first in goals allowed in the Big Ten with 14 conceded so far. The Carlsbad, California, native is also ranked seventh in the conference in saves with 29.

The Trojans are coming off their best conference performance, drawing 1-1 with Oregon; they outshot the Ducks 14-7 and possessed the ball 68% of the match. USC will face No. 8 Ohio State on Thursday before heading to Happy Valley. USC enters the game on a struggling year, just looking to get in the win column.

title: Wellness darties | How to bring wellness into your everyday life
author: Ally Sons | The Daily Collegian
description:
“Wellness darties” have been the talk of TikTok for the last couple of weeks. The trend started with a video posted by a student at the University of Florida, featuring a fraternity and sorority mixer where attendees did yoga and went for a run.

This trend was also seen at schools like The University of Alabama, which surprised people since it's ranked as the number one party school in the state. This may seem like a foreign concept to a lot of college students nowadays, but it seems to be taking Greek life and social media by storm.

If you’re not involved in Greek life, or if this isn’t the content of your mixers, there are still ways to integrate wellness into your everyday life here at Penn State.

Switch from coffee to matcha

The first step to reducing your caffeine intake is realizing you might love coffee a little too much. But switching from your usual latte or cold brew to a matcha in the mornings is an easy solution.

The usual latte clocks in at about 60-100 mg of caffeine, while matcha comes in at about 40 mg for a cup. Matcha seems to be all the rage recently, and the flavors are expanding and diversifying every day.

Luckily there are a large number of great matcha options right downtown. Vibe Coffee Co., located on Beaver Avenue, is currently featuring a “banana bread matcha” that seems to be a popular choice.

Start utilizing the salad places in town

From Roots to Mezeh to the salad bar at the HUB-Robeson Center, there are tons of great build-your-own salad bowl places right near campus.

These kinds of restaurants are a great way to meet your protein and vegetable goals in a really delicious way. They not only offer create-your-own bowls but also featured menu items that keep it easy on those busy days.

If you’re in the market for a protein packed lunch or dinner that is convenient and makes you feel good, look no further.

Sunday resets

Sunday resets are one of the best ways to start the week off on a good note. Come Sunday, you’re done with the excitement of the weekend, and you're preparing for the week ahead.

You could take this day to clean your apartment or dorm, do your laundry, meal prep, take an everything shower or, if you really want to incorporate wellness to the fullest, have a full spa day at home.

Regardless of what happened during the week, Sunday is your opportunity to start fresh and go into the new week feeling ready to take it on.

Phone-free mornings

Going phone free for any period of time nowadays is definitely one of those things that’s easier said than done. However, it can feel worth it to start your day off in a relaxing way free from Snapchat notifications, Canvas alerts and the risk of doom-scrolling.

Start by setting a calming alarm that wakes you up peacefully, then start your day before you check your phone.

Whether that means you have to set your phone on the other side of the room or lock your apps, it's worth it to start your day before you start your device.

Use the wellness services included in your tuition

Students can sometimes forget about all the options Penn State offers in terms of wellness opportunities right here on campus.

With the Campus Recreation center offering free classes for yoga, pilates and so much more, you and your friends can sign up for a fun daytime class to try something new. Also included in your student membership are things like the IM building's “Well-being Areas” and hydromassage chairs in the R&R Lounge.

You don’t have to be a Los Angeles wellness influencer to bring health and wellness into your life. You can do it right on campus as a Penn State student.

Hike Mount Nittany

If you're looking for a good place to really experience the outdoors in State College, planning a Mount Nittany hike with your friends is a great way to do so.

About a 10-minute drive from campus, Mount Nittany trailhead can be very accessible to students and State College residents. Featuring a variety of different trail lengths and difficulty levels, this hiking experience is attainable for a wide array of people.

It can be a great way to reconnect with nature on an ordinary day or a great opportunity if you feel you need to decompress after a night out.

title: QB Rocco Becht’s win-first mentality drives approach in final season at Penn State
author: Noah Aberegg | The Daily Collegian
description:
Through three weeks, Rocco Becht has proven to be one of the best quarterbacks in the nation.

On Saturday, Becht surpassed 10,000 career passing yards, a record held by only two other active quarterbacks. However, the milestone doesn’t mean much to him.

“Wins, that’s all I care about,” Becht said on Tuesday. “I’m just trying to go out there and do everything that I possibly can to go win the game.”

Becht entered the season as the winningest returning quarterback in college football and has continued to improve his play, throwing for 751 yards and nine touchdowns with 70.3% accuracy this season.

Despite his success through the air, he acknowledged the need to become more of a threat with his legs to win in the Big Ten. He tallied negative rushing yards through the nonconference slate, including multiple instances when he ran out of bounds behind the line of scrimmage.

“I consider myself a pocket passer, and if nothing is there, I’m able to move around and scramble and get yards for the team,” Becht said. “To win games, the quarterback’s gonna have to scramble and make some plays with his legs.”

While he hasn’t done much of that this season, he knows his responsibility with the biggest games of the season looming.

That slate begins this weekend, as Becht will make his Big Ten debut against Wisconsin. Despite the tougher opponent, he’s approaching this weekend the same.

“I’m going to prepare for it the same like I have the past four years and keep everything level-headed,” Becht said. “I’m going into another week playing another good team and that’s my thought in my mind going into this week and that’s going to be my headspace going into the next eight weeks.”

Linebacker Kooper Ebel said Tuesday the Big Ten is more of an “NFL style of play.” Fortunately for Becht, he has former Iowa State quarterback Brock Purdy to lean on, who now plays for the San Francisco 49ers.

Purdy was one of the reasons that Becht went to play for Campbell, knowing his offense was tailored to someone with a similar build and playstyle of Becht. Purdy has also been a mentor and resource to Becht throughout his journey.

“He’s always a person I can go out and reach out to if I have any information that I need or any knowledge that I want and need for a big game, things like that,” Becht said. “He’s definitely a resource that I have that I’m able to use that I’m super grateful for.”

As Becht plays through his final season of collegiate eligibility, he’s been pleased as various parts of Penn State’s offense have come together.

However, he knows there’s still room to grow and make improvements as he makes the most of his last year.

“Just on my end, continuing to be better with decisions, with my detail and precision on all the plays,” Becht said postgame on Saturday. “I got to continue to be better on my part for the offense, and we’re going to go out of this week and be prepared for conference games.”

title: Agostino Abbatiello seeks ‘speedy trial,’ defense requests jury selection begin in early December
author: Grace Levy | News Editor
description:
Agostino S. Abbatiello, one of the alleged ringleaders in the fraternity-led cocaine-trafficking ring at Penn State has requested a “speedy trial,” according to a court filing from Sept. 16.

Abbatiello, 24, of Westbury, New York, was charged with distributing cocaine through his involvement in the off-campus Sigma Chi fraternity at Penn State, according to authorities. He was charged on Aug. 17, along with 13 other defendants.

Abbatiello’s preliminary hearing occurred on Sept. 2, where he was represented by attorney Philip M. Masorti.

In the new filing, Masorti requested for Abbatiello's case to proceed to trial in December 2026. Jury selection for the trial is slated to occur on Dec. 7, 2026.

Masorti said that the charges have “imposed substantial stress and hardship” on Abbatiello and his family, aggravated by what he described as “extenstive, and at times, excessive media attention.”

“Time is of the essence,” Masorti said. “The Defendant intends to fully exercise and insist upon his constitutional right to a prompt and speedy trial.”

Additionally, Masorti argued that the Commonwealth has had “substantial opportunity” to gather and analyze evidence, and requested the discovery period for evidence begin now.

The filing states the Commonwealth has had over two years to prepare its case, with co-defendant Thomas M. Robinson first being charged in Dec. 2024.

Masorti said he preemptively objects to any request to delay or continue the trial from prosecutors.

At the Sept. 2 hearing, Masorti requested a bail modification, and Abbatiello was granted $250,000 secured bail.

Abbatiello posted bail on Sept. 22, according to court documents.

title: Clearfield County board of commissioners votes to extend Moshannon ICE contract
author: Fabiola González-Cruz | The Daily Collegian
description:
The Clearfield County Board of Commissioners voted 2-1 on Tuesday to extend its contract involving the Moshannon Valley Processing Center, one of the largest immigration detention facilities in the Northeast, for another six months, according to Spotlight PA.

Under the agreement, which began in September 2021, Clearfield County acts as an intermediary between the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and GEO Group, the private company that owns and operates the facility. The county receives $200,000 annually through the arrangement.

Commissioners Tim Winters and John Sobel voted in favor of the extension, while Commissioner Dave Glass voted against it.

The facility has faced allegations concerning conditions for detainees. According to previous reporting by Spotlight PA, detainees and advocates have alleged inadequate medical and dental care, rotten or insect-infested food, and lack of access to toilet paper or hand soap inside Moshannon.

GEO Group has disputed allegations of inadequate conditions and has said its operations are monitored by ICE and comply with federal detention standards.

The contract extension comes amid increased scrutiny of Moshannon’s operations. Seven Democrats of Pennsylvania’s congressional delegation allegedly sought financial records and communications from ICE, GEO Group and Clearfield County regarding the facility and federal taxpayer dollars.

The facility’s future after the six-month extension remains uncertain. ICE has sought proposals for detention services that identify Moshannon as a historical location, while federal officials have also considered different arrangements for detention facilities.
